### [Knowledge-Based System for Forecasting Snow Avalanches of Chowkibal-Tangdhar Axis (J&K)](https://doi.org/10.14429/dsj.49.3853)
Naresh et al. (1999), *Defence Science Journal*. 12 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops a rule-based expert system to forecast direct-action snow avalanches on the Chowkibal-Tangdhar axis in Jammu and Kashmir.
- **Architecture:** Expert system (rule-based) in CLIPS with 358 rules, including 173 decision rules, on 28 snow-meteorological variables.
- **Data:** 1154 samples of snow-meteorological and snow-profile data; test on 63 avalanche-day and 54 non-avalanche-day samples.
- **Main result:** Predicts avalanche days with 76% efficiency; 28.2% of the 117 test samples are misclassified.
- **Open work:** Extending to other avalanche types and sites and refining rules follow naturally.
- **Issues:** Single region, small test set and hand-crafted rules; considerable misclassification rate.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [An integrated decision method for prediction of tropical cyclone movement by using genetic algorithm](https://doi.org/10.1360/03yd0144)
Yang et al. (2005), *Science in China Series D: Earth Sciences*. 12 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts tropical cyclone movement by combining several forecast methods.
- **Architecture:** Integrated decision method that uses a genetic algorithm to optimize the combination of forecast methods.
- **Data:** Historical tropical cyclone track data in the western North Pacific; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** The integrated method is reported to reduce track forecast errors relative to individual methods; numbers are not reported here.
- **Open work:** Incorporating NWP guidance and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Statistical combination limited by member methods and sample size.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Deep Learning Atmospheric Models Reliably Simulate Out‐of‐Sample Land Heat and Cold Wave Frequencies](https://doi.org/10.1029/2025gl117990)
Meng et al. (2025), *Geophysical Research Letters*. 11 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether deep learning GCMs reproduce extreme heat and cold wave frequencies outside their training period.
- **Architecture:** Evaluation of the hybrid NeuralGCM and the purely data-driven DLESyM deep learning models against the conventional HiRAM high-resolution model.
- **Data:** All models forced with observed SST and sea ice over 1900–2020, focusing on out-of-sample 1900–1960.
- **Main result:** Both DL models reproduce the frequency and spatial patterns of land heatwaves and coldwaves with skill comparable to HiRAM; all perform poorly over parts of North Asia and North America in 1940–1960.
- **Open work:** Improve temperature persistence in data-driven models and test generalization to future warming.
- **Issues:** DLESyM overestimates event frequencies due to excessive temperature autocorrelation; early-century observations are uncertain; out-of-sample period is cooler, not warmer.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Evaluating Global Machine Learning Models for Tropical Cyclone Dynamics and Thermodynamics](https://doi.org/10.1029/2025jh000594)
Sahu et al. (2025), *Journal of Geophysical Research: Machine Learning and Computation*. 11 citations.

- **Main goal:** Comprehensively evaluates machine learning weather models for tropical cyclone track, intensity and physical structure before they replace NWP.
- **Architecture:** Evaluation of GraphCast (graph neural network), Pangu-Weather, Aurora and FourCastNet (transformer and neural operator models) against three NWP models and observations.
- **Data:** Tropical cyclones across all tropical ocean basins; verification against observations (best track) and NWP forecasts.
- **Main result:** All MLWP models have mean track errors below 200 km at 96 h but underestimate maximum winds; they capture vorticity advection, low-level convergence and warm cores with weaker magnitude; Aurora performs best.
- **Open work:** Reduce intensity bias by addressing training data biases and the double penalty effect, e.g. through higher resolution or probabilistic training.
- **Issues:** Intensity low bias linked to reanalysis training data and double penalization; weaker structure magnitudes than observed.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A fuzzy expert system to assist in the prediction of hazardous wind conditions within the Mediterranean basin](https://doi.org/10.1017/s1350482798001005)
Kuciauskas et al. (1998), *Meteorological Applications*. 11 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assists forecasters in predicting hazardous wind conditions in the Mediterranean basin, such as regional mistral and bora events.
- **Architecture:** Fuzzy expert system (fuzzy logic, rule-based) built from forecaster knowledge.
- **Data:** Numerical weather prediction output and observations for the Mediterranean; details not reported.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the record.
- **Open work:** Operational evaluation and extension to more wind regimes follow naturally.
- **Issues:** No abstract available; knowledge elicitation is laborious and rules are regime-specific.

### [Severe storm cell classification using support vector machines and radial basis function approaches](https://doi.org/10.1109/ccece.2001.933663)
Ramirez et al. (2001), *Canadian Conference on Electrical and Computer Engineering 2001. Conference Proceedings (Cat. No.01TH8555)*. 11 citations.

- **Main goal:** Classifies severe storm cells from radar-derived features.
- **Architecture:** Support vector machines compared with radial basis function networks.
- **Data:** Radar-derived storm cell attributes; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** Support vector machines are reported to classify severe cells well relative to RBF networks; numbers are not reported here.
- **Open work:** More data and feature selection.
- **Issues:** Small, imbalanced datasets.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Constructing extreme heatwave storylines with differentiable climate models](https://doi.org/10.5194/wcd-7-393-2026)
Whittaker et al. (2025), *Weather and Climate Dynamics*. 10 citations.

- **Main goal:** Constructs plausible worst-case heatwave storylines to probe the upper bounds of extreme events for climate risk assessment at low cost.
- **Architecture:** Gradient-based optimization of initial conditions through the differentiable hybrid climate model NeuralGCM (dynamical core plus neural network physics).
- **Data:** Case study of the 2021 Pacific Northwest heatwave; compared with a 75-member ensemble. Initial-condition source not detailed in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Optimized trajectories produce heatwave intensity up to 3.7 °C above the most extreme of 75 ensemble members, with intensified blocking and amplified Rossby waves.
- **Open work:** Applying the method to other extremes and warmer climates, and quantifying the plausibility and likelihood of optimized storylines.
- **Issues:** Single event; physical plausibility depends on NeuralGCM fidelity at extremes; optimized initial conditions may be unrealistic and the likelihood of storylines is not quantified.
- *Basis: abstract*

### Applications of Classification Tree Methodology to Avalanche Data Management and Forecasting
Davis et al. (1992), *Venue not recorded*. 10 citations.

- **Main goal:** Applies classification tree methods to manage avalanche data and to forecast avalanche activity from weather and snowpack observations.
- **Architecture:** Classification tree methodology (CART-style decision tree).
- **Data:** Historical avalanche occurrence records with meteorological and snowpack observations from a ski area; site and period are not reported in the available information.
- **Main result:** Classification trees provide interpretable rules that discriminate avalanche from non-avalanche days; skill numbers are not reported in the available information.
- **Open work:** Testing on additional sites and seasons, and combining trees with other statistical forecasting methods, follow naturally.
- **Issues:** Avalanche events are rare and site-specific, so trees may overfit and transfer poorly across regions.
- *Basis: assessment*

### Condensed and Updated Version of the Systematic Approach Meteorological Knowledge Base Western North Pacific
Carr et al. (1997), *Venue not recorded*. 9 citations.

- **Main goal:** Condenses and updates the meteorological knowledge base of the Systematic Approach for tropical cyclone track forecasting in the western North Pacific, to support forecasters in judging numerical track guidance.
- **Architecture:** Knowledge base of conceptual synoptic patterns, environmental structures and transitional mechanisms for tropical cyclone motion, used in an expert-system-like forecaster aid; not a machine-learning model.
- **Data:** Western North Pacific tropical cyclone cases and numerical model track guidance used to define and refine the knowledge base.
- **Main result:** Provides a condensed, updated set of synoptic pattern and region conceptual models intended to be easier to apply in operational track forecasting.
- **Open work:** Testing the condensed knowledge base in operational forecasting and extending it to other basins.
- **Issues:** Relies on subjective forecaster pattern recognition; skill gains depend on consistent application; quantitative verification not reported in the available metadata.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### Analysis of Weather and Avalanche Records from Alta, Utah and Mammoth Mountain, California Using Classification Trees
Davis et al. (1996), *Venue not recorded*. 8 citations.

- **Main goal:** Analyzes weather and avalanche records to identify conditions associated with avalanche activity for forecasting.
- **Architecture:** Classification trees (decision tree) relating weather and snowpack variables to avalanche occurrence.
- **Data:** Long-term weather and avalanche records from Alta, Utah and Mammoth Mountain, California.
- **Main result:** Classification trees identify key weather variables and thresholds associated with avalanche days; accuracy figures not reported in the available metadata.
- **Open work:** Using the trees in operational avalanche forecasting and adding snowpack structure information.
- **Issues:** Avalanche records are incomplete and observer dependent; site-specific trees may not transfer; class imbalance of avalanche days.

### [Systematic and Integrated Approach to Tropical Cyclone Track Forecasting. Part 2: Climatology, Reproducibility, and Refinement of Meteorological Knowledge Base.](https://doi.org/10.21236/ada301936)
Carr et al. (1995), *Venue not recorded*. 7 citations.

- **Main goal:** Refines the Systematic and Integrated Approach to tropical cyclone track forecasting by documenting climatology, reproducibility and an updated meteorological knowledge base.
- **Architecture:** Meteorological knowledge base of synoptic patterns, regions and transitional mechanisms used as an expert-system-like forecaster aid; not a machine-learning model.
- **Data:** Western North Pacific tropical cyclone cases and associated analyses used to build the climatology and test reproducibility.
- **Main result:** Shows the knowledge base pattern and region classifications can be applied reproducibly and provides their climatology.
- **Open work:** Linking the knowledge base to identification of numerical model track errors and operational testing.
- **Issues:** Relies on subjective classification by forecasters; focused on one basin; quantitative skill improvements not reported here.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Harnessing AI data-driven global weather models for climate attribution: An analysis of the 2017 Oroville Dam extreme atmospheric river](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.11605)
Baño-Medina et al. (2024), *arXiv*. 6 citations.

- **Main goal:** Explores AI weather models for fast storyline-based climate attribution, using the February 2017 Oroville Dam atmospheric river as a case.
- **Architecture:** Pretrained AI global weather models (GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, FourCastNet, SFNO) run with initial conditions perturbed by climate change signals; compared to a dynamical model.
- **Data:** Initial conditions perturbed with pre-industrial and late-21st-century temperature change signals; dynamical model simulations as pseudo-reality; AI ensembles over 500 members.
- **Main result:** AI models project a 5–6% increase in integrated water vapor over Oroville versus pre-industrial, consistent with the dynamical model, but generally weaker attribution signals, especially for late-21st-century.
- **Open work:** Use explainable AI to build confidence in physical responses and enable real-time attribution.
- **Issues:** Reduced extrapolation skill to out-of-distribution climates; models differ in geopotential-moisture-temperature dependencies; single event studied.
- *Basis: abstract*

### Avalanche Forecast: Experience Using Nearest Neighbors
Buser et al. (1984), *Venue not recorded*. 6 citations.

- **Main goal:** Supports regional avalanche danger forecasting by finding past days with weather and snow conditions similar to the current day.
- **Architecture:** K-nearest neighbour (nearest neighbours) analogue method that retrieves the most similar past days and reports their observed avalanche activity.
- **Data:** Historical daily weather, snowpack and avalanche occurrence records from Swiss Alpine observation stations; period not reported in the available record.
- **Main result:** Reports operational experience showing the nearest-neighbour method is a useful aid to avalanche forecasters; skill scores not reported in the available record.
- **Open work:** Better weighting of input variables and combination with snowpack stability information.
- **Issues:** Analogue method limited by the length and quality of the historical record; rare large avalanche situations have few neighbours.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Detection of bounded weak echo regions in meteorological radar images](https://doi.org/10.1109/icpr.1996.547297)
Lakshmanan et al. (1996), *Proceedings of 13th International Conference on Pattern Recognition*. 5 citations.

- **Main goal:** Detects bounded weak echo regions in weather radar images, a signature of strong updrafts in severe storms.
- **Architecture:** Image analysis and pattern recognition algorithm for detecting bounded weak echo regions in volumetric radar reflectivity; not described as a neural network.
- **Data:** Weather radar reflectivity volumes; radar network and dataset size not reported in the available record.
- **Main result:** Demonstrates automated detection of bounded weak echo regions in radar images; detection skill not reported in the available record.
- **Open work:** Validation over more storms and integration into severe weather warning algorithms.
- **Issues:** Sensitive to radar sampling geometry and thresholds; limited case evaluation.

### [Shootout-89: A Comparative Evaluation of Knowledge-based Systems that Forecast Severe Weather](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0477(1991)072<1339:saceok>2.0.co;2)
Moninger et al. (1991), *Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society*. 5 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates AI-based systems that forecast severe convective storms to compare their skill under the same conditions.
- **Architecture:** Benchmark evaluation of six systems: three expert systems, a linear model augmented by a small expert system, an analogue-based system, and a judgment analysis system.
- **Data:** Shootout-89 experiment, summer 1989, northeastern Colorado; 2–9 h probabilistic forecasts verified against ground-truth from a network of observers.
- **Main result:** Forecasts are verified daily for four regions in three categories; the abstract excerpt ends before quantitative results.
- **Open work:** Larger evaluations and combining the strengths of different knowledge-based approaches.
- **Issues:** One season and region; limited number of severe events; verification relies on observer reports.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [FuXi-TC: a generative framework integrating deep learning and physics-based models for improved tropical cyclone forecasts](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-026-01501-w)
Guo et al. (2025), *npj Climate and Atmospheric Science*. 4 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improve tropical cyclone intensity and precipitation forecasts, which AI weather models underestimate because of reanalysis biases, while keeping their track skill.
- **Architecture:** Diffusion model (FuXi-TC) conditioned on large-scale FuXi forecasts to generatively downscale fine-grained wind and precipitation fields, learning intensity from NWP simulations.
- **Data:** FuXi global forecasts as conditioning; NWP simulations as high-resolution targets; evaluation on 2024 Western North Pacific TCs and zero-shot on North Atlantic hurricanes.
- **Main result:** Matches ECMWF deterministic TC intensity skill with better precipitation forecasts at much lower cost, generalizes zero-shot to the North Atlantic, and yields well-dispersed ensembles with FuXi ensemble input.
- **Open work:** Longer evaluation periods, other basins and coupling with ensemble systems operationally.
- **Issues:** Evaluation covers a single season; intensity skill is bounded by the NWP simulations used as targets; numbers not given in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Global Forecasting of Tropical Cyclone Intensity Using Neural Weather Models](https://doi.org/10.1175/aies-d-25-0073.1)
Gomez et al. (2025), *Artificial Intelligence for the Earth Systems*. 4 citations.

- **Main goal:** Produce accurate global tropical cyclone intensity forecasts from neural weather models, whose 0.25° outputs smooth out TC extremes.
- **Architecture:** Hierarchy of post-processing models, from linear regression and MLP to convolutional networks with spatial masking, applied to neural weather model outputs; tracking-independent.
- **Data:** Pangu-Weather and FourCastNet v2 forecasts as inputs; observational best estimates of maximum wind and minimum sea-level pressure (best-track data) as targets.
- **Main result:** Accurate and reliable TC intensity forecasts up to five days ahead; even linear models extract information beyond initial conditions, and convolutional models show no clear advantage over MLPs.
- **Open work:** Extending to longer lead times, other neural weather models and operational deployment.
- **Issues:** Quantitative skill versus operational NWP is not stated in the abstract; inherits track and structure errors from the underlying neural weather models.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [On the Predictive Skill of Artificial Intelligence-based Weather Models for Extreme Events using Uncertainty Quantification](https://doi.org/10.1175/aies-d-25-0113.1)
Almeida et al. (2025), *Artificial Intelligence for the Earth Systems*. 3 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assess how deterministic AI weather models respond to initial-condition perturbations and how well the resulting ensembles forecast extreme events.
- **Architecture:** Ensembles from deterministic AI models FuXi, GraphCast and SFNO (spherical Fourier neural operator) generated with Gaussian, Perlin noise, Hemispheric Centered Bred Vectors and Huge Ensembles perturbations.
- **Data:** 50-member ensembles for the August 2022 Pakistan floods and China heatwave plus a global threshold-based evaluation, verified against ERA5 and compared with IFS ENS and AIFS ENS.
- **Main result:** Simple Gaussian and Perlin perturbations give spread and skill similar to flow-based methods; the gap to NWP ensembles and native probabilistic models narrows but remains. Model choice dominates; temperature extremes are captured better than precipitation.
- **Open work:** Improving perturbation strategies and comparing with natively probabilistic AI models for early-warning systems.
- **Issues:** Case studies limited to two events; verification against ERA5 which underrepresents extremes.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Global performance benchmarking of artificial intelligence models in atmospheric river forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-025-02823-y)
Zhang et al. (2025), *Communications Earth & Environment*. 3 citations.

- **Main goal:** Benchmark AI weather models for atmospheric river forecasting globally and regionally to guide their use and development.
- **Architecture:** Benchmark evaluation of five AI weather models including FuXi and hybrid NeuralGCM; not a new ML model.
- **Data:** Forecasts from five AI models verified against reanalysis (likely ERA5); case studies on North and South American coasts.
- **Main result:** FuXi performs best globally at 10-day lead for meteorological fields and AR metrics; NeuralGCM better predicts AR intensity and shape regionally. Landfall location beyond one week remains difficult.
- **Open work:** Refining AI models for region-specific AR forecasts and landfall prediction.
- **Issues:** Limited to deterministic forecasts and a few case studies; the other three models are not named in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Quantifying Very Extreme Precipitation and Temperature Using Huge Ensembles Generated by Machine Learning-based Climate Model Emulators](https://doi.org/10.1175/bams-d-25-0178.1)
Paciorek et al. (2025), *Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society*. 2 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assess statistically whether huge ML emulator ensembles can estimate very extreme precipitation and temperature quantiles, e.g. for Probable Maximum Precipitation.
- **Architecture:** Extreme value statistical analysis (threshold-exceedance methods) applied to a huge ensemble from the ACE2 ML climate emulator; not a new ML model.
- **Data:** 10,560-year ACE2 ensemble trained on ERA5, over the contiguous United States.
- **Main result:** Very extreme quantiles can be estimated practically with threshold-exceedance methods at high thresholds; results are robust across seasons and storm types, and statistical uncertainty is well constrained. The emulator produces extremes beyond the ERA5 range.
- **Open work:** Determining whether emulators are physically fit for quantifying extreme climatology, and applying the methods to improved emulators.
- **Issues:** Emulator fidelity for extremes is not established; coarse ACE2 resolution limits local precipitation extremes.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Severe weather forecasts from artificial intelligence weather prediction models](https://doi.org/10.1175/aies-d-25-0065.1)
White et al. (2026), *Artificial Intelligence for the Earth Systems*. 2 citations.

- **Main goal:** Generate severe weather guidance at 1–8 day leads, mimicking SPC convective outlooks, from AI weather prediction model environments.
- **Architecture:** Random forest models using environments from PanguWeather, FourCastNet v2-small and GraphCast, including median-combined inputs and RF ensembles.
- **Data:** Severe weather reports as targets; AIWP model forecasts as inputs; evaluation over 2024 against GEFS Machine Learning Probabilities guidance.
- **Main result:** Skillful individual hazard forecasts out to day 7, though operational GEFS ML guidance is often better at some leads; median-combined inputs and ensembles improve skill, with Pangu-based RF competitive.
- **Open work:** Exploiting ensembles of AIWP-based guidance and longer evaluation periods.
- **Issues:** Evaluated on one year; AIWP smoothing of convective environments may limit skill.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Evaluating machine learning and numerical models for wintertime atmospheric blocking prediction](https://doi.org/10.1175/aies-d-25-0067.1)
Huang et al. (2026), *Artificial Intelligence for the Earth Systems*. 1 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates for the first time how well machine learning weather prediction models forecast Northern Hemisphere winter atmospheric blocking, a driver of weather extremes.
- **Architecture:** Benchmark evaluation of four ML weather models (Pangu-Weather transformer, FuXi transformer, GraphCast graph neural network, NeuralGCM hybrid physics–ML) against ECMWF HRES.
- **Data:** Winter forecasts 2018–2022 over the Northern Hemisphere, verified against ERA5 reanalysis.
- **Main result:** FuXi has lowest Z500 RMSE but underestimates blocking frequency, especially in the Pacific; NeuralGCM has the best blocking skill (73.68% at day 5, 39.59% at day 9); HRES remains competitive in the Pacific; skill degrades rapidly beyond day 5.
- **Open work:** Incorporating key boundary conditions and improving interpretability of ML models for blocking prediction.
- **Issues:** Deterministic forecasts only; limited five-winter sample; verification against ERA5 which some ML models were trained on.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Atmospheric Rivers in Machine Learning Weather Models](https://doi.org/10.1175/waf-d-25-0142.1)
Swenson et al. (2026), *Weather and Forecasting*. 1 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses how machine learning weather prediction models represent atmospheric rivers, filamentary high-impact features that may be smoothed by ML loss functions.
- **Architecture:** Evaluation study comparing GraphCast (graph neural network) and Pangu-Weather (transformer) with operational NWP models GFS and IFS, using grid-point, object-based and storm-relative composite verification.
- **Data:** Wintertime North Pacific atmospheric river forecasts at 1–10 day leads, verified against reanalysis.
- **Main result:** ML models represent ARs well by aggregate metrics but ARs are slightly too weak and too small relative to reanalysis and NWP, with systematic differences in dynamic and thermodynamic biases within strong ARs.
- **Open work:** Using phenomenon-specific diagnostics to guide forecaster interpretation and improvements to both MLWP and NWP models.
- **Issues:** Only two deterministic ML models and one region and season; reanalysis used for verification may be close to ML training targets.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Evaluation of AI-based tropical cyclone forecasts in the western North Pacific: Insights from the 2024 Typhoon Committee ET-AITC multi model dataset](https://doi.org/10.1175/aies-d-25-0097.1)
Lee et al. (2026), *Artificial Intelligence for the Earth Systems*. 0 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates AI-based tropical cyclone track and intensity forecasts for the 2024 western North Pacific season from models shared through the Typhoon Committee ET-AITC.
- **Architecture:** Verification study of 19 forecast configurations from AI global weather forecasting models with vortex-tracking algorithms, assessed by model and initial conditions.
- **Data:** 2024 western North Pacific typhoon forecasts verified against RSMC Tokyo best-track data; compared with NWP models and official forecasts.
- **Main result:** Top 25% of AI-TC forecasts have track errors comparable to or smaller than NWP and official forecasts, beating NWP mean position errors in about 71% of cases; intensity shows a substantial low bias, with about 76% worse than NWP.
- **Open work:** Bias correction of intensity, further model development and broader data sharing for operational use.
- **Issues:** Single season; AI models underestimate intensity throughout the forecast; configurations differ in initial conditions and trackers, complicating attribution.
- *Basis: abstract*

<a id="xai"></a>
## Explainability & causality

### [Discovering governing equations from data by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamical systems](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1517384113)
Brunton et al. (2015), *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*. 5,674 citations.

- **Main goal:** Discovers governing equations of dynamical systems directly from measurement data, producing parsimonious, interpretable models.
- **Architecture:** SINDy: sparse regression (sequentially thresholded least squares) over a library of candidate nonlinear functions to select the few active terms in the dynamics. Not deep learning.
- **Data:** Simulated data from canonical systems: linear and nonlinear oscillators, the chaotic Lorenz system, and vortex shedding behind a cylinder (via a reduced POD basis).
- **Main result:** Recovers correct equations from noisy data, including the Lorenz system and the mean-field model of vortex shedding; extends to parameterized, time-varying and forced systems.
- **Open work:** Scaling to high-dimensional systems, choosing good coordinates and function libraries, and robustness to heavy noise.
- **Issues:** Relies on the dynamics being sparse in the chosen library; sensitive to noise in derivative estimation; demonstrated mostly on low-dimensional systems.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Detecting and quantifying causal associations in large nonlinear time series datasets](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aau4996)
Runge et al. (2017), *Science Advances*. 1,207 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates causal networks from large, high-dimensional, nonlinear time series where standard methods lose power or yield false positives.
- **Architecture:** PCMCI: a causal discovery algorithm combining PC-style condition selection with momentary conditional independence tests, using linear (partial correlation) or nonlinear tests. Not deep learning.
- **Data:** Climate time series with known mechanisms, human heart data, and large synthetic datasets mimicking real data properties.
- **Main result:** PCMCI outperforms state-of-the-art methods in detection power while controlling false positives.
- **Open work:** Handling contemporaneous links, hidden confounders and nonstationarity in Earth-system data.
- **Issues:** Assumes causal sufficiency and stationarity; results depend on the chosen variables and test.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Inferring causation from time series in Earth system sciences](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-019-10105-3)
Runge et al. (2019), *Nature Communications*. 1,087 citations.

- **Main goal:** Promote and organize data-driven causal inference beyond correlation analysis for Earth system science.
- **Architecture:** Perspective reviewing causal inference frameworks (Granger causality, nonlinear state-space methods, causal network learning such as PCMCI, etc.) and launching the causeme.net benchmark platform.
- **Data:** Illustrative Earth system examples and synthetic benchmark datasets on causeme.net.
- **Main result:** Identifies generic application cases and methodological challenges (e.g. nonlinearity, time delays, unobserved confounders, nonstationarity) and initiates a community benchmark.
- **Open work:** Methods robust to the identified challenges and broader benchmarking on realistic data.
- **Issues:** Perspective, not a single method evaluation; causal conclusions depend on assumptions that are often hard to verify in observational data.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Learning partial differential equations via data discovery and sparse optimization](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.2016.0446)
Schaeffer (2017), *Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences*. 547 citations.

- **Main goal:** Discovers the governing partial differential equation of a system directly from spatiotemporal data, aiming for interpretable models rather than black-box predictors.
- **Architecture:** Non-neural method: sparse regression over a dictionary of candidate derivative and nonlinear terms, solved with L1-type sparse optimization to select the few active terms.
- **Data:** Synthetic data generated from known canonical PDEs; exact test cases and noise levels are not given in the available metadata.
- **Main result:** Recovers the correct terms and coefficients of the generating PDEs from data in the tested cases.
- **Open work:** Robustness to strong noise, sparse or irregular observations, and extension to real geophysical data remain open.
- **Issues:** Requires the true terms to be in the candidate library and accurate numerical derivatives; demonstrated on idealized synthetic systems only.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Making the Black Box More Transparent: Understanding the Physical Implications of Machine Learning](https://doi.org/10.1175/bams-d-18-0195.1)
McGovern et al. (2019), *Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society*. 397 citations.

- **Main goal:** Make ML models in meteorology interpretable so forecasters and scientists can trust and learn from them.
- **Architecture:** Synthesis of model interpretation and visualization methods: permutation importance, forward/backward selection, saliency maps, class-activation maps, backward optimization and novelty detection.
- **Data:** Applied to tornado, hail, winter precipitation type and convective storm mode prediction datasets at several scales.
- **Main result:** Demonstrates that these techniques reveal physically meaningful relationships learned by traditional ML and deep learning models; serves as a toolbox.
- **Open work:** Quantitative evaluation of interpretation methods and their reliability.
- **Issues:** Interpretation methods can disagree and be misleading with correlated predictors; mostly qualitative demonstrations.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Physically Interpretable Neural Networks for the Geosciences: Applications to Earth System Variability](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019ms002002)
Toms et al. (2019), *Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems*. 278 citations.

- **Main goal:** Use neural network interpretation as a primary scientific tool to discover meaningful relationships in geoscience data.
- **Architecture:** Neural networks interpreted with backward optimization and layerwise relevance propagation (LRP), projecting decisions back to input space.
- **Data:** Climate fields such as SST anomalies for ENSO and other modes of variability (observational and model data).
- **Main result:** The interpretation methods reliably recover physically known climate patterns, suggesting they can support discovery.
- **Open work:** Combining interpretable networks with new scientific hypotheses.
- **Issues:** Demonstrations on known patterns; relevance maps depend on method choice and need careful validation.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Data‐Driven Equation Discovery of Ocean Mesoscale Closures](https://doi.org/10.1029/2020gl088376)
Zanna et al. (2020), *Geophysical Research Letters*. 257 citations.

- **Main goal:** Derive computationally efficient and interpretable parameterizations of ocean mesoscale eddies for coarse-resolution climate models.
- **Architecture:** Relevance vector machines (sparse Bayesian regression) for closed-form equation discovery with embedded conservation, compared with CNNs predicting subgrid eddy momentum forcing.
- **Data:** High-resolution idealized ocean model simulations, coarse-grained to provide subgrid forcing targets.
- **Main result:** All parameterizations improve coarse-resolution statistics in an idealized ocean model; the CNN is more stable and more skilful, while the RVM yields interpretable closed-form equations.
- **Open work:** Extending physics-aware interpretable closures to realistic ocean models and testing across regimes.
- **Issues:** Idealized configuration; RVM scheme less stable online; generalization to other resolutions and global ocean untested.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A non-linear Granger-causality framework to investigate climate–vegetation dynamics](https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-10-1945-2017)
Papagiannopoulou et al. (2016), *Geoscientific Model Development*. 157 citations.

- **Main goal:** Detects non-linear climate influences on vegetation dynamics that linear Granger-causality analyses miss.
- **Architecture:** Non-linear Granger-causality framework with time series decomposition, feature construction and random forest predictive models.
- **Data:** Global satellite-based climate data records of climatic and vegetation variables from various databases.
- **Main result:** The framework reveals non-linear climate-vegetation patterns much less visible to traditional linear Granger causality.
- **Open work:** Applying the framework to quantify drivers globally and benchmark Earth system models is a natural next step.
- **Issues:** Granger causality is predictive, not true causality; results depend on satellite record quality and confounders.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [How Interpretable Machine Learning Can Benefit Process Understanding in the Geosciences](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024ef004540)
Jiang et al. (2024), *Earth's Future*. 150 citations.

- **Main goal:** Shows how interpretable machine learning can advance process understanding in the geosciences, and guards against careless use.
- **Architecture:** Review and perspective on interpretable machine learning, including application scenarios, a practical workflow, common pitfalls and good practices.
- **Data:** Not applicable; draws on geoscientific examples.
- **Main result:** Identifies scenarios such as quantifying relationships, generating mechanism hypotheses and evaluating process-based models, plus pitfalls that lead to misleading conclusions.
- **Open work:** Broader yet more careful integration of interpretable ML, and linking explanations with causal inference and domain knowledge.
- **Issues:** Perspective without new quantitative experiments; explanations describe the model, not necessarily the physical system.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Interpretable machine learning for weather and climate prediction: A review](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.atmosenv.2024.120797)
Yang et al. (2024), *Atmospheric Environment*. 135 citations.

- **Main goal:** Surveys interpretable machine learning methods for weather and climate prediction, where opaque models limit trust and scientific insight.
- **Architecture:** Review of interpretable and explainable machine learning techniques (e.g. feature attribution and intrinsically interpretable models) applied to weather and climate prediction.
- **Data:** Review of published literature; no new data.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the available information; the review organises existing interpretability approaches and their uses in the field.
- **Open work:** Develop evaluation standards for explanations and physically consistent interpretable models.
- **Issues:** Card based on the title only; scope and conclusions could not be verified.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Using Machine Learning to Analyze Physical Causes of Climate Change: A Case Study of U.S. Midwest Extreme Precipitation](https://doi.org/10.1029/2021gl093787)
Davenport et al. (2021), *Geophysical Research Letters*. 123 citations.

- **Main goal:** Uses ML to understand how circulation changes contribute to trends in US Midwest extreme precipitation.
- **Architecture:** CNN classifier of extreme-precipitation circulation patterns (EPCPs) from daily sea level pressure and 500 hPa geopotential height anomalies, with visualization methods for interpretation.
- **Data:** Daily reanalysis circulation fields and observed Midwest precipitation extremes over roughly four decades.
- **Main result:** The CNN identifies 91% of observed extremes. EPCPs have become more frequent over the past two decades, but trends over four decades are insignificant. Moisture transport and precipitation intensity during EPCPs have increased.
- **Open work:** Apply to climate model projections to reduce uncertainty about future changes in extremes.
- **Issues:** Short observational record for trends, a single region, and possible false positives from classification on daily maps.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Viewing Forced Climate Patterns Through an AI Lens](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019gl084944)
Barnes et al. (2019), *Geophysical Research Letters*. 108 citations.

- **Main goal:** Extract forced climate change signals from internal variability and model uncertainty without explicit signal-noise separation.
- **Architecture:** Shallow artificial neural network trained to predict the year of a temperature or precipitation map, interpreted with layerwise relevance propagation to obtain indicator patterns.
- **Data:** Large multimodel climate simulations (CMIP-class) under historical and future scenarios, applied to observed surface temperature maps.
- **Main result:** The ANN identifies spatial indicator patterns of forced change and can date maps; forced patterns are detectable from the 1960s onward in simulated and observed temperature.
- **Open work:** Apply the approach to other variables and detection-attribution problems and to deeper diagnosis of model-observation differences.
- **Issues:** Indicator patterns are nonlinear mixtures of signal and noise and depend on the training ensemble; performance on observations relies on models capturing real forced patterns.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Investigating the fidelity of explainable artificial intelligence methods for applications of convolutional neural networks in geoscience](https://doi.org/10.1175/aies-d-22-0012.1)
Mamalakis et al. (2022), *Artificial Intelligence for the Earth Systems*. 106 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluate how faithfully popular explainable-AI methods explain CNN decisions in geoscience, to guide best practice.
- **Architecture:** Intercomparison of XAI attribution methods (e.g. gradient, SmoothGrad, input times gradient, integrated gradients, LRP variants, DeepSHAP) applied to CNNs.
- **Data:** An idealized synthetic attribution benchmark with known ground truth, and a CNN predicting the number of atmospheric rivers in climate-simulation snapshots.
- **Main result:** Reveals issues such as gradient shattering, inability to distinguish attribution sign and insensitivity to zero inputs that can distort interpretation of CNN strategies.
- **Open work:** Further study of XAI fidelity, better baselines, and benchmarks for other architectures and tasks.
- **Issues:** Limited to a subset of methods and CNNs; conclusions depend on the benchmark design.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Neural network attribution methods for problems in geoscience: A novel synthetic benchmark dataset](https://doi.org/10.1017/eds.2022.7)
Mamalakis et al. (2021), *Environmental Data Science*. 94 citations.

- **Main goal:** Enables objective evaluation of explainable AI (XAI) attribution methods for geoscience, where ground-truth attributions are usually unknown.
- **Architecture:** Framework that builds synthetic regression benchmarks from additively separable functions, giving a known ground-truth attribution. A fully connected network is trained, and XAI heatmaps (gradient-based, LRP variants and others) are compared with the ground truth.
- **Data:** Synthetic dataset with climate-like spatial inputs (for example SST-like anomaly fields) and outputs generated from known functions.
- **Main result:** Shows where specific XAI methods perform well or poorly against the known attribution, which makes XAI assessment less subjective.
- **Open work:** Extend benchmarks to non-additive functions, classification tasks and more complex architectures such as CNNs.
- **Issues:** Additive separability is a simplifying assumption, and real geophysical relations are often non-additive and interacting.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Indicator Patterns of Forced Change Learned by an Artificial Neural Network](https://doi.org/10.1029/2020ms002195)
Barnes et al. (2020), *Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems*. 94 citations.

- **Main goal:** Identify reliable regional indicator patterns of forced climate change amid internal variability and model differences.
- **Architecture:** ANN trained to predict the year from annual-mean temperature or precipitation maps, visualized with layerwise relevance propagation and backward optimization; designed so indicators vary in time.
- **Data:** CMIP5 forced climate model simulations; observations used to compare with simulated patterns.
- **Main result:** Produces time-evolving indicator patterns of forced change, compared with signal-to-noise and multilinear regression; backward optimization highlights where model-observation disagreements matter most.
- **Open work:** Apply to other variables and use the indicators for model evaluation and detection.
- **Issues:** Patterns depend on the model ensemble and ANN design; LRP explanations can be method-dependent.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Finding the right XAI method - A Guide for the Evaluation and Ranking of Explainable AI Methods in Climate Science](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.00652)
Bommer et al. (2023), *arXiv*. 94 citations.

- **Main goal:** Help climate scientists choose an explainable AI (XAI) method when ground-truth explanations are missing, by evaluating XAI methods on defined properties.
- **Architecture:** Benchmark/evaluation framework scoring XAI methods on robustness, faithfulness, randomization, complexity and localization, applied to an MLP and a convolutional neural network (CNN).
- **Data:** Case study predicting the decade from annual-mean temperature maps from climate model simulations, following earlier work.
- **Main result:** Integrated Gradients, layer-wise relevance propagation and input times gradients are robust, faithful and low-complexity but weak on randomization; sensitivity methods trade faithfulness and complexity for randomization; results depend on architecture.
- **Open work:** Task-specific XAI evaluation for other climate problems and architectures.
- **Issues:** Single case study with simple networks; evaluation metrics are proxies since true explanations are unknown.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Creating and Evaluating Uncertainty Estimates with Neural Networks for Environmental-Science Applications](https://doi.org/10.1175/aies-d-22-0061.1)
Haynes et al. (2023), *Artificial Intelligence for the Earth Systems*. 70 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provide environmental scientists with practical methods to create and evaluate uncertainty estimates from neural networks.
- **Architecture:** Tutorial/review of six NN uncertainty-quantification approaches plus four evaluation graphics and eight scores for judging uncertainty quality; Jupyter notebooks provided.
- **Data:** Two demonstrations: vertical dewpoint profile estimation (regression) and convection prediction over Taiwan from Himawari-8 imagery (classification).
- **Main result:** Shows how the UQ methods and evaluation tools can be applied and compared on real regression and classification problems.
- **Open work:** Broader adoption and systematic comparison of UQ methods across environmental applications.
- **Issues:** Tutorial scope; method rankings are demonstration-specific and not a general benchmark.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Observed Statistical Connections Overestimate the Causal Effects of Arctic Sea Ice Changes on Midlatitude Winter Climate](https://doi.org/10.1175/jcli-d-20-0293.1)
Blackport et al. (2021), *Journal of Climate*. 69 citations.

- **Main goal:** Quantifies how much Arctic sea ice variability causally affects midlatitude winter climate, separating cause from effect.
- **Architecture:** Non-ML study: regression analysis applied to observations and to large initial-condition ensembles of multiple climate models, in coupled and AMIP (prescribed sea ice/SST) configurations.
- **Data:** Observations and reanalysis plus large ensembles from several climate models, coupled and AMIP-style.
- **Main result:** Coupled models reproduce the observed sea ice and temperature links, but these are absent or much weaker in AMIP runs forced only by sea ice. Statistical links are inflated by circulation driving sea ice, so the causal effect is much weaker.
- **Open work:** Clarify whether models underestimate the true response, and refine estimates of the stratospheric pathway.
- **Issues:** Relies on models simulating the coupling correctly. Members span only 35 years, and internal variability makes individual estimates noisy.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Evaluation, Tuning and Interpretation of Neural Networks for Meteorological Applications](https://doi.org/10.1175/bams-d-20-0097.1)
Ebert-Uphoff et al. (2020), *Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society*. 68 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provide practical guidance for evaluating, tuning and interpreting neural networks applied to meteorological imagery.
- **Architecture:** Tutorial and perspective covering receptive fields, meteorological performance measures, and interpretation via synthetic experiments and layerwise relevance propagation, for classification and image-to-image tasks.
- **Data:** Illustrated with examples such as satellite-to-radar translation (GOES to synthetic reflectivity).
- **Main result:** Frames interpretation as an iterative, meteorologist-driven discovery process with hypothesis testing; highlights underused strategies.
- **Open work:** Develop community best practices and interpretation tools for image-to-image networks.
- **Issues:** Guidance rather than systematic benchmarking; examples drawn from a limited set of applications.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Meteorology and Climate Science: Model Fine-Tuning, Calibrating Trust and Learning New Science](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-04083-2_16)
Mamalakis et al. (2020), *xxAI@ICML*. 48 citations.

- **Main goal:** Discusses how explainable AI can help meteorology and climate science fine-tune neural networks, calibrate trust in their predictions and extract new physical insight.
- **Architecture:** Review and perspective on post hoc explainable AI (attribution) methods applied to neural networks for weather and climate problems; specific network families are not specified in the available metadata.
- **Data:** Abstract not available; the work presumably illustrates methods on climate datasets, but the data used are not reported in the metadata.
- **Main result:** Argues that XAI can reveal whether networks learn physically sensible strategies, help diagnose and fine-tune models, and occasionally reveal new science. No quantitative results available.
- **Open work:** Develop benchmark tests to evaluate the fidelity of XAI methods and guidance on choosing among them for geoscience applications.
- **Issues:** Abstract missing; attribution methods can disagree and their fidelity is hard to verify without ground truth.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [A graph‐based approach to find teleconnections in climate data](https://doi.org/10.1002/sam.11181)
Kawale et al. (2013), *Statistical Analysis and Data Mining: The ASA Data Science Journal*. 43 citations.

- **Main goal:** Automatically discovers teleconnections, such as pressure dipoles, in global climate data rather than relying on predefined indices.
- **Architecture:** Graph-based data mining: a climate network built from correlations between grid points, with clustering to find dipole teleconnection patterns.
- **Data:** Gridded reanalysis climate data (e.g., sea level pressure anomalies); exact products not confirmed here.
- **Main result:** No abstract is available; the approach recovers known teleconnections such as major climate dipoles and can identify new candidate patterns.
- **Open work:** Evaluation of discovered patterns in climate model output and their predictive value.
- **Issues:** Abstract missing; correlation-based networks do not establish causality and depend on the reanalysis used.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Are AI weather models learning atmospheric physics? A sensitivity analysis of cyclone Xynthia](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-025-00949-6)
Baño-Medina et al. (2025), *npj Climate and Atmospheric Science*. 38 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether AI weather models learn physically meaningful dynamics by using them for initial-condition sensitivity analysis of an extreme cyclone.
- **Architecture:** Backpropagation gradients of a forecast metric through an AI weather model with respect to initial fields, compared with an adjoint of a dynamical NWP model.
- **Data:** Cyclone Xynthia (2010) case at 36-hour lead time; the AI model is trained on reanalysis. Specific model and data products are not named in the abstract.
- **Main result:** AI-model sensitivities closely resemble adjoint sensitivities, and evolved perturbations produce similar impacts, indicating physically meaningful learned spatio-temporal links.
- **Open work:** Using AI gradients for observing network design and dynamics studies at nonlinear lead times beyond 5 days.
- **Issues:** Single case study at one lead time; agreement with an adjoint does not prove physical realism in general.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Learning Closed‐Form Equations for Subgrid‐Scale Closures From High‐Fidelity Data: Promises and Challenges](https://doi.org/10.1029/2023ms003874)
Jakhar et al. (2023), *Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems*. 29 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether equation discovery can learn interpretable closed-form subgrid-scale closures from high-fidelity data, and why such closures fail online.
- **Architecture:** Sparse-regression equation discovery with expansive term libraries applied to filtered DNS fluxes.
- **Data:** Filtered direct numerical simulations of 2D turbulence and Rayleigh-Benard convection with Gaussian, box and other filters.
- **Main result:** Robustly recovers the nonlinear gradient model (leading Taylor-series term), with offline flux correlations above 0.95, but LES with these closures is unstable due to no inter-scale energy transfer (2D) and poor backscatter (RBC).
- **Open work:** Physics-informed libraries, loss functions and metrics to discover accurate, stable closures.
- **Issues:** Idealized flows; SGS 'truth' depends on filtering and is non-unique; offline accuracy does not guarantee online stability.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Discovery of interpretable structural model errors by combining Bayesian sparse regression and data assimilation: A chaotic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky test case.](https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0091282)
Mojgani et al. (2021), *Chaos: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Nonlinear Science*. 22 citations.

- **Main goal:** Discovers interpretable closed-form representations of structural model errors from sparse, possibly noisy observations.
- **Architecture:** MEDIDA framework: non-neural method combining ensemble Kalman filter data assimilation with equation discovery by relevance vector machine (sparse Bayesian regression).
- **Data:** Chaotic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky system with synthetic noise-free and noisy sporadic observations.
- **Main result:** Accurately discovers different structural and parametric model errors representing missing physics, with both noise-free and noisy observations.
- **Open work:** Applying to higher-dimensional systems such as atmospheric and ocean models and real observations.
- **Issues:** 1D idealized test case; requires an adequate library of candidate terms for sparse regression.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Moving beyond post hoc explainable artificial intelligence: a perspective paper on lessons learned from dynamical climate modeling](https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-18-787-2025)
O’Loughlin et al. (2025), *Geoscientific Model Development*. 19 citations.

- **Main goal:** Argues that trust in AI climate models should be built not only through post hoc explainable AI but also via lessons from physics-based dynamical climate model development.
- **Architecture:** Review and perspective proposing instrumental, statistical and component-level understanding as a framework for evaluating trust in dynamical and AI models; non-ML conceptual method.
- **Data:** No new data; draws on the history of climate model intercomparison projects and examples from the AI climate science literature.
- **Main result:** Post hoc XAI mainly adds statistical understanding; component-level understanding, as achieved through intercomparison projects, requires AI models with interpretable components.
- **Open work:** Build AI climate models with interpretable, modular components amenable to component-level diagnosis and intercomparison.
- **Issues:** Conceptual paper without quantitative tests; cited successes in component-level understanding of AI models remain limited.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Towards mechanistic understanding in a data-driven weather model: internal activations reveal interpretable physical features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24440)
MacMillan et al. (2025), *arXiv*. 18 citations.

- **Main goal:** Investigates whether the internal representations of a data-driven weather model are interpretable and physically consistent, toward mechanistic understanding.
- **Architecture:** Mechanistic interpretability of GraphCast, a graph neural network, using sparse autoencoders on intermediate layer activations, plus feature interventions during prediction.
- **Data:** GraphCast activations from forecasts initialized from ERA5-like global states; specific periods are not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Finds interpretable features for tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, diurnal and seasonal cycles, precipitation patterns, geography and sea ice; editing a cyclone feature produces physically consistent hurricane changes.
- **Open work:** Extend interpretability analyses to other data-driven models and use feature interventions for scientific discovery and trust assessment.
- **Issues:** Qualitative case-study evidence; features found may depend on sparse autoencoder settings, and physical consistency of interventions is assessed for few cases.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Learning Physically Interpretable Atmospheric Models From Data With WSINDy](https://doi.org/10.1029/2025jh000602)
Minor et al. (2024), *Journal of Geophysical Research: Machine Learning and Computation*. 9 citations.

- **Main goal:** Discovers interpretable governing equations for atmospheric phenomena as an alternative to opaque neural weather models.
- **Architecture:** Weak-form sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (WSINDy), a sparse-regression equation-discovery method (not a neural network), adapted to high-dimensional fluid data.
- **Data:** Simulated atmospheric data and assimilated (reanalysis) data; specific products not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** WSINDy learns effective symbolic PDE models of atmospheric dynamics from both simulated and assimilated data.
- **Open work:** Scaling to more complex, multivariate and 3D atmospheric systems and assessing forecast skill of discovered models.
- **Issues:** Demonstration-focused without detailed skill comparison against ML models; library choice constrains discoverable physics.
- *Basis: assessment*

<a id="ocean"></a>
## Ocean

### [Machine Learning for the Detection of Oil Spills in Satellite Radar Images](https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1007452223027)
Kubát et al. (1998), *Machine Learning*. 1,326 citations.

- **Main goal:** Automatically detects oil spills in satellite synthetic aperture radar images to reduce the manual screening burden.
- **Architecture:** Machine-learning classification pipeline on segmented dark regions, including a learner tailored to highly imbalanced classes (the SHRINK approach) compared with standard classifiers such as decision trees and nearest neighbour.
- **Data:** Spaceborne SAR images (RADARSAT and ERS-1) with a small number of labeled oil slicks and many look-alike dark patches.
- **Main result:** Shows that class imbalance and image-batched data strongly affect learning, and that imbalance-aware learning and suitable evaluation metrics give a usable detector.
- **Open work:** More labeled images, better handling of look-alikes and transfer across sensors and image batches.
- **Issues:** Very few positive examples; evaluation on a small image set; accuracy metrics misleading under imbalance.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Oil spill detection by satellite remote sensing](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2004.11.015)
Brekke et al. (2005), *Remote Sensing of Environment*. 1,120 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews methods for detecting marine oil spills from satellite remote sensing, important for environmental monitoring and enforcement.
- **Architecture:** Review of oil spill detection: dark-spot segmentation, feature extraction and classification (statistical classifiers and neural networks) applied mainly to SAR imagery.
- **Data:** Spaceborne SAR (e.g. ERS, RADARSAT, ENVISAT ASAR) and optical sensors as discussed in the literature.
- **Main result:** Summarizes the state of automatic and semi-automatic SAR oil spill detection and the difficulty of separating oil from look-alikes.
- **Open work:** Better discrimination of look-alikes, use of wind information and operational integration.
- **Issues:** Review; no new quantitative benchmark.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [The MERIS Case 2 water algorithm](https://doi.org/10.1080/01431160600821127)
Doerffer et al. (2007), *International Journal of Remote Sensing*. 550 citations.

- **Main goal:** Retrieves water constituents from MERIS reflectances in optically complex coastal (Case 2) waters.
- **Architecture:** Inverse multilayer perceptron neural networks trained on radiative transfer simulations, with a forward network to check out-of-scope spectra.
- **Data:** Bio-optical radiative transfer simulations of water-leaving reflectance; Envisat MERIS observations.
- **Main result:** The algorithm retrieves absorption and scattering coefficients and derived chlorophyll, suspended matter and yellow substance concentrations as an operational MERIS product.
- **Open work:** Validation with in situ data and regional adaptation of the bio-optical model.
- **Issues:** Accuracy depends on the assumed bio-optical model and atmospheric correction.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Seamless retrievals of chlorophyll-a from Sentinel-2 (MSI) and Sentinel-3 (OLCI) in inland and coastal waters: A machine-learning approach](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2019.111604)
Pahlevan et al. (2020), *Remote Sensing of Environment*. 509 citations.

- **Main goal:** Retrieves chlorophyll-a consistently across Sentinel-2 MSI and Sentinel-3 OLCI in optically complex inland and coastal waters.
- **Architecture:** Mixture Density Network (MDN), a neural network that outputs a Gaussian mixture distribution of Chla given remote sensing reflectance.
- **Data:** In situ database of co-located Chla (n = 2943) and hyperspectral radiometry resampled to MSI and OLCI bands, plus independent satellite matchups; Chla 0.2–1209 mg/m3.
- **Main result:** Compared with state-of-the-art algorithms, MAE and bias drop by 40–60%, and RMSLE and MAPE improve two to three times for both sensors.
- **Open work:** Extend MDN to other water-quality parameters and sensors, and quantify retrieval uncertainty further.
- **Issues:** Performance depends on atmospheric correction for satellite data and on representativeness of the in situ training set.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Reconstruction of sea-surface temperatures from assemblages of planktonic foraminifera: multi-technique approach based on geographically constrained calibration data sets and its application to glacial Atlantic and Pacific Oceans](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.quascirev.2004.07.014)
Kučera et al. (2005), *Quaternary Science Reviews*. 444 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reconstructs Last Glacial Maximum sea surface temperatures from planktonic foraminifera assemblages with consistent, cross-checked statistical techniques.
- **Architecture:** Multi-technique transfer-function approach including artificial neural networks, modern analogue technique, revised analogue method and SIMMAX, with geographically constrained calibration sets.
- **Data:** Core-top planktonic foraminifera calibration datasets and glacial assemblages from Atlantic and Pacific Ocean sediment cores.
- **Main result:** The techniques produce broadly consistent glacial SST estimates; combining them with regional calibration improves robustness of the reconstructions.
- **Open work:** Better treatment of no-analogue glacial assemblages and fuller uncertainty quantification.
- **Issues:** Reconstructions depend on calibration coverage and assume stable species-temperature relationships.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Global Patterns and Predictions of Seafloor Biomass Using Random Forests](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0015323)
Wei et al. (2010), *PLoS ONE*. 439 citations.

- **Main goal:** Builds global maps of seafloor biomass and abundance to inform deep-sea food web models, carbon cycling and management.
- **Architecture:** Random forest regression predicting benthic standing stocks from environmental predictors.
- **Data:** Seafloor biomass and abundance database from 24 institutions within the Census of Marine Life, with predictors of surface primary production, water-column and export POC flux, seafloor relief and bottom-water properties.
- **Main result:** Models explain 63–88% of stock variance by size group; biomass is highest at the poles, on upwelling margins and equatorial divergence zones, lowest on central abyssal plains.
- **Open work:** Incorporating the maps into mechanistic deep-sea food web and carbon cycle models and filling sampling gaps.
- **Issues:** Uneven sampling across ocean basins and depths; predictions in unsampled regions are extrapolations; static climatological view.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Prediction of Sea Surface Temperature Using Long Short-Term Memory](https://doi.org/10.1109/lgrs.2017.2733548)
Zhang et al. (2017), *IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Letters*. 411 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts sea surface temperature at daily, weekly and monthly scales as a time series regression problem.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network followed by a fully connected dense layer.
- **Data:** SST and SST anomaly data for coastal seas of China; product name not given in the abstract.
- **Main result:** The LSTM predicts 1- and 3-day SST and weekly and monthly means effectively, and supports online updating.
- **Open work:** Using spatial information (e.g. convolutional LSTM) and longer leads.
- **Issues:** Point-wise time series model ignores spatial structure; limited region; baselines unclear in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Recent variability of the global ocean carbon sink](https://doi.org/10.1002/2014gb004853)
Landschützer et al. (2014), *Global Biogeochemical Cycles*. 407 citations.

- **Main goal:** Quantifies recent variability of the global ocean CO2 sink from observations.
- **Architecture:** Two-step neural network (SOM-FFN): a self-organizing map clusters ocean provinces and a feedforward neural network reconstructs surface ocean pCO2 within each.
- **Data:** Surface ocean pCO2 observations from the SOCAT database with satellite and reanalysis predictors (SST, salinity, chlorophyll, mixed layer depth), roughly 1998–2011.
- **Main result:** The ocean sink weakened in the 1990s and strengthened substantially in the 2000s, showing large decadal variability.
- **Open work:** Attribution of drivers, better coverage in poorly sampled regions such as the Southern Ocean.
- **Issues:** Sparse, uneven observations especially in the Southern Ocean; mapping uncertainty and gas-exchange parameterization errors.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Decadal variations and trends of the global ocean carbon sink](https://doi.org/10.1002/2015gb005359)
Landschützer et al. (2016), *Global Biogeochemical Cycles*. 379 citations.

- **Main goal:** Quantifies decadal variations and trends of the global ocean CO2 sink from observations, to test whether the sink keeps pace with rising emissions.
- **Architecture:** Two-step neural network approach (SOM-FFN): a self-organizing map clusters the ocean into biogeochemical provinces and a feedforward neural network maps surface pCO2 from predictors.
- **Data:** SOCAT surface ocean pCO2 observations with predictors such as SST, salinity, mixed layer depth and chlorophyll, covering roughly 1982–2011.
- **Main result:** The sink shows strong decadal variability: it weakened through the 1990s and reinvigorated substantially from the early 2000s, departing from a steady trend expected from rising atmospheric CO2.
- **Open work:** Attributing the variability to physical and biological drivers and extending the reconstruction with more observations.
- **Issues:** Abstract not available; sparse pCO2 sampling, especially in the Southern Ocean and early decades, makes decadal estimates uncertain.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Applications of Deep Learning to Ocean Data Inference and Subgrid Parameterization](https://doi.org/10.1029/2018ms001472)
Bolton et al. (2018), *Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems*. 365 citations.

- **Main goal:** Uses ML to infer unresolved ocean processes: subgrid eddy momentum forcing for coarse models and subsurface flow from surface data.
- **Architecture:** Convolutional neural networks, optionally constrained to conserve global momentum.
- **Data:** Coarse-grained output from a high-resolution quasi-geostrophic ocean model (idealized double-gyre configuration).
- **Main result:** CNNs reproduce spatiotemporal variability of subgrid eddy forcing, generalize across dynamical regimes, work with 10-20% of the training data, and predict subsurface flow from surface fields.
- **Open work:** Implementing and testing the parameterization online in coarse-resolution ocean and climate models.
- **Issues:** Offline, idealized QG setting; online stability and realism in primitive-equation models untested.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A machine learning framework to forecast wave conditions](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.coastaleng.2018.03.004)
James et al. (2017), *Coastal Engineering*. 364 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides fast estimates of ocean wave conditions as a surrogate for a physics-based wave model.
- **Architecture:** Supervised machine learning surrogates: an MLP regression model for wave height and a support vector machine classifier for characteristic period, trained on wave model runs.
- **Data:** Thousands of SWAN-type physics-based wave model runs for Monterey Bay forced by measured waves, ocean-current nowcasts and winds.
- **Main result:** Wave heights reproduced with RMSE of 9 cm and over 90% of characteristic periods identified correctly, at under 1/1,000 of the physics model's cost.
- **Open work:** Applying to other coasts and to forecast-mode forcing.
- **Issues:** Emulates the physical model rather than observations, so inherits its errors; single site.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Deep-learning-based information mining from ocean remote-sensing imagery](https://doi.org/10.1093/nsr/nwaa047)
Li et al. (2020), *National Science Review*. 351 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews deep learning for mining information from big ocean remote sensing data archives.
- **Architecture:** Review of two deep learning frameworks for ocean remote sensing image classification, with eight application examples.
- **Data:** Ocean remote sensing imagery of various types (e.g. SAR and optical) for internal waves, eddies, oil spills, coastal inundation, sea ice, green algae, ships and coral reefs.
- **Main result:** Shows that the deep learning frameworks are effective across the eight applications.
- **Open work:** Adapting the frameworks to other kinds of remote sensing imagery.
- **Issues:** Largely showcases the authors' own work; limited quantitative comparison.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Real time wave forecasting using neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0029-8018(97)10025-7)
Deo et al. (1998), *Ocean Engineering*. 349 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts ocean wave heights a few hours ahead in real time for coastal and offshore operations.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward artificial neural network (multilayer perceptron) using recent observed wave heights.
- **Data:** Observed wave height time series from a buoy off the west coast of India.
- **Main result:** The neural networks give satisfactory forecasts for short leads, with accuracy decreasing as lead time increases.
- **Open work:** Use of wind inputs and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Univariate inputs; single site; skill falls at longer leads.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Short and mid-term sea surface temperature prediction using time-series satellite data and LSTM-AdaBoost combination approach](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2019.111358)
Xiao et al. (2019), *Remote Sensing of Environment*. 325 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts short and mid-term daily sea surface temperature anomalies, which matter for extreme weather and climate.
- **Architecture:** LSTM recurrent neural network and AdaBoost ensemble trained separately and averaged (LSTM-AdaBoost), after polynomial removal of seasonality.
- **Data:** Time series of satellite SST anomaly in the East China Sea.
- **Main result:** For daily SSTA up to 10 days ahead, the combination outperforms LSTM, AdaBoost, optimized SVR, BPNN and a stacking variant.
- **Open work:** Extending to longer leads, larger regions and multivariate predictors.
- **Issues:** Pointwise time series without explicit spatial context; single region; no uncertainty estimates.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Global ocean methane emissions dominated by shallow coastal waters](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-019-12541-7)
Weber et al. (2019), *Nature Communications*. 322 citations.

- **Main goal:** Constrains global ocean methane emissions, a highly uncertain term in the atmospheric CH4 budget, despite sparse sampling.
- **Architecture:** Machine learning models (an ensemble of artificial neural networks and random forests) mapping surface methane disequilibrium from environmental predictors.
- **Data:** Compiled in situ dissolved CH4 measurements and gridded oceanographic predictors.
- **Main result:** Diffusive flux of 2–6 Tg CH4/yr and total oceanic emissions of 6–12 Tg CH4/yr, narrowing prior ranges by a factor of three; dominated by shallow coastal waters.
- **Open work:** More coastal and seafloor sampling and better constraints on ebullitive fluxes.
- **Issues:** Sparse observations, uncertain gas transfer velocities, and extrapolation into unsampled regions.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Neural network for emulation of an inverse model: operational derivation of Case II water properties from MERIS data](https://doi.org/10.1080/014311699212443)
Schiller et al. (1999), *International Journal of Remote Sensing*. 309 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides an operational algorithm for retrieving optically complex Case II water constituents from MERIS ocean colour data, where simple band-ratio methods fail.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer perceptron trained to emulate the inverse of a radiative transfer model, mapping top-of-atmosphere or water-leaving reflectances to water constituent concentrations.
- **Data:** Large set of simulated MERIS reflectances generated with a radiative transfer model over ranges of chlorophyll, suspended matter and yellow substance.
- **Main result:** The network reproduces the inverse model accurately and is fast enough for operational processing of MERIS data.
- **Open work:** Validation against in situ match-ups once MERIS data become available and extension to coupled atmosphere-water retrievals.
- **Issues:** Trained only on simulations, so accuracy depends on the realism of the bio-optical and radiative transfer model; pre-launch study without real-data validation.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Neural networks for wave forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0029-8018(00)00027-5)
Deo et al. (2001), *Ocean Engineering*. 305 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts ocean wave height and period from wind information as an alternative to empirical and numerical wave models.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward artificial neural network (MLP) trained with different learning algorithms, using wind speed as input.
- **Data:** Wind and wave measurements from an offshore location; exact dataset not reported here.
- **Main result:** Neural networks forecast significant wave height and average wave period with satisfactory accuracy.
- **Open work:** Including fetch, wind direction and duration and testing at other sites.
- **Issues:** Site-specific training; cannot represent swell from distant sources; limited data.
- *Basis: assessment*

### Evolution of the C2RCC Neural Network for Sentinel 2 and 3 for the Retrieval of Ocean Colour Products in Normal and Extreme Optically Complex Waters
Brockmann et al. (2016), *Venue not recorded*. 284 citations.

- **Main goal:** Retrieves ocean colour products in normal and extremely optically complex coastal and inland waters from Sentinel-2 and Sentinel-3.
- **Architecture:** Case-2 Regional CoastColour (C2RCC) processor: neural networks (MLP) inverting reflectances to inherent optical properties and concentrations, extended for extreme waters.
- **Data:** Training on simulated reflectances from radiative transfer modelling, applied to Sentinel-2 MSI and Sentinel-3 OLCI.
- **Main result:** Describes the evolution of C2RCC for the new sensors and extended training ranges for extreme waters; quantitative validation not reported here.
- **Open work:** Broader in-situ validation and refinement of bio-optical models for extreme waters.
- **Issues:** Relies on simulated training data and assumed bio-optical models; abstract not available.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Oil Spill Identification from Satellite Images Using Deep Neural Networks](https://doi.org/10.3390/rs11151762)
Krestenitis et al. (2019), *Remote Sensing*. 268 citations.

- **Main goal:** Detects oil spills in SAR images and separates them from look-alikes, and provides a common benchmark so methods can be compared.
- **Architecture:** Semantic segmentation with deep convolutional neural networks; several known models (U-Net-style and DeepLab variants) are compared, with DeepLabv3+ best. Also introduces a benchmark dataset.
- **Data:** New public SAR oil spill dataset with pixel-wise labels for oil spills, look-alikes, ships, land and sea; built from Sentinel-1 imagery per the authors.
- **Main result:** DeepLabv3+ gives the best test accuracy and inference time; discriminating oil from look-alikes remains the hardest part.
- **Open work:** Use the benchmark to develop methods that better separate look-alikes and add contextual data such as wind.
- **Issues:** Class imbalance and look-alike confusion persist; single-sensor dataset; no wind or ancillary inputs.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A Neural Network Model for Estimating Sea Surface Chlorophyll and Sediments from Thematic Mapper Imagery](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0034-4257(98)00054-6)
Keiner et al. (1998), *Remote Sensing of Environment*. 265 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates sea surface chlorophyll and suspended sediment concentrations in coastal waters from Landsat TM imagery.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer perceptron neural network mapping TM band radiances to constituent concentrations, compared with regression methods.
- **Data:** Landsat Thematic Mapper imagery of Delaware Bay with concurrent in situ chlorophyll and sediment measurements.
- **Main result:** The neural network gives lower errors than regression-based algorithms for both chlorophyll and sediments.
- **Open work:** Application to more scenes, seasons and sensors with better spectral resolution.
- **Issues:** Limited in situ match-ups; TM bands are not designed for ocean colour; atmospheric correction uncertainties.
