### [Spatiotemporal patterns of PM10 concentrations over China during 2005-2016: A satellite-based estimation using the random forests approach.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envpol.2018.07.012)
Chen et al. (2018), *Environmental Pollution*. 154 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates historical daily PM10 exposure across China from satellite aerosol data to study long-term trends and health effects.

- **Data:** Daily PM10 at 1479 sites (2014-2016), two MODIS AOD products, land use and meteorological data; predictions at 0.1 degree for 2005-2016.
- **Main result:** Cross-validated R2 0.78 daily (RMSE 31.5 ug/m3), 0.82 monthly and 0.81 annually; about one-third of China exceeded the Grade II standard; PM10 peaked in 2006-2007 and declined after 2008.
- **Open work:** Applying the estimates to long-term health studies and improving coverage where AOD is missing.
- **Issues:** Back-extrapolation to 2005-2013 relies on a model trained on 2014-2016 monitoring data; AOD gaps and random CV may overstate skill.

### [Artificial Intelligence Technologies for Forecasting Air Pollution and Human Health: A Narrative Review](https://doi.org/10.3390/su14169951)
Subramaniam et al. (2022), *Sustainability*. 154 citations.

Fan et al. (2017), *ISPRS Annals of the Photogrammetry, Remote Sensing and Spatial Information Sciences*. 153 citations.

- **Main result:** The DRNN framework outperforms deep feed-forward networks and GBDT; missing-value strategies affect performance.

### [Automated detection and monitoring of methane super-emitters using satellite data](https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-23-9071-2023)
Schuit et al. (2023), *Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics*. 153 citations.

- **Main goal:** Automates detection of methane super-emitter plumes in TROPOMI data, where manual inspection of millions of daily observations is infeasible.

- **Data:** TROPOMI methane data, training on pre-2021 data and application to 2021; GHGSat, PRISMA and Sentinel-2 for facility-level follow-up.
- **Main result:** 2974 plumes detected in 2021 (mean source 44 t/h) from 94 persistent clusters; sources are urban areas/landfills 35%, gas 24%, oil 21%, coal 20%.

- **Issues:** Detection limited by TROPOMI resolution and retrieval artifacts; emission rate estimates are uncertain.

Paschalidou et al. (2011), *Environmental Science and Pollution Research*. 153 citations.

Zhou et al. (2023), *Scientific Reports*. 149 citations.

### [Estimating Regional Ground‐Level PM2.5 Directly From Satellite Top‐Of‐Atmosphere Reflectance Using Deep Belief Networks](https://doi.org/10.1029/2018jd028759)
Shen et al. (2017), *Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres*. 133 citations.

Turquety et al. (2004), *Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres*. 129 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides an operational algorithm for retrieving atmospheric trace gas columns (CO, CH4, O3) from the Infrared Atmospheric Sounding Interferometer before the instrument's launch.

### [A 24-h forecast of ozone peaks and exceedance levels using neural classifiers and weather predictions](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envsoft.2006.08.002)
Dutot et al. (2007), *Environmental Modelling & Software*. 127 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts next-day hourly maximum ozone and threshold exceedances in an urban area of central France for real-time air quality warnings.
- **Architecture:** MultiLayer Perceptron (MLP) neural network with a BIC-like regularisation and confidence intervals, plus an MLP neural classifier with sigmoid output giving exceedance probability, compared with logistic regression.
- **Data:** Model output statistics of weather predictions from the French National Weather Service and ozone measurements from an urban air quality network; validation in summer 2003.
- **Main result:** Ozone peaks are predicted with agreement index 92%; the neural classifier reaches a 78% success index versus 65–72% for classical MLPs and detected six of seven peaks in summer 2003.

### [Application of random forest regression to the calculation of gas-phase chemistry within the GEOS-Chem chemistry model v10](https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-12-1209-2019)
Keller et al. (2018), *Geoscientific Model Development*. 125 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests replacing the costly gas-phase chemistry integrator of an atmospheric chemistry transport model with a machine-learning surrogate.

- **Data:** One month (July 2013) of GEOS-Chem v10 output of chemical and physical state.
- **Main result:** Online ozone errors grow slowly: after 5 days NMB 4.2%, RMSE 35%, R2 0.9; after 30 days 13%, 67%, 0.75. Polluted regions are within 10%, but some species (inorganic bromine, short-lived nitrogen) have very large errors.
- **Open work:** Optimizing speed and implementation, improving error accumulation in remote regions, and operational air quality applications.
- **Issues:** Proof-of-concept is 1.8x slower than the numerical integrator; one month of training data; errors accumulate in remote areas and for several species; no mass conservation guarantees.
- *Basis: abstract*

- **Main goal:** Reviews how interpretable machine learning has been used for air pollution forecasting, since most studies favour accuracy over interpretability.

- **Issues:** Station-based statistical models; limited interpretability and transferability.

### [A Simple Feedforward Neural Network for the PM10 Forecasting: Comparison with a Radial Basis Function Network and a Multivariate Linear Regression Model](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11270-008-9950-2)
Caselli et al. (2009), *Water, Air, and Soil Pollution*. 101 citations.

### [A blended TROPOMI+GOSAT satellite data product for atmospheric methane using machine learning to correct retrieval biases](https://doi.org/10.5194/amt-16-3787-2023)
Balasus et al. (2023), *Atmospheric Measurement Techniques*. 85 citations.

- **Main goal:** Corrects TROPOMI methane retrieval biases by reference to GOSAT to create a blended product for quantifying methane emissions.
- **Architecture:** Gradient-boosted decision tree model (LightGBM) trained to predict the TROPOMI minus GOSAT difference using only TROPOMI retrieval variables, then applied to the full TROPOMI record.
- **Data:** Co-located TROPOMI and GOSAT XCH4 retrievals, applied to TROPOMI from April 2018 onward; validation against TCCON ground-based columns.
- **Main result:** Spatially variable bias over land falls from 14.3 to 10.4 ppb versus GOSAT; against TCCON, variable bias drops from 4.7 to 4.4 ppb and precision from 14.5 to 11.9 ppb.
- **Open work:** Applying the method to other new satellite instruments and removing residual coastal biases with additional filters.
- **Issues:** Inherits GOSAT errors as reference; TCCON sites cover only low-albedo surfaces; residual coastal biases remain.

### [Ozone ensemble forecast with machine learning algorithms](https://doi.org/10.1029/2008jd009978)
Mallet et al. (2009), *Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres*. 84 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves ozone forecasts by combining an ensemble of air-quality model runs rather than relying on a single model.

- **Data:** An ensemble of about 48 chemistry-transport model configurations from the Polyphemus platform over Europe, evaluated against ground ozone observations for a summer season.
- **Main result:** Aggregated forecasts outperform the best single model and the ensemble mean, reducing RMSE of daily ozone peaks substantially (on the order of 20%).

- **Issues:** Weights are station-based and need a training period; gains depend on ensemble diversity.

Li et al. (2023), *Environment International*. 82 citations.

- **Issues:** Single city and season; SHAP attributions reflect correlation rather than causation and include co-varying chemical species.

### [Toward Stable, General Machine‐Learned Models of the Atmospheric Chemical System](https://doi.org/10.1029/2020jd032759)
Kelp et al. (2020), *Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres*. 67 citations.

- **Main goal:** Build fast ML emulators of atmospheric chemistry solvers that remain stable over long simulations.

- **Data:** Simulations from a reference atmospheric chemical mechanism solver, initialized with random conditions.
- **Main result:** About 260x speedup (about 1,900x on specialized hardware); stable beyond one week; 24 h ozone median error 2.7 ppb and below 19 ppb in 99% of cases; PM median error 16 ug/m3.

Sturm et al. (2021), *Geoscientific Model Development*. 62 citations.

- **Main goal:** Prevents nonphysical predictions from neural network surrogates of atmospheric chemistry by enforcing conservation laws in the architecture.

### [Advancing Sophisticated Photochemistry Simulation in Atmospheric Numerical Models With Artificial Intelligence PhotoChemistry (AIPC) Scheme Using the Feature‐Mapping Subspace Self‐Attention Algorithm](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024ms004646)
Xia et al. (2025), *Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems*. 6 citations.

- **Main goal:** Accelerates full atmospheric photochemistry simulation in 3D models by replacing a complex chemical solver with a stable AI scheme.
- **Architecture:** Transformer-style Feature-Mapping Subspace Self-Attention (FMSSA) network forming the AIPC scheme, compared with MLP and ResNet baselines; coupled online in WRF-Chem.
- **Data:** WRF-Chem simulations with the full SAPRC-99 mechanism (79 species, 229 reactions); monthly online tests in August and February.
- **Main result:** FMSSA cuts attention cost by 91%, reaches mean NRMSE of 3.09% for 69 species offline, and runs stably online in August with 77% faster computation than the numerical solver.
- **Open work:** Expand training data, refine the architecture and test across broader spatiotemporal regimes.

### [mloz: A Highly Efficient Machine Learning‐Based Ozone Parameterization for Climate Sensitivity Simulations](https://doi.org/10.1029/2025ms005459)
Ma et al. (2025), *Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems*. 4 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provide interactive tropospheric and stratospheric ozone in climate models that lack costly chemistry schemes, for climate sensitivity simulations where ozone feedbacks matter.
- **Architecture:** Machine-learning ozone parameterization (mloz) that predicts daily ozone from atmospheric temperature profiles only, coupled online in climate models; network family not specified in the abstract.
- **Data:** Trained on UKESM simulations with interactive chemistry; transferred online to the ICON model without chemistry.
- **Main result:** Stable decadal online simulations with high fidelity, including two-way ozone–QBO interactions; about 31 times faster than UKESM chemistry and under 4% of total model runtime.
- **Open work:** Adoption in CMIP-class models without interactive chemistry and evaluation under a wider range of forcing scenarios.
- **Issues:** Temperature-only input omits explicit dependence on ozone-depleting substances and emissions, so applicability is targeted at climate sensitivity experiments; inherits biases of the UKESM chemistry it learned from.
- *Basis: abstract*

Pang et al. (2026), *Geophysical Research Letters*. 4 citations.

Liu et al. (2026), *Science Advances*. 2 citations.

- **Main goal:** Rapidly simulate daily PM2.5 and its chemical composition in response to emission reductions, replacing costly chemical transport model runs for policy evaluation.
- **Architecture:** CleanAir, a residual symmetric three-dimensional U-Net emulating a chemical transport model.

### [Deep Learning Ensemble Emulation for NASA’s Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS) Composition Forecast](https://doi.org/10.1175/aies-d-24-0117.1)
Sleeman et al. (2025), *Artificial Intelligence for the Earth Systems*. 1 citations.

- **Main goal:** Emulates ensembles of NASA's GEOS Composition Forecast to extend air-quality forecasts beyond five days and provide probabilistic estimates at low cost.
- **Architecture:** Air quality conditional generative adversarial network (AQcGAN) emulating ensemble mean and spread; FourCastNet-type models are shown to be inadequate and unstable for composition.
- **Data:** GEOS-CF composition forecasts and ensembles for carbon monoxide, nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide and ozone.
- **Main result:** AQcGAN forecasts ten days ahead, generating ensemble mean and spread in seconds with competitive low RMSE against true ensemble statistics; used as the ensemble in an operational data assimilation study.
- **Open work:** Authors plan integration with data assimilation methods and the operational GEOS-CF system.
- **Issues:** Trained and verified against GEOS-CF model output rather than observations; GAN training can be unstable; limited set of species.

### [A chemistry-informed deep learning network for mitigating the stratospheric OH data gap](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aee2319)
Yin et al. (2026), *Science Advances*. 0 citations.

- **Main goal:** Fills the gap in global stratospheric hydroxyl (OH) observations, absent from satellites since 2009, which is key for ozone chemistry.
- **Architecture:** DRCAT: a chemistry-informed deep learning network predicting stratospheric OH profiles from coincident satellite observations of chemically related species.
- **Data:** Satellite observations of OH and related species, trained on only 2 years of data, producing a reconstruction from late 2004 to present; specific instruments not named in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Outperforms a chemical transport model and an observation-constrained steady-state approximation, and captures anomalous OH enhancements after the 2022 Hunga eruption outside the training regime.
- **Open work:** Applying the framework to reconstruct other short-lived chemical species.
- **Issues:** Very short training period; reconstruction depends on continued availability of the input satellite species; uncertainty not described in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

## Hydrology & water resources

### [Neural networks for the prediction and forecasting of water resource variables: a review of modelling issues and applications](https://doi.org/10.1016/s1364-8152(99)00007-9)
Maier et al. (2000), *Environmental Modelling & Software*. 2,397 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews how artificial neural networks were developed for predicting and forecasting water resource variables, to identify good modelling practice.
- **Architecture:** Review of feedforward neural network (mostly MLP with backpropagation) modelling practice: input selection, data division, preprocessing, architecture choice, training and validation.
- **Data:** No new data; examines 43 published papers on ANN prediction of water resource variables, mainly river flow and water quality.
- **Main result:** Finds that the modelling process is often poorly described and suboptimal, especially input determination, data division and validation, and proposes a structured modelling protocol.
- **Open work:** Calls for systematic methods for input selection, data division and architecture determination, and for consistent reporting of model development.
- **Issues:** Abstract not available; relies on knowledge of the paper. Covers pre-2000 feedforward networks only.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Recent decline in the global land evapotranspiration trend due to limited moisture supply](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature09396)
Jung et al. (2010), *Nature*. 2,170 citations.

- **Main goal:** Explains why the global land evapotranspiration trend changed after the late 1990s, testing whether moisture supply rather than energy limits recent evapotranspiration growth.
- **Architecture:** Model tree ensemble (MTE), a tree-based machine learning upscaling of eddy covariance fluxes, combined with diagnostic analysis and an ensemble of process-based land models.
- **Data:** FLUXNET eddy covariance evapotranspiration, satellite vegetation (fAPAR) and gridded meteorological data, 1982–2008, plus process-model simulations for comparison.
- **Main result:** Global land evapotranspiration rises from 1982 to about 1997, then the trend stalls, mainly because soil moisture limitation in Southern Hemisphere regions such as Africa and Australia.
- **Open work:** Longer records and better soil moisture observations are needed to tell whether the pause reflects decadal variability or a lasting shift in the water cycle.
- **Issues:** Upscaled fluxes depend on sparse, Northern Hemisphere biased tower coverage and on satellite forcing quality; trend attribution over a short record is uncertain.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Rainfall–runoff modelling using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-22-6005-2018)
Kratzert et al. (2018), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 1,818 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether a purely data-driven recurrent network can simulate daily rainfall-runoff, including snow-driven storage effects, as an alternative to conceptual hydrological models.
- **Architecture:** Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network trained per catchment, regionally across many catchments, and with regional pretraining followed by fine-tuning on individual catchments.
- **Data:** 241 catchments of the CAMELS dataset (contiguous US) with daily meteorological forcing and discharge; benchmark is SAC-SMA coupled with Snow-17.
- **Main result:** LSTMs fine-tuned from a regional model outperform SAC-SMA + Snow-17 and single-catchment LSTMs, showing that regional learning transfers process understanding to individual basins.
- **Open work:** Adding static catchment attributes, testing in ungauged basins and probing interpretability of the learned storage states are natural next steps.
- **Issues:** Evaluated only on CAMELS US catchments; no uncertainty estimates; purely data-driven with no physical constraints, so extrapolation to unseen climates is untested.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Artificial Neural Network Modeling of the Rainfall‐Runoff Process](https://doi.org/10.1029/95wr01955)
Hsu et al. (1995), *Water Resources Research*. 1,537 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether artificial neural networks can model the nonlinear rainfall-runoff process as well as conventional time-series and conceptual hydrological models.
- **Architecture:** Three-layer feedforward neural network (MLP) trained with a procedure combining linear least squares and simplex search, compared with ARMAX time-series models and the SAC-SMA conceptual model.
- **Data:** Daily rainfall and streamflow data from the Leaf River basin, Mississippi.
- **Main result:** The ANN gives better streamflow simulations than the linear ARMAX model and performance comparable to or better than the conceptual SAC-SMA model.
- **Open work:** Need to improve physical interpretability and to test networks on other basins and with additional inputs.
- **Issues:** Abstract not available; relies on knowledge of the paper. Single basin; black-box model with limited physical interpretation.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Flood Prediction Using Machine Learning Models: Literature Review](https://doi.org/10.3390/w10111536)
Mosavi et al. (2018), *Water*. 1,514 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews machine learning models for flood prediction to guide hydrologists and climate scientists in choosing suitable methods for short- and long-term flood forecasting.
- **Architecture:** Review of machine learning methods for flood prediction, including artificial neural networks (MLP), support vector machines, neuro-fuzzy systems, decision trees, wavelet-based and hybrid or ensemble models.
- **Data:** Published studies benchmarking ML flood models; no new data are used.
- **Main result:** Hybridization, data decomposition, algorithm ensembles and model optimization are reported as the most effective strategies for improving ML flood prediction; promising methods are identified for short- and long-term floods.
- **Open work:** Further development of hybrid and ensemble models and more systematic benchmarking are suggested.
- **Issues:** Qualitative comparison across studies with heterogeneous data and metrics; predates the widespread use of LSTM-based rainfall-runoff models.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Artificial Neural Networks in Hydrology. I: Preliminary Concepts](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2000)5:2(115))
Null (2000), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 1,433 citations.

- **Main goal:** Introduces artificial neural network concepts to hydrologists, as the first part of an ASCE task committee report on ANNs in hydrology.
- **Architecture:** Review and tutorial of artificial neural networks for hydrology, mainly feedforward MLP networks with backpropagation, plus other network types and training methods.
- **Data:** No new data; conceptual overview with references to hydrological applications.
- **Main result:** Sets out the basic concepts, network types and training procedures relevant to hydrological modelling.
- **Open work:** Points to the applications review in Part II and to open questions on network design and physical interpretation.
- **Issues:** Abstract not available and author list missing in metadata (ASCE Task Committee report); card relies on knowledge of the paper. Predates deep learning.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A Transdisciplinary Review of Deep Learning Research and Its Relevance for Water Resources Scientists](https://doi.org/10.1029/2018wr022643)
Shen (2017), *Water Resources Research*. 1,182 citations.

- **Main goal:** Introduces deep learning to water resources scientists and argues it can address hydrologic challenges such as scaling, equifinality, data discoverability and parameter regionalization.
- **Architecture:** Review and technical overview of deep learning (convolutional neural networks, LSTM recurrent networks, generative models) and of interpretability methods termed AI neuroscience.
- **Data:** Literature from water sciences and other physical and geoscientific disciplines; no new data.
- **Main result:** Finds that DL is especially suited to image-like and sequential data, can serve as an exploratory scientific tool, and that interpretation techniques can extract insights from trained networks.
- **Open work:** Calls for wider DL adoption in hydrology, interpretable DL, and networks that mimic physical organizing units to reveal emergent behaviour.
- **Issues:** Perspective-style review written early in hydrologic DL adoption; offers few quantitative comparisons.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Towards learning universal, regional, and local hydrological behaviors via machine learning applied to large-sample datasets](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-23-5089-2019)
Kratzert et al. (2019), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 1,021 citations.

- **Main goal:** Addresses regional rainfall-runoff modelling, where traditional models degrade when calibrated across many basins, by training one model on large-sample data.
- **Architecture:** Single LSTM recurrent neural network trained on all basins, plus the Entity-Aware LSTM (EA-LSTM) whose input gate is conditioned on static catchment attributes to learn catchment similarity.
- **Data:** 531 basins from the CAMELS dataset with meteorological forcing time series and static catchment attributes; compared against several regionally and individually calibrated hydrological benchmark models.
- **Main result:** A single regional LSTM significantly outperforms regionally calibrated and even basin-wise calibrated hydrological models; EA-LSTM embeddings yield catchment similarities consistent with hydrological understanding.
- **Open work:** Applying the approach to ungauged basins and other regions and exploiting the learned embeddings for hydrological insight.
- **Issues:** Limited to CAMELS US basins; deterministic predictions without uncertainty; no physical constraints.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Flood susceptibility mapping using a novel ensemble weights-of-evidence and support vector machine models in GIS](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2014.03.008)
Tehrany et al. (2014), *Journal of Hydrology*. 930 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps flood susceptibility to support flood risk management, combining statistical and machine learning methods.
- **Architecture:** Ensemble of weights-of-evidence (bivariate statistical model) and support vector machine within a GIS.
- **Data:** Flood inventory and GIS flood conditioning factors (topography, hydrology, land use, geology) for a study area in Malaysia; split into training and validation sets.
- **Main result:** The ensemble improves susceptibility prediction over the individual models in terms of success and prediction rate curves; exact figures not reported here.
- **Open work:** Testing in other catchments and with other ensemble combinations.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; results are site-specific and depend on inventory quality; static susceptibility, not event forecasting.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Hydrological modelling using artificial neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1177/030913330102500104)
Dawson et al. (2001), *Progress in Physical Geography: Earth and Environment*. 890 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews the use of artificial neural networks in hydrological modelling, especially rainfall-runoff and flow forecasting.
- **Architecture:** Review of artificial neural networks in hydrology, mainly multilayer perceptrons trained by backpropagation and radial basis function networks, including data preprocessing and model selection.
- **Data:** Published hydrological ANN studies; no new dataset.
- **Main result:** Finds ANNs perform well but notes a lack of standard protocols for model development and evaluation.
- **Open work:** Calls for consistent development protocols, physical interpretation and comparison with conventional models.
- **Issues:** Review; quantitative comparison across studies is limited.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Methods used for the development of neural networks for the prediction of water resource variables in river systems: Current status and future directions](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envsoft.2010.02.003)
Maier et al. (2010), *Environmental Modelling & Software*. 867 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews how neural networks for predicting water resource variables in river systems were developed, to assess progress and future directions.
- **Architecture:** Review of neural network development methods (mostly MLP feedforward networks) covering input selection, data division, architecture, calibration and validation.
- **Data:** No new data; reviews about 210 journal papers published 1999–2007 on river flow and water quality prediction.
- **Main result:** Finds most studies use MLPs, with ad hoc input selection and data division and little progress on validation and uncertainty, despite advances since 2000.
- **Open work:** Calls for better input selection methods, model validation, uncertainty quantification and a generic modelling protocol.
- **Issues:** Abstract not available; relies on knowledge of the paper, and the paper count should be spot-checked.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Comparison of the ARMA, ARIMA, and the autoregressive artificial neural network models in forecasting the monthly inflow of Dez dam reservoir](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2012.11.017)
Valipour et al. (2013), *Journal of Hydrology*. 839 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts monthly reservoir inflow to support dam operation and water resources planning.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of ARMA, ARIMA and an autoregressive artificial neural network for time series forecasting.
- **Data:** Historical monthly inflow records of the Dez dam reservoir, Iran.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the abstract here; the study ranks the linear time-series models against the autoregressive neural network for monthly inflow, with ARIMA improving on ARMA.
- **Open work:** Testing other neural and hybrid models and other reservoirs.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; single reservoir, univariate inputs, and result details should be spot-checked.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [A comparison of performance of several artificial intelligence methods for forecasting monthly discharge time series](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2009.06.019)
Wang et al. (2009), *Journal of Hydrology*. 814 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares AI methods for monthly river discharge forecasting to support hydropower reservoir management and scheduling.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of ARMA models, artificial neural networks, adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS), genetic programming and support vector machine (SVM) regression.
- **Data:** Long-term monthly river flow discharge observations at two river sites in China.
- **Main result:** ANFIS, GP and SVM give the best performance across R, Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency, RMSE and MAPE during training and validation.
- **Open work:** Combining methods or hybrid models, and testing at other sites and lead times.
- **Issues:** Only two sites and monthly scale; no single method dominates across all criteria.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A Nearest Neighbor Bootstrap For Resampling Hydrologic Time Series](https://doi.org/10.1029/95wr02966)
Lall et al. (1996), *Water Resources Research*. 806 citations.

- **Main goal:** Resamples hydrologic time series by bootstrap while preserving their dependence structure, without assuming linear dependence or Gaussian distributions.
- **Architecture:** Nonparametric k-nearest neighbour bootstrap based on multivariate nearest neighbour probability density estimation; related to Markov processes; not a neural network.
- **Data:** Monthly streamflow records and synthetic series from linear and nonlinear autoregressive models.
- **Main result:** The method reproduces the behavior of linear and nonlinear autoregressive series and handles monthly streamflow with asymmetric and bimodal marginal densities.
- **Open work:** Choice of neighbourhood size and embedding, and extension to multisite and longer-memory settings.
- **Issues:** Resampling cannot generate values outside the historical record; sensitivity to the number of neighbours and lag structure.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Application of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) Neural Network for Flood Forecasting](https://doi.org/10.3390/w11071387)
Le et al. (2019), *Water*. 797 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops an LSTM model for flood forecasting in a transboundary basin where downstream flows can change suddenly.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network using daily discharge and rainfall as inputs.
- **Data:** Daily discharge and rainfall from the Da River basin, Vietnam, before 1985 (pre Hoa Binh dam), forecasting flow at Hoa Binh station.
- **Main result:** Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency reaches 99%, 95% and 87% for one-, two- and three-day ahead forecasts.
- **Open work:** Extending to post-dam regulated conditions and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Single basin with pre-dam data; skill drops with lead time and regulation effects are not modelled.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Toward Improved Predictions in Ungauged Basins: Exploiting the Power of Machine Learning](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019wr026065)
Kratzert et al. (2019), *Water Resources Research*. 772 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether LSTMs can predict streamflow in ungauged basins, a long-standing hydrological challenge.
- **Architecture:** Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) recurrent neural networks using meteorological forcing and static catchment attributes, evaluated with k-fold cross-validation over basins.
- **Data:** 531 CAMELS basins (4-2,000 km2) with about 30 years of daily data; benchmarked against basin-calibrated SAC-SMA and the NOAA National Water Model reanalysis over a 15-year validation period.
- **Main result:** Out-of-sample LSTM median Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency is 0.69, above calibrated SAC-SMA (0.64) and the National Water Model (0.58).
- **Open work:** Adding physical constraints to LSTMs (physics-guided machine learning) is suggested as future research.
- **Issues:** Limited to US catchments with good attribute data; ungauged performance relies on informative catchment attributes; no uncertainty quantification.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Artificial neural networks as rainfall-runoff models](https://doi.org/10.1080/02626669609491511)
Minns et al. (1996), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 764 citations.

- **Main goal:** Investigates whether artificial neural networks can serve as rainfall-runoff models and learn catchment response.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural network trained by backpropagation mapping rainfall to runoff.
- **Data:** Mainly synthetic rainfall and runoff series generated from a conceptual storage model; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** ANNs can emulate rainfall-runoff behaviour well, with performance sensitive to data scaling and the range of training data.
- **Open work:** Testing on real catchment data and improving extrapolation to events outside the training range.
- **Issues:** Abstract not available; data details should be spot-checked. Synthetic data and poor extrapolation to extremes.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Flood susceptibility assessment using GIS-based support vector machine model with different kernel types](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.catena.2014.10.017)
Tehrany et al. (2015), *CATENA*. 757 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses flood susceptibility using support vector machines with different kernel functions in GIS.
- **Architecture:** Support vector machine with linear, polynomial, radial basis function and sigmoid kernels, compared with frequency ratio style approaches.
- **Data:** Flood inventory and GIS conditioning factors for a catchment in Malaysia; specific layers not reported here.
- **Main result:** Kernel choice affects susceptibility map accuracy; detailed figures not reported here.
- **Open work:** Ensemble and hybrid susceptibility models and transfer to other regions.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; site-specific results depending on inventory quality; static susceptibility only.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Flood hazard risk assessment model based on random forest](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2015.06.008)
Wang et al. (2015), *Journal of Hydrology*. 738 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses flood hazard risk spatially using machine learning to identify high-risk areas and important risk factors.
- **Architecture:** Random forest model for flood hazard risk classification, with variable importance analysis and comparison to a support vector machine.
- **Data:** Historical flood records and geospatial risk indices (e.g. rainfall, terrain, river network) for a river basin in China; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** Random forest is reported to outperform SVM for flood hazard risk assessment; exact scores not given here.
- **Open work:** Applying to other basins and adding dynamic or climate-change drivers.
- **Issues:** Abstract not available; study area and indices should be spot-checked. Static assessment depends on historical flood inventory quality.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [What Role Does Hydrological Science Play in the Age of Machine Learning?](https://doi.org/10.1029/2020wr028091)
Nearing et al. (2020), *Water Resources Research*. 721 citations.

- **Main goal:** Asks what role hydrological process understanding should play as machine learning increasingly dominates rainfall-runoff modelling.
- **Architecture:** Commentary/perspective (non-ML method) derived from a keynote; discusses deep learning (LSTM) results relative to process-based models.
- **Data:** Draws on recent deep learning rainfall-runoff experiments on large-sample datasets such as CAMELS; no new dataset.
- **Main result:** Argues large-scale hydrological datasets contain more information than current theory or models capture, and that preferences for process-based models are often not evidence-based.
- **Open work:** Calls for quantitative assessment of where and when process understanding adds value in an ML-dominated modelling discipline.
- **Issues:** Opinion piece with only preliminary examples; conclusions rest largely on streamflow prediction rather than other hydrological variables.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A comparative assessment of decision trees algorithms for flash flood susceptibility modeling at Haraz watershed, northern Iran.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2018.01.266)
Khosravi et al. (2018), *Science of The Total Environment*. 714 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps flash flood susceptibility in the Haraz watershed, Iran, to identify flood-prone areas.
- **Architecture:** Four decision-tree classifiers: logistic model trees, reduced error pruning trees, naive Bayes trees and alternating decision trees.
- **Data:** Spatial database of 201 flood locations and eleven factors (slope, altitude, curvature, SPI, TWI, land use, rainfall, river density, distance from river, lithology, NDVI).
- **Main result:** Alternating decision trees performs best, followed by NBT, LMT and REPT, based on ROC and Friedman and Wilcoxon tests.
- **Open work:** Testing in other watersheds and with ensemble or hybrid decision-tree models.
- **Issues:** Single watershed with small inventory; static susceptibility mapping.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [An ensemble prediction of flood susceptibility using multivariate discriminant analysis, classification and regression trees, and support vector machines.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2018.10.064)
Choubin et al. (2019), *Science of The Total Environment*. 705 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps flood susceptibility in the Khiyav-Chai watershed, Iran, with an ensemble of models for watershed management.
- **Architecture:** Multivariate discriminant analysis, classification and regression trees and support vector machine combined in an ensemble, admitting only models above 80% accuracy.
- **Data:** Flood inventory and conditioning factors (altitude, slope, aspect, curvature, distance from river, TWI, drainage density, soil depth, soil groups, land use, lithology).
- **Main result:** MDA reaches 89% accuracy, SVM 88% and CART 83%; slope, drainage density and distance from river are most important.
- **Open work:** Applying the accuracy-filtered ensemble framework to other watersheds and prioritizing remediation in exposed residential areas.
- **Issues:** Single watershed; static susceptibility; the abstract reports CART accuracy inconsistently.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Developing a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) based model for predicting water table depth in agricultural areas](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2018.04.065)
Zhang et al. (2018), *Journal of Hydrology*. 702 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts long-term water table depth in heterogeneous agricultural areas as a cheaper alternative to physical groundwater models.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) layer with dropout followed by a fully connected layer, compared with a feedforward neural network and a double-LSTM model.
- **Data:** Monthly water diversion, evaporation, precipitation, temperature and time for five sub-areas of Hetao Irrigation District, China; 2000–2011 training, 2012–2013 validation.
- **Main result:** LSTM reaches R2 of 0.789–0.952 versus 0.004–0.495 for FFNN and 0.170–0.864 for double-LSTM; dropout significantly reduces overfitting.
- **Open work:** Applying to other regions and data-scarce areas, and longer prediction horizons.
- **Issues:** Short 14-year record and a two-year validation period; single irrigation district.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Support vector machine applications in the field of hydrology: A review](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.asoc.2014.02.002)
Raghavendra et al. (2014), *Applied Soft Computing*. 697 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews the use of support vector machines in hydrology to summarize applications and guide future work.
- **Architecture:** Review of support vector machine (SVM) and support vector regression applications in hydrology, including hybrid variants.
- **Data:** No new data; surveys hydrological studies on rainfall-runoff, streamflow, groundwater, evaporation and related variables.
- **Main result:** Finds SVMs perform well, often comparably to or better than ANNs, in many hydrological prediction problems.
- **Open work:** Calls for better kernel and parameter selection and more hybrid approaches.
- **Issues:** Abstract not available; relies on general knowledge of the paper's scope.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [The FLUXCOM ensemble of global land-atmosphere energy fluxes](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-019-0076-8)
Jung et al. (2018), *Scientific Data*. 697 citations.

- **Main goal:** Produces global gridded land-atmosphere energy flux estimates with uncertainties to constrain land-atmosphere interactions and benchmark land models.
- **Architecture:** Ensemble of machine learning methods (including tree-based and neural network regressors) in a full factorial design across methods, forcings and energy balance corrections.
- **Data:** FLUXNET eddy covariance energy fluxes, MODIS remote sensing (0.0833°) and remote sensing plus meteorological forcing (0.5°), 2001–2013.
- **Main result:** FLUXCOM provides 147 products; global net radiation about 75–78 W m-2, sensible heat 32–36 W m-2 and latent heat about 39 W m-2.
- **Open work:** Use FLUXCOM to benchmark land surface models and study land-atmosphere interactions.
- **Issues:** Limited tower representativeness and energy balance closure issues; uncertainty only from the ensemble spread.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Applications of hybrid wavelet–Artificial Intelligence models in hydrology: A review](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2014.03.057)
Nourani et al. (2014), *Journal of Hydrology*. 690 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews hybrid models coupling wavelet transforms with artificial intelligence for hydrological forecasting.
- **Architecture:** Review of wavelet-artificial neural network, wavelet-fuzzy and related hybrid models, including choice of mother wavelet and decomposition level.
- **Data:** Literature applications to rainfall-runoff, streamflow, groundwater, sediment and precipitation modelling.
- **Main result:** Wavelet preprocessing generally improves AI models by capturing multiscale features; details not reported here.
- **Open work:** Guidance on wavelet selection and avoiding use of future information in decomposition.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; boundary effects and look-ahead leakage in wavelet preprocessing can overstate skill.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Groundwater level forecasting using artificial neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2004.12.001)
Daliakopoulos et al. (2005), *Journal of Hydrology*. 681 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts groundwater levels with artificial neural networks to support aquifer management under declining water tables.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of several neural network types, including feedforward multilayer perceptrons with different training algorithms, Elman recurrent and radial basis function networks.
- **Data:** Monthly groundwater level, precipitation, temperature and streamflow data from the Messara Valley, Crete, Greece.
- **Main result:** A feedforward network trained with Levenberg-Marquardt gives the most accurate forecasts, up to about 18 months ahead.
- **Open work:** Extending to other aquifers and including pumping data.
- **Issues:** Single aquifer, limited data length and no uncertainty quantification.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [An artificial neural network approach to rainfall-runoff modelling](https://doi.org/10.1080/02626669809492102)
Dawson et al. (1998), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 679 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests artificial neural networks as rainfall-runoff models for flood forecasting in small catchments.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer perceptron trained by backpropagation compared with a radial basis function network.
- **Data:** Rainfall and flow records at 15-minute resolution from two UK catchments (Rivers Amber and Mole).
- **Main result:** The neural networks forecast flows several hours ahead with reasonable accuracy; the multilayer perceptron generally performs better than the radial basis function network.
- **Open work:** Guidelines for input selection, network design and extrapolation to extreme floods.
- **Issues:** Two catchments only; limited ability to extrapolate beyond training range; no uncertainty.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A neuro-fuzzy computing technique for modeling hydrological time series](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2003.12.010)
Nayak et al. (2004), *Journal of Hydrology*. 676 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models hydrological time series (river flow) with a neuro-fuzzy approach for better forecasting.
- **Architecture:** Adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) compared with artificial neural network and ARMA models.
- **Data:** River flow series from the Baitarani River basin, India.
- **Main result:** ANFIS preserves flow statistics and performs comparably to or better than ANN and ARMA models.
- **Open work:** Applications to other basins and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Single basin; limited lead times.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Scaling carbon fluxes from eddy covariance sites to globe: synthesis and evaluation of the FLUXCOM approach](https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-2019-368)
Jung et al. (2019), *Biogeosciences*. 672 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates FLUXCOM machine-learning upscaling of eddy covariance carbon fluxes (GPP and NEE) from flux towers to the globe.
- **Architecture:** Ensemble of machine learning methods (e.g., random forests, neural networks, model trees, kernel methods) with different forcing data and predictor sets; evaluation study rather than a new model.
- **Data:** FLUXNET eddy covariance sites with remote sensing (MODIS) and meteorological forcing; compared with atmospheric inversions, sun-induced fluorescence (SIF) and dynamic global vegetation models.
- **Main result:** Global mean GPP is 106-130 PgC/yr; seasonal SIF agrees better with FLUXCOM (R2~0.75) than DGVMs (~0.6); NEE seasonality matches inversions (R2>0.92), but interannual NEE variability is underestimated.
- **Open work:** Exploiting more Earth observation data and machine learning concepts and improving flux tower quantity and quality, especially in the tropics.
- **Issues:** Too strong tropical carbon sink likely from eddy covariance biases and missing site history; no CO2 fertilization, so flux trends are unrealistic.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A comparative assessment of flood susceptibility modeling using Multi-Criteria Decision-Making Analysis and Machine Learning Methods](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2019.03.073)
Khosravi et al. (2019), *Journal of Hydrology*. 667 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares multi-criteria decision-making and machine learning methods for flood susceptibility in the Ningdu Catchment, China.
- **Architecture:** VIKOR, TOPSIS and SAW decision-making methods versus naive Bayes trees and naive Bayes classifiers.
- **Data:** Flood inventory and twelve conditioning factors (NDVI, lithology, land use, distance from river, curvature, altitude, STI, TWI, SPI, soil type, slope, rainfall).
- **Main result:** All models perform well (AUC above 0.95); the naive Bayes tree performs best with AUC 0.98.
- **Open work:** Testing in other catchments and with ensemble or hybrid models.
- **Issues:** Single catchment; high AUCs may reflect spatial autocorrelation in validation points.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A Brief Review of Random Forests for Water Scientists and Practitioners and Their Recent History in Water Resources](https://doi.org/10.3390/w11050910)
Tyralis et al. (2019), *Water*. 651 citations.

- **Main goal:** Popularizes random forests and their variants for water scientists and assesses how they have been used in water resources.
- **Architecture:** Review of random forest algorithms and variants (e.g. quantile regression forests), related concepts such as variable importance, and R implementations.
- **Data:** No new data; reviews published random forest applications in water resources.
- **Main result:** Finds most applications use only Breiman's original algorithm, leaving useful variants underexploited.
- **Open work:** Encourages use of random forest variants for diverse practical problems in the water sector.
- **Issues:** Descriptive review without quantitative benchmarking of methods.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A wavelet neural network conjunction model for groundwater level forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2011.06.013)
Adamowski et al. (2011), *Journal of Hydrology*. 640 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts groundwater levels by coupling wavelet decomposition with neural networks, to support groundwater resource management.
- **Architecture:** Wavelet-artificial neural network conjunction model (WA-ANN), compared with ANN and ARIMA.
- **Data:** Monthly groundwater level, precipitation and temperature data from wells in Quebec, Canada.
- **Main result:** WA-ANN gives more accurate forecasts than ANN and ARIMA; numbers not reported here.
- **Open work:** Longer forecast horizons, more wells and other aquifers.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; wavelet decomposition of the full series may leak future information and inflate skill.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [An artificial neural network model for flood simulation using GIS: Johor River Basin, Malaysia](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12665-011-1504-z)
Kia et al. (2012), *Environmental Earth Sciences*. 635 citations.

- **Main goal:** Simulates floods and maps flood-prone areas in the Johor River Basin, Malaysia.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network model coupled with GIS layers to simulate flooding; network configuration not specified here.
- **Data:** Rainfall, slope, elevation, flow accumulation, soil, land use and geology layers in GIS.
- **Main result:** The ANN produces flood-prone area maps consistent with historical floods; numbers not reported here.
- **Open work:** Application to other basins and use of finer-resolution and dynamic rainfall inputs.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; single basin; static mapping with limited validation; details should be spot-checked.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [An enhanced extreme learning machine model for river flow forecasting: State-of-the-art, practical applications in water resource engineering area and future research direction](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2018.11.069)
Yaseen et al. (2019), *Journal of Hydrology*. 624 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts river flow in a tropical river with an enhanced extreme learning machine and reviews ELM use in water resources.
- **Architecture:** Enhanced extreme learning machine using complete orthogonal decomposition to tune output weights, compared with ELM and support vector regression.
- **Data:** River flow records from the Kelantan River, peninsular Malaysia, used for training and testing the models.
- **Main result:** EELM achieves NSE 0.80 versus 0.74 (ELM) and 0.67 (SVR), with RMSE and MAE reduced by 12–23% and 8–9%.
- **Open work:** Improved ELM variants for other water resource engineering problems, as outlined in the review part.
- **Issues:** Single river; univariate setting; no uncertainty estimates.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Operating rules for multireservoir systems](https://doi.org/10.1029/96wr03745)
Oliveira et al. (1997), *Water Resources Research*. 616 citations.

- **Main goal:** Derives operating rules for multireservoir water supply systems that perform well over many hydrologic conditions.
- **Architecture:** Genetic algorithm searching parameterized release and storage-balancing rules, evaluated by simulating the reservoir system.
- **Data:** Simulated operation of example multireservoir systems driven by historical or synthetic inflow sequences.
- **Main result:** The genetic algorithm finds operating policies that improve system performance compared with initial rules.
- **Open work:** Multiple objectives, larger systems and robustness to inflow uncertainty.
- **Issues:** Computational cost of simulation-based search; rules restricted to an assumed parametric form.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Daily reservoir inflow forecasting using artificial neural networks with stopped training approach](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-1694(00)00214-6)
Coulibaly et al. (2000), *Journal of Hydrology*. 609 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts daily reservoir inflow with neural networks while avoiding overfitting.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer perceptron neural network trained with early stopping (stopped training).
- **Data:** Daily inflow and meteorological data for a hydropower reservoir in Quebec, Canada.
- **Main result:** Stopped training improves generalization and gives accurate short-range inflow forecasts.
- **Open work:** Comparing with other regularization methods and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Single reservoir; no uncertainty estimation.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Artificial Neural Networks in Hydrology](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-015-9341-0)
Govindaraju et al. (2010), *Venue not recorded*. 609 citations.

- **Main goal:** Presents applications of artificial neural networks to hydrological problems, as an alternative to conceptual and physically based models.
- **Architecture:** Book covering artificial neural networks (mainly multilayer perceptrons) for hydrological modelling.
- **Data:** Applications such as rainfall-runoff, streamflow, groundwater and water quality modelling; no single dataset.
- **Main result:** Not reported; the volume shows the potential of ANNs as hydrological modelling tools.
- **Open work:** Physical interpretability, extrapolation and generalization of neural network hydrological models remain open.
- **Issues:** Abstract and venue unavailable; the catalog year may not match the original edition; early-generation ANN work.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Short-term runoff prediction with GRU and LSTM networks without requiring time step optimization during sample generation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2020.125188)
Gao et al. (2020), *Journal of Hydrology*. 607 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts short-term runoff with recurrent networks without tuning the input time step.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent unit (GRU) networks compared with an artificial neural network.
- **Data:** Hourly discharge at one station and hourly rainfall at four stations, Yutan catchment, Fujian, China, 2000–2014.
- **Main result:** LSTM and GRU accuracy rises with time step then stabilizes; both beat ANN; GRU matches LSTM with faster training.
- **Open work:** Applying large time steps in operational runoff prediction and testing other catchments and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Single catchment with few rain gauges; short-term forecasts only; no uncertainty quantification.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A Rainfall‐Runoff Model With LSTM‐Based Sequence‐to‐Sequence Learning](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019wr025326)
Xiang et al. (2020), *Water Resources Research*. 599 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts hourly runoff for the next 24 hours to improve short-term flood forecasting.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) encoder-decoder sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) model, compared with linear, Lasso, Ridge, support vector, Gaussian process regression and plain LSTM.
- **Data:** Rainfall observations and forecasts, runoff observations and monthly evapotranspiration for Clear Creek and Upper Wapsipinicon River watersheds, Iowa.
- **Main result:** LSTM-seq2seq outperforms all baselines at all stations in NSE, correlation, bias and normalized RMSE.
- **Open work:** Use in operational short-term flood forecasting and other hydrological time-series tasks.
- **Issues:** Two watersheds only; quality depends on rainfall forecast inputs.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A comparative study of artificial neural networks and support vector machines for predicting groundwater levels in a coastal aquifer](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2010.11.002)
Yoon et al. (2011), *Journal of Hydrology*. 598 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts groundwater level fluctuations in a coastal aquifer influenced by rainfall and tides, to support groundwater management.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network and support vector machine regression models compared for time-series forecasting.
- **Data:** Groundwater level, precipitation and tide level records from monitoring wells in a coastal aquifer in Korea; period not reported here.
- **Main result:** Both models forecast groundwater levels reasonably; the support vector machine generally shows better or more robust performance than the neural network, notably for longer horizons.
- **Open work:** Testing on more wells and aquifers and adding other drivers such as pumping.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; few wells at one site; result details should be spot-checked.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [The Genetic Algorithm and Its Application to Calibrating Conceptual Rainfall-Runoff Models](https://doi.org/10.1029/91wr01305)
Wang (1991), *Water Resources Research*. 594 citations.

- **Main goal:** Calibrates conceptual rainfall-runoff model parameters automatically, avoiding local optima that trap traditional search methods.
- **Architecture:** Genetic algorithm used as a global optimizer of model parameters; non-neural method.
- **Data:** Applied to calibrate the Xinanjiang conceptual rainfall-runoff model; details of catchment data not reported here.
- **Main result:** The genetic algorithm reliably locates the global optimum of the calibration objective in repeated runs.
- **Open work:** Efficiency for higher-dimensional problems and comparison with other global optimizers.
- **Issues:** Many model evaluations are required; parameter identifiability is not addressed.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Ensemble machine learning paradigms in hydrology: A review](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2021.126266)
Zounemat‐Kermani et al. (2021), *Journal of Hydrology*. 578 citations.

- **Main goal:** Surveys how ensemble machine learning is used in hydrology to improve accuracy and robustness over single models.
- **Architecture:** Review of ensemble learning paradigms (bagging, boosting, stacking and related resampling/combination schemes) including random forest and gradient boosting, as applied to hydrological prediction.
- **Data:** Published hydrology studies covering streamflow, rainfall, floods, groundwater, sediment, evaporation and water quality; no new data.
- **Main result:** Ensemble methods generally outperform their single base learners across hydrological tasks; boosting and bagging dominate the literature.
- **Open work:** Broader use of stacking and heterogeneous ensembles, better uncertainty quantification and more interpretable ensembles for hydrology.
- **Issues:** Literature review: comparisons across studies use different data and metrics, so performance claims are not directly comparable.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A novel hybrid artificial intelligence approach for flood susceptibility assessment](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envsoft.2017.06.012)
Chapi et al. (2017), *Environmental Modelling & Software*. 578 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps flood susceptibility to support flood risk management, proposing a hybrid ensemble classifier for better spatial prediction.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid ensemble Bagging-LMT (bagging of logistic model trees), compared with logistic model tree, logistic regression, Bayesian logistic regression and random forest classifiers.
- **Data:** Flood inventory and GIS conditioning factors (topography, hydrology, land use, lithology, rainfall) for a watershed in Iran; split into training and validation sets.
- **Main result:** The Bagging-LMT ensemble gives the highest AUC and best goodness-of-fit among compared models; exact scores not reported here.
- **Open work:** Transfer the hybrid to other basins and compare with deep learning and other ensemble schemes.
- **Issues:** Single-catchment study; static susceptibility without hydrodynamics or rainfall scenarios; results depend on inventory quality.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Using support vector machines for long-term discharge prediction](https://doi.org/10.1623/hysj.51.4.599)
Lin et al. (2006), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 568 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts long-term (monthly) river discharge for reservoir and hydropower planning.
- **Architecture:** Support vector machine (SVM) regression, compared with ARMA time-series models and artificial neural networks.
- **Data:** Long-term monthly river discharge records; site details not reported here.
- **Main result:** SVM is reported to outperform ARMA and ANN for monthly discharge prediction.
- **Open work:** Improving SVM parameter selection and testing at more stations.
- **Issues:** Abstract not available; data details should be spot-checked.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Support vector regression for real-time flood stage forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2006.01.021)
Yu et al. (2006), *Journal of Hydrology*. 567 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts river flood stage in real time for flood warning.
- **Architecture:** Support vector regression (SVR) with systematic parameter calibration.
- **Data:** Hourly stage and rainfall data from typhoon events in the Lan-Yang River basin, Taiwan.
- **Main result:** SVR gives accurate flood stage forecasts for lead times of 1–6 hours.
- **Open work:** Longer lead times and use of rainfall forecasts.
- **Issues:** Limited number of events; single basin.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Input determination for neural network models in water resources applications. Part 1—background and methodology](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2004.06.021)
Bowden et al. (2005), *Journal of Hydrology*. 554 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews methods for selecting inputs to neural network models in water resources, an often neglected step.
- **Architecture:** Review and methodology for input determination: model-based and model-free approaches, including partial mutual information, self-organizing maps and genetic algorithm-general regression neural network.
- **Data:** Synthetic and literature-based examples; applications appear in Part 2.
- **Main result:** Highlights shortcomings of ad hoc input selection and presents methods that handle nonlinear dependence and redundancy.
- **Open work:** Testing the methods on real case studies, as done in the companion paper.
- **Issues:** Methodological; quantitative performance is in the companion paper.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A review of surrogate models and their application to groundwater modeling](https://doi.org/10.1002/2015wr016967)
Asher et al. (2015), *Water Resources Research*. 550 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews surrogate models that replace expensive groundwater simulations in calibration, uncertainty analysis and optimization.
- **Architecture:** Review of surrogate modelling approaches, grouped into data-driven (e.g. neural networks, Gaussian processes, polynomial chaos), projection-based reduced-order and multifidelity/hierarchical surrogates.
- **Data:** Published groundwater modelling studies; no new data.
- **Main result:** Surrogates can greatly reduce computational cost, but their suitability depends on the application, and their errors are often insufficiently characterised.
- **Open work:** Better validation and error characterisation of surrogates, adaptive sampling, and guidance on choosing surrogate types for groundwater problems.
- **Issues:** Review; surrogate accuracy outside the training range and impact on decision-relevant outputs are recurrent concerns.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Short term streamflow forecasting using artificial neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-1694(98)00242-x)
Zealand et al. (1998), *Journal of Hydrology*. 540 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts streamflow a short time ahead for hydropower and flood operations in a large river system.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward artificial neural network (multilayer perceptron) with different input configurations and hidden-layer sizes.
- **Data:** Flow, precipitation and temperature records from a basin in the Winnipeg River system, Canada.
- **Main result:** The neural networks outperform a conventional forecasting model at the tested lead times.
- **Open work:** Systematic selection of inputs and network structure, and testing in other basins.
- **Issues:** Single basin; network design by trial and error; no uncertainty estimates.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Comparison of short-term rainfall prediction models for real-time flood forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-1694(00)00344-9)
Toth et al. (2000), *Journal of Hydrology*. 538 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares short-term rainfall prediction models as inputs to real-time flood forecasting.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of ARMA models, artificial neural networks and k-nearest neighbour methods for rainfall prediction, fed to a rainfall-runoff model.
- **Data:** Rainfall and flow data from the Sieve River basin, Italy.
- **Main result:** Neural networks give the best improvement in flood forecasts relative to no rainfall prediction.
- **Open work:** Using radar or NWP information for rainfall prediction.
- **Issues:** Single basin; univariate rainfall histories only.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A Comprehensive Review of Deep Learning Applications in Hydrology and Water Resources](https://doi.org/10.31223/osf.io/xs36g)
Sit et al. (2020), *Water Science and Technology*. 532 citations.

- **Main goal:** Systematically reviews deep learning applications in hydrology and the water sector for monitoring, management, governance and communication.
- **Architecture:** Systematic review of deep learning approaches (CNNs, LSTM recurrent networks, generative adversarial networks, autoencoders and others) for generation, prediction, enhancement and classification tasks.
- **Data:** Published literature on water-related deep learning applications; no new data.
- **Main result:** Provides a guide to state-of-the-art deep learning in water resources and discusses key issues including ethics for decision-making.
- **Open work:** Gives recommendations and future directions for deep learning in hydrology and water resources.
- **Issues:** Broad scope limits depth of comparison; performance claims are not benchmarked across studies.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Deep Learning with a Long Short-Term Memory Networks Approach for Rainfall-Runoff Simulation](https://doi.org/10.3390/w10111543)
Hu et al. (2018), *Water*. 529 citations.

- **Main goal:** Simulates event-based rainfall–runoff for flood forecasting, testing whether deep learning improves on conventional neural networks and process models.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) network compared with a standard artificial neural network (ANN).
- **Data:** 98 rainfall–runoff flood events (1971–2013) in the Fen River basin, China, from 14 rain gauges and one hydrologic station; 86 events training, 12 test.
- **Main result:** Both networks beat conceptual and physically based models; LSTM outperforms ANN with R2 and NSE above 0.9 and is more stable across lead times.
- **Open work:** Testing on more basins and longer lead times for operational flood forecasting.
- **Issues:** Single basin and small test set of 12 events; no uncertainty quantification.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Estimating Evapotranspiration using Artificial Neural Network](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)0733-9437(2002)128:4(224))
Kumar et al. (2002), *Journal of Irrigation and Drainage Engineering*. 528 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates reference evapotranspiration from climate variables with a neural network.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward multilayer perceptron neural network trained by backpropagation.
- **Data:** Daily climate data (CIMIS station, Davis, California) with lysimeter or Penman-Monteith reference values.
- **Main result:** The ANN estimates evapotranspiration more accurately than conventional empirical methods.
- **Open work:** Testing with fewer inputs and in other climates.
- **Issues:** Single site; limited generalization tests.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Artificial intelligence based models for stream-flow forecasting: 2000-2015](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2015.10.038)
Yaseen et al. (2015), *Journal of Hydrology*. 511 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews artificial intelligence methods used for streamflow forecasting between 2000 and 2015 to summarize progress and guide model choice.
- **Architecture:** Review of AI-based streamflow models such as artificial neural networks, fuzzy and neuro-fuzzy systems, support vector machines, genetic programming and wavelet-hybrid models.
- **Data:** Covers published streamflow studies from 2000–2015 across many catchments; no new data.
- **Main result:** Summarizes the growth and relative performance of AI models for streamflow forecasting; detailed findings are not available in the provided metadata.
- **Open work:** Hybrid models and better input selection are typical suggested directions.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; predates deep learning models such as LSTM in hydrology.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Application of a neural network technique to rainfall-runoff modelling](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-1694(96)03330-6)
Shamseldin (1997), *Journal of Hydrology*. 510 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates neural networks for daily rainfall-runoff modelling against established black-box models.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer perceptron (feedforward neural network) with different input scenarios including rainfall indices and seasonal flow information.
- **Data:** Daily rainfall and discharge records from six catchments of different climates.
- **Main result:** The neural network generally matches or outperforms simple linear and linear perturbation models, depending on inputs used.
- **Open work:** Combination with other models and better use of input information.
- **Issues:** Black-box model with limited physical interpretability; performance varies between catchments.

### [Flood susceptibility modelling using advanced ensemble machine learning models](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gsf.2020.09.006)
Islam et al. (2020), *Geoscience Frontiers*. 506 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps flash flood susceptibility in the Teesta River basin, northern Bangladesh, to support flood risk management.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid ensembles Dagging and Random Subspace coupled with artificial neural network, random forest and support vector machine base models.
- **Data:** 413 current and former flood points and twelve flood influencing factors in a GIS for the Teesta River basin.
- **Main result:** All models have ROC AUC above 0.80; Dagging performs best, followed by RF, ANN, SVM and Random Subspace.

- **Issues:** Static susceptibility from a limited inventory; spatial autocorrelation in validation not addressed.

### [Evaluation of CatBoost method for prediction of reference evapotranspiration in humid regions](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2019.04.085)
Huang et al. (2019), *Journal of Hydrology*. 503 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates daily reference evapotranspiration with limited meteorological data in humid regions of China for irrigation and water management.
- **Architecture:** CatBoost (gradient-boosted decision trees with categorical feature support) compared with random forest and support vector machine.
- **Data:** Daily meteorological data (Rs, Tmax, Tmin, humidity, wind) from five weather stations in South China, 2001–2015, with eight input combinations; FAO-56 Penman-Monteith target.
- **Main result:** SVM is most accurate with incomplete inputs, CatBoost with complete inputs; CatBoost is faster and lighter than RF and SVM; generalized models lose under 10% in RMSE or MAPE.
- **Open work:** Test CatBoost in other humid regions worldwide.
- **Issues:** Few stations; the target is a Penman-Monteith estimate rather than measured ET; humid climates only.

### [FloodNet: A High Resolution Aerial Imagery Dataset for Post Flood Scene Understanding](https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2021.3090981)
Rahnemoonfar et al. (2020), *IEEE Access*. 503 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides high-resolution UAV imagery for post-flood damage assessment, which existing low-resolution satellite datasets cannot support.

- **Issues:** Single event and region; class imbalance between flooded and non-flooded classes may affect baselines.

### [A review of advances in flash flood forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.8040)
Hapuarachchi et al. (2011), *Hydrological Processes*. 499 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews advances in flash flood forecasting given its short lead times and high impacts.

- **Data:** Published studies and operational systems; no new data.
- **Main result:** Forecast skill is limited by rainfall estimation and quantitative precipitation forecasting; integrated systems combining remote sensing, NWP and distributed models are advancing.
- **Open work:** Improve rainfall nowcasting, data assimilation and uncertainty quantification for flash floods.
- **Issues:** Review; machine learning plays a minor role, and limitations of individual systems are summarized rather than tested.

### [Estimating soil moisture using remote sensing data: A machine learning approach](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.advwatres.2009.10.008)
Ahmad et al. (2010), *Advances in Water Resources*. 494 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates soil moisture from remote sensing data with machine learning as an alternative to physically based retrieval.
- **Architecture:** Support vector machine (support vector regression).

- **Main result:** Reports that the machine learning approach estimates soil moisture with reasonable accuracy; specific scores are not available here.
- **Open work:** Extending to other regions and sensors and comparing with in situ networks.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; target data may come from a land surface model rather than observations, inheriting its biases.

### [Extreme gradient boosting (Xgboost) model to predict the groundwater levels in Selangor Malaysia](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.asej.2020.11.011)
Osman et al. (2021), *Ain Shams Engineering Journal*. 493 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts groundwater levels in populated towns of Selangor, Malaysia, where levels are declining.

- **Issues:** Very short record; high skill relies on the previous day's groundwater level (persistence).

### [Delineation of inundated area and vegetation along the Amazon floodplain with the SIR-C synthetic aperture radar](https://doi.org/10.1109/36.406675)
Hess et al. (1995), *IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing*. 491 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps inundation extent and vegetation type on the Amazon floodplain, important for wetland hydrology and methane studies.

- **Issues:** Limited image dates and ground truth; thresholds specific to sensor and site.

Karunanithi et al. (1994), *Journal of Computing in Civil Engineering*. 487 citations.

### [Evaluation of SVM, ELM and four tree-based ensemble models for predicting daily reference evapotranspiration using limited meteorological data in different climates of China](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agrformet.2018.08.019)
Fan et al. (2018), *Agricultural and Forest Meteorology*. 477 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates daily reference evapotranspiration with limited meteorological data across different climates of China.

Chen et al. (2019), *Science of The Total Environment*. 472 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares data-driven methods for flood susceptibility mapping in the Quannan area, China.

Feng et al. (2019), *Water Resources Research*. 468 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves daily streamflow forecasts by integrating recent discharge observations of varied types into an LSTM model at continental scale.

Campolo et al. (1999), *Water Resources Research*. 468 citations.

Adamowski et al. (2012), *Water Resources Research*. 468 citations.

### [Rainfall-Runoff Modeling Using Artificial Neural Networks](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(1999)4:3(232))
Tokar et al. (1999), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 467 citations.

Ma et al. (2021), *Journal of Hydrology*. 467 citations.

Kim et al. (2003), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 456 citations.

### [Review of Machine Learning Approaches for Biomass and Soil Moisture Retrievals from Remote Sensing Data](https://doi.org/10.3390/rs71215841)
Ali et al. (2015), *Remote Sensing*. 453 citations.
