- **Architecture:** Review of machine learning retrieval approaches for remote sensing, covering methods such as artificial neural networks, support vector regression and other non-linear regressors applied to biomass and soil moisture.
- **Data:** Literature on airborne and spaceborne optical, radar and microwave observations plus ground measurements, with attention to the Sentinel satellite family.
- **Main result:** Machine learning methods are flexible, handle many inputs and non-linear relations, and are well suited to exploit the growing Sentinel data volume for biomass and soil moisture retrieval.
- **Open work:** Exploiting dense Sentinel time series, multi-sensor fusion and better ground reference data for training and validation of retrieval models.
- **Issues:** Qualitative review without a quantitative benchmark; retrievals depend on sparse, heterogeneous in situ reference data and may transfer poorly across regions.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Differentiable modelling to unify machine learning and physical models for geosciences](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43017-023-00450-9)
Shen et al. (2023), *Nature Reviews Earth & Environment*. 450 citations.

- **Main goal:** Proposes differentiable modelling as a way to unify process-based models and machine learning in the geosciences, combining interpretability with data-driven skill.
- **Architecture:** Perspective on differentiable modelling: physics-based models implemented in differentiable form and coupled with neural networks (e.g., LSTM or MLP) for parameter learning and process representation; physics-informed machine learning.
- **Data:** Examples drawn from hydrological modelling, e.g., large-sample streamflow datasets such as CAMELS; no single new dataset.
- **Main result:** Differentiable models achieve accuracy similar to pure ML with less data, better interpretability and extrapolation, and outperform ML under data scarcity for dynamics and decadal trends.
- **Open work:** Address computational challenges, reduce uncertainty and verify the physical significance of learned outputs.
- **Issues:** Perspective with examples mostly from hydrology; computational cost and physical validation remain open.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Application of Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, and Genetic Algorithm Optimized Random Forest Models in Groundwater Potential Mapping](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11269-017-1660-3)
Naghibi et al. (2017), *Water Resources Management*. 446 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps groundwater potential to guide water resource exploration and management in a data-scarce region of Iran.
- **Architecture:** Compares support vector machine, random forest and a random forest whose parameters are optimized by a genetic algorithm, trained on spring locations and conditioning factors.
- **Data:** Spring occurrence inventory and GIS-derived topographic, hydrological, geological and land use conditioning factors for a watershed in Iran; exact factors not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** All models produce usable potential maps; the genetic-algorithm-optimized random forest gives the best ROC-based performance in the comparison.
- **Open work:** Testing in other hydrogeological settings and adding further optimizers or ensemble learners.
- **Issues:** Single study area; spring locations are an indirect proxy for groundwater potential; validation relies on AUC of a held-out inventory.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Global prediction of extreme floods in ungauged watersheds](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07145-1)
Nearing et al. (2024), *Nature*. 441 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides reliable flood warnings for extreme riverine events in ungauged watersheds worldwide, where gauge networks are sparse.
- **Architecture:** LSTM-based recurrent neural network (encoder-decoder hindcast/forecast LSTMs) trained across thousands of gauged basins and applied to ungauged basins.
- **Data:** Global streamflow gauge records (e.g., GRDC/Caravan) with meteorological reanalysis and forecast forcings (e.g., ERA5-Land, IFS HRES) and catchment attributes; benchmarked against GloFAS.
- **Main result:** AI forecasts at up to five-day lead time are as reliable as or better than GloFAS nowcasts, and skill for five-year return-period events matches GloFAS skill for one-year events.
- **Open work:** Increasing availability of hydrological data to further improve global flood warnings; model is operational in over 80 countries.
- **Issues:** Performance depends on sparse gauge data, especially in data-poor regions; extreme events remain few for evaluation.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Predictive models for forecasting hourly urban water demand](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2010.04.005)
Herrera et al. (2010), *Journal of Hydrology*. 440 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts hourly urban water demand to support operation of water supply networks.
- **Architecture:** Compares artificial neural networks, projection pursuit regression, multivariate adaptive regression splines, random forest and support vector regression, plus a naive baseline.
- **Data:** Hourly water demand and associated weather and calendar variables for a city in southeastern Spain.
- **Main result:** Support vector regression gives the most accurate hourly forecasts, followed by MARS, projection pursuit regression and random forest.
- **Open work:** Testing on other networks and longer horizons, and adding uncertainty estimates.
- **Issues:** Single city; short-horizon deterministic forecasts only; limited set of predictors.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Long-term SPI drought forecasting in the Awash River Basin in Ethiopia using wavelet neural network and wavelet support vector regression models](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2013.10.052)
Belayneh et al. (2014), *Journal of Hydrology*. 437 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts long-term drought, expressed by the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), in the Awash River Basin, Ethiopia, to support drought preparedness.
- **Architecture:** Wavelet neural network (wavelet transform plus artificial neural network) and wavelet support vector regression, compared with ARIMA, ANN and SVR.
- **Data:** SPI time series (e.g. SPI 12 and SPI 24) derived from rain gauge records in the Awash River Basin.
- **Main result:** Wavelet-coupled models, especially the wavelet neural network, forecast long-term SPI better than the non-wavelet models.
- **Open work:** Testing other lead times, basins and drought indices.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; wavelet decomposition can leak future information if applied to the whole series.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Flood susceptibility mapping using novel ensembles of adaptive neuro fuzzy inference system and metaheuristic algorithms.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2017.09.262)
Razavi-Termeh et al. (2018), *Science of The Total Environment*. 437 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps flood susceptibility for flood risk management using hybrid neuro-fuzzy models.
- **Architecture:** Adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) combined in ensembles with metaheuristic optimization algorithms that tune its parameters.
- **Data:** Flood inventory and GIS-derived conditioning factors for a study area in Iran; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** The metaheuristic-optimized ANFIS ensembles produce accurate susceptibility maps and improve on the standalone model in ROC-based validation; exact values not reported here.
- **Open work:** Transfer to other catchments and comparison with deep learning and ensemble tree methods.
- **Issues:** Single region; static susceptibility without flood dynamics or rainfall forcing; inventory quality limits validation.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Flood susceptibility analysis and its verification using a novel ensemble support vector machine and frequency ratio method](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00477-015-1021-9)
Tehrany et al. (2015), *Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment*. 436 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves flood susceptibility mapping by combining a statistical weighting method with a kernel machine.
- **Architecture:** Ensemble of frequency ratio (bivariate statistics) and support vector machine classification with tested kernel types.
- **Data:** Flood inventory and GIS conditioning factors (topography, hydrology, geology, land use) for a flood-prone region in Malaysia.
- **Main result:** The FR–SVM ensemble yields higher success and prediction rates than standalone models; exact rates not reported here.
- **Open work:** Applying the ensemble to other regions and adding dynamic triggering factors.
- **Issues:** Single study area; static susceptibility only; dependent on inventory completeness.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A data‐driven algorithm for constructing artificial neural network rainfall‐runoff models](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.554)
Sudheer et al. (2002), *Hydrological Processes*. 435 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides a systematic, data-driven way to choose inputs when building neural network rainfall-runoff models, instead of trial and error.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (feedforward MLP) rainfall-runoff model with input selection based on statistical cross-, auto- and partial autocorrelation analysis.
- **Data:** Rainfall and runoff records from a river basin in India; specific periods not reported here.
- **Main result:** The statistically guided input selection yields parsimonious networks with accurate runoff simulation compared with ad hoc input choices.
- **Open work:** Testing in other basins and incorporating nonlinear dependence measures for input selection.
- **Issues:** Linear correlation measures may miss nonlinear relationships; single case study.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Light Gradient Boosting Machine: An efficient soft computing model for estimating daily reference evapotranspiration with local and external meteorological data](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agwat.2019.105758)
Fan et al. (2019), *Agricultural Water Management*. 427 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates daily reference evapotranspiration when meteorological data at the target station are incomplete or short.
- **Architecture:** Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM, gradient boosting trees) compared with M5 model tree, random forest and four empirical equations.
- **Data:** Daily Tmax, Tmin, humidity, wind speed and radiation from 49 stations in humid subtropical China (16 in Jiangxi), 2001–2015, in eight input combinations.
- **Main result:** LightGBM beats M5Tree and RF locally (RMSE 0.08–0.58 vs 0.11–0.62 and 0.13–0.60 mm/d) and in cross-station use; all ML models beat empirical equations; Rs is the most influential input.
- **Open work:** Testing in other climates and with remote sensing or reanalysis inputs.
- **Issues:** Targets are FAO-56 Penman-Monteith estimates, not lysimeter measurements; one climatic region.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Soil moisture mapping using Sentinel-1 images: Algorithm and preliminary validation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2013.02.027)
Paloscia et al. (2013), *Remote Sensing of Environment*. 426 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops and tests a soil moisture retrieval algorithm for the Sentinel-1 SAR mission ahead of launch.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network retrieval trained on simulated backscatter from an electromagnetic surface scattering model, then applied to SAR images.
- **Data:** Model-simulated backscatter for training; validation with SAR images from precursor C-band missions (such as ENVISAT ASAR) and ground soil moisture measurements at test sites.
- **Main result:** The ANN algorithm retrieves soil moisture with accuracy suited to Sentinel-1 product requirements in preliminary validation; exact errors not reported here.
- **Open work:** Validation with real Sentinel-1 data, vegetation correction and operational high-resolution products.
- **Issues:** Preliminary validation on precursor data; vegetated and rough surfaces challenge retrieval; training relies on model simulations.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Deep Learning Methods for Flood Mapping: A Review of Existing Applications and Future Research Directions](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-2021-614)
Bentivoglio et al. (2021), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 424 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews deep learning for flood mapping to identify the state of the art, knowledge gaps and future directions.
- **Architecture:** Review of 45 publications on deep learning for flood susceptibility, inundation and hazard mapping.
- **Data:** Reviewed studies use varied data, including hydraulic model outputs, remote sensing and topography; no new data.
- **Main result:** Convolutional models are usually more accurate; deep learning is more accurate than traditional methods and faster than numerical models, but all reviewed models are deterministic.
- **Open work:** Graph neural networks and neural operators for generalization, real-time warning and flood risk, and Deep Gaussian Processes for probabilistic prediction.
- **Issues:** Generalization to unseen sites and uncertainty quantification are largely missing in the field.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Widespread increasing vegetation sensitivity to soil moisture](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-31667-9)
Li et al. (2022), *Nature Communications*. 423 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses long-term changes in global vegetation sensitivity to soil moisture and whether land surface models capture them.
- **Architecture:** Explainable machine learning with feature attribution relating leaf area index anomalies to hydro-climate anomalies; the model type is not specified in the abstract.
- **Data:** Observation-based leaf area index and hydro-climate anomaly data, 1982–2017, compared with state-of-the-art land surface model (TRENDY-type) simulations.
- **Main result:** LAI sensitivity to soil moisture increases significantly across many semi-arid and arid regions, strongest where precipitation declines; land surface models do not reproduce the trend.
- **Open work:** Improving land surface model representation of water-limited vegetation and assessing carbon-uptake consequences under future drought.
- **Issues:** Relies on satellite LAI and soil moisture products with their own errors; sensitivities are statistical attributions, not causal.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Development of a coupled wavelet transform and neural network method for flow forecasting of non-perennial rivers in semi-arid watersheds.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2010.06.033)
Adamowski et al. (2010), *Journal of Hydrology*. 418 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts streamflow in non-perennial rivers of semi-arid watersheds, where intermittent flow challenges standard models.
- **Architecture:** Coupled wavelet transform and artificial neural network (WA-ANN) compared with a standalone ANN.
- **Data:** Daily flow records from two non-perennial rivers in semi-arid watersheds of Cyprus.
- **Main result:** WA-ANN forecasts 1 and 3 days ahead more accurately than the standalone ANN.
- **Open work:** Longer lead times, other climates and inclusion of rainfall inputs.
- **Issues:** Two rivers only; wavelet preprocessing can introduce boundary effects or leakage.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Ensemble machine-learning-based geospatial approach for flood risk assessment using multi-sensor remote-sensing data and GIS](https://doi.org/10.1080/19475705.2017.1294113)
Mojaddadi et al. (2017), *Geomatics, Natural Hazards and Risk*. 417 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses flood probability, hazard and risk for a Malaysian catchment to support flood risk management.
- **Architecture:** Ensemble of frequency ratio weighting with a support vector machine (RBF kernel), combined with a 2D high-resolution sub-grid hydraulic model for inundation depth.
- **Data:** Thirteen conditioning factors from multi-sensor remote sensing and GIS (topography indices, distance to river, geology, soil, runoff, LULC) plus rainfall for the Damansara River catchment.
- **Main result:** The approach produces flood probability, hazard and risk maps judged effective for flood management along the expressway and replicable elsewhere.
- **Open work:** Validation with more flood events and application in other catchments.
- **Issues:** Single catchment; quantitative accuracy not reported in the abstract; vulnerability weights are subjective.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Predicting monthly streamflow using data‐driven models coupled with data‐preprocessing techniques](https://doi.org/10.1029/2007wr006737)
Wu et al. (2009), *Water Resources Research*. 414 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves monthly streamflow prediction by coupling data-driven models with data-preprocessing techniques.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of ARMA, k-nearest neighbour (KNN) and artificial neural network models, coupled with moving average, singular spectrum analysis and wavelet multiresolution preprocessing.
- **Data:** Monthly streamflow series from several catchments in China.
- **Main result:** Data preprocessing improves forecasts substantially, with the neural network combined with moving average preprocessing performing best.
- **Open work:** Assessing other preprocessing methods and the practical lag introduced by smoothing.
- **Issues:** Preprocessing with centred filters can leak future information and introduce lags; limited sites.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Drought and flood monitoring for a large karst plateau in Southwest China using extended GRACE data](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2014.08.006)
Long et al. (2014), *Remote Sensing of Environment*. 403 citations.

- **Main goal:** Monitors drought and flood over the Yunnan-Guizhou karst plateau in Southwest China using terrestrial water storage beyond the GRACE record.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network used to extend GRACE terrestrial water storage anomalies from hydro-climatic predictors.
- **Data:** GRACE terrestrial water storage, precipitation, temperature and other hydro-climate data over the karst plateau.
- **Main result:** Extended GRACE data capture the severe 2009–2010 drought and flood events in the region.
- **Open work:** Applying the reconstruction to other regions and longer periods, and merging with hydrological models.
- **Issues:** Reconstruction outside the GRACE period depends on predictor relationships staying stable; coarse GRACE resolution.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Artificial neural network modeling of water table depth fluctuations](https://doi.org/10.1029/2000wr900368)
Coulibaly et al. (2001), *Water Resources Research*. 401 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models and forecasts water table depth fluctuations in an aquifer to support groundwater management in a data-scarce region.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of input delay neural networks, recurrent neural networks and radial basis function networks.
- **Data:** Water table depth, precipitation and temperature records from the Gondo aquifer, Burkina Faso.
- **Main result:** Neural networks reproduce water table fluctuations well, with the recurrent network giving the most accurate forecasts.
- **Open work:** Testing longer horizons and other aquifers, and including pumping information.
- **Issues:** Short records from one aquifer; no uncertainty estimates.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Model trees as an alternative to neural networks in rainfall—runoff modelling](https://doi.org/10.1623/hysj.48.3.399.45291)
Solomatine et al. (2003), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 396 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests model trees as an interpretable alternative to neural networks for rainfall-runoff forecasting.
- **Architecture:** M5 model trees (piecewise linear regression trees) compared with artificial neural networks (MLP).
- **Data:** Hourly rainfall and discharge data from the Sieve catchment, Italy, with forecasts several hours ahead.
- **Main result:** Model trees achieve accuracy similar to neural networks while being faster to train and more transparent.
- **Open work:** Testing on other catchments and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Single catchment; performance degrades for longer horizons as for ANNs.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Process‐Guided Deep Learning Predictions of Lake Water Temperature](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019wr024922)
Read et al. (2019), *Water Resources Research*. 394 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts depth-specific lake water temperature with a hybrid model that integrates physical theory with deep learning.
- **Architecture:** Process-Guided Deep Learning (PGDL): LSTM recurrent neural network with an energy-conservation penalty in the loss and pretraining on outputs of a process-based lake model.
- **Data:** In situ lake temperature observations and process-based (General Lake Model) simulations for two detailed study lakes and 68 additional lakes.
- **Main result:** PGDL beats DL and process-based models; across 68 lakes median test RMSE is 1.65 °C versus 1.78 °C (DL) and 2.03 °C (PB).
- **Open work:** Applying process-guided deep learning to other environmental variables and larger lake populations.
- **Issues:** Gains depend on pretraining data having more variability than the training period; in some lakes PB or DL is more accurate.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Artificial neural network simulation of hourly groundwater levels in a coastal aquifer system of the Venice lagoon](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.engappai.2012.02.009)
Taormina et al. (2012), *Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence*. 391 citations.

- **Main goal:** Simulates hourly groundwater levels in a coastal aquifer near the Venice lagoon.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward artificial neural network (MLP) driven by external forcings to simulate groundwater levels over long periods.
- **Data:** Hourly groundwater levels, rainfall and evapotranspiration records for the coastal aquifer system of the Venice lagoon.
- **Main result:** The ANN reproduces hourly groundwater level dynamics accurately in long-term simulation, not only one-step prediction.
- **Open work:** Applying to other aquifers and including more drivers.
- **Issues:** Single site; extrapolation outside training conditions is uncertain.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A review of the artificial intelligence methods in groundwater level modeling](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2018.12.037)
Rajaee et al. (2019), *Journal of Hydrology*. 386 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews artificial intelligence methods for groundwater level modelling and forecasting to provide practical guidelines.
- **Architecture:** Review of 67 papers (2001–2018) on AI methods such as artificial neural networks, neuro-fuzzy, support vector machines and hybrid models for groundwater level.
- **Data:** Reviewed studies on groundwater level time series in various aquifers; no new data.
- **Main result:** Properly developed AI methods can simulate and forecast groundwater level, though many modelling steps rely on trial and error.
- **Open work:** Proposes new ideas for innovative methods and improved modelling quality.
- **Issues:** Qualitative synthesis; predates widespread deep learning use.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Streamflow Forecasting Using Different Artificial Neural Network Algorithms](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2007)12:5(532))
Kisi (2007), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 383 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts streamflow with artificial neural networks and compares different network training algorithms.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural networks trained with different algorithms; the network family beyond ANN is not specified in the available metadata.
- **Data:** Streamflow time series; the river and period are not reported in the available metadata.
- **Main result:** Compares forecast skill across training algorithms; specific results are not available here.
- **Open work:** Testing on other basins and with additional inputs.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; single-variable time series forecasting.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Application of fuzzy weight of evidence and data mining techniques in construction of flood susceptibility map of Poyang County, China.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2017.12.256)
Hong et al. (2018), *Science of The Total Environment*. 383 citations.

- **Main goal:** Builds a flood susceptibility map for Poyang County, China, to support flood mitigation and preparedness.
- **Architecture:** Fuzzy weight of evidence used to delineate non-flood areas and weight factors, combined with logistic regression, random forest and support vector machine classifiers.
- **Data:** Flood inventory for Poyang County with eleven conditioning factors (lithology, soil, elevation, slope, aspect, TWI, SPI, STI, curvatures, distance to rivers).
- **Main result:** Fuzzy WofE-SVM performs best (AUC 0.9865), significantly above fuzzy WofE-RF (0.9756) and fuzzy WofE-LR (0.9652).
- **Open work:** Testing transferability to other basins and adding dynamic rainfall drivers.
- **Issues:** Single small study area; very high AUCs may reflect spatial autocorrelation between training and test points; static susceptibility only.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Urban Water Demand Forecasting: Review of Methods and Models](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)wr.1943-5452.0000314)
Donkor et al. (2014), *Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management*. 381 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews methods and models for forecasting urban water demand, to guide utilities in choosing forecasting approaches.
- **Architecture:** Review of urban water demand forecasting literature, spanning regression, time-series, artificial neural network and other soft-computing and hybrid methods.
- **Data:** Published urban water demand forecasting studies; no new data.
- **Main result:** Categorizes studies by forecast horizon and method; specific quantitative conclusions are not reported here.
- **Open work:** Better treatment of forecast uncertainty and of the link between forecast horizon and planning decisions.
- **Issues:** Abstract not available; card based on title and general knowledge; review predates recent deep learning work.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Urban flood risk mapping using the GARP and QUEST models: A comparative study of machine learning techniques](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2018.12.002)
Darabi et al. (2019), *Journal of Hydrology*. 378 citations.

- **Main goal:** Produces an urban flood risk map for Sari, Iran, with limited hydrological and hydraulic data.
- **Architecture:** Genetic Algorithm Rule-Set Production (GARP) and Quick Unbiased Efficient Statistical Tree (QUEST, a decision tree) for hazard, with Fuzzy Analytical Network Process weighting for vulnerability.
- **Data:** 113 flooded points from reports and field surveys; hazard factors (precipitation, slope, curve number, distances, groundwater depth, land use, elevation) and socio-economic vulnerability factors.
- **Main result:** GARP (AUC-ROC 93.5%, Kappa 0.86) outperforms QUEST (89.2%, 0.79); distance to channel, land use and elevation dominate hazard.
- **Open work:** Coupling with hydraulic modelling where data allow and testing in other cities.
- **Issues:** Small inventory of 113 points in one city; vulnerability weights rely on expert judgement.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Interpretable spatio-temporal attention LSTM model for flood forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2020.04.110)
Ding et al. (2020), *Neurocomputing*. 377 citations.

- **Main goal:** Builds an accurate and interpretable deep learning flood forecasting model, addressing low robustness of hydrological models and opacity of ML.
- **Architecture:** Spatio-temporal attention long short-term memory (STA-LSTM) network with dynamic spatial and temporal attention, trained with Adam.
- **Data:** Hydrological data from three small and medium basins in China.
- **Main result:** STA-LSTM outperforms HA, FCN, CNN, GCN, LSTM, SA-LSTM and TA-LSTM in most cases, and attention weights are physically reasonable.
- **Open work:** Testing on larger basins and more systematic interpretability evaluation.
- **Issues:** Attention weights are a limited form of interpretation; only three basins.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Drought forecasting using feed-forward recursive neural network](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2006.04.017)
Mishra et al. (2006), *Ecological Modelling*. 377 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts drought, measured by the Standardized Precipitation Index, at several lead times to aid drought planning.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward neural networks applied with recursive multistep and direct multistep forecasting strategies.
- **Data:** SPI series from a river basin in India (Kansabati basin); details should be checked.
- **Main result:** Neural network approaches give useful drought forecasts, with differences between recursive and direct strategies by lead time; numbers not available here.
- **Open work:** Hybrid stochastic–neural models and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; single-basin study.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Improved weighting methods, deterministic and stochastic data-driven models for estimation of missing precipitation records](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2005.02.015)
Teegavarapu et al. (2005), *Journal of Hydrology*. 375 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates missing daily precipitation records at rain gauges, a common gap-filling problem for hydrological analysis.
- **Architecture:** Compares improved inverse-distance and correlation-based weighting schemes with data-driven models, including an artificial neural network (MLP) and kriging-type stochastic interpolation.
- **Data:** Long-term daily precipitation records from a rain gauge network in Kentucky, USA.
- **Main result:** Modified weighting methods and the neural network improve on the classical inverse distance weighting method for filling missing records.
- **Open work:** Testing in other climates and gauge densities and handling of dry/wet day classification remain open.
- **Issues:** Single regional gauge network; performance depends on correlation between neighbouring stations and may degrade for extremes.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Application of ANN for Reservoir Inflow Prediction and Operation](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)0733-9496(1999)125:5(263))
Jain et al. (1999), *Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management*. 371 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts reservoir inflow and derives operating rules to improve reservoir management.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward artificial neural network (multilayer perceptron) for inflow forecasting and for releases, compared with time series models.
- **Data:** Inflow and operation records of the Indravati reservoir, India.
- **Main result:** The neural network forecasts inflows better than conventional time series models, notably for high flows, and helps model operation rules.
- **Open work:** Integration with optimization and broader validation.
- **Issues:** Single reservoir; network design by trial and error.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Multi-criteria calibration of a conceptual runoff model using a genetic algorithm](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-4-215-2000)
Seibert (2000), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 371 citations.

- **Main goal:** Calibrates a conceptual runoff model against several output variables to obtain reliable simulations of internal catchment processes and reduce parameter uncertainty.
- **Architecture:** Non-ML optimisation: a genetic algorithm combined with local optimisation for automatic single- and multi-criteria calibration of the HBV conceptual runoff model.
- **Data:** Observed runoff and groundwater level time series in two catchments with different geology, plus a synthetic error-free test case.
- **Main result:** The algorithm usually recovers true parameters in the synthetic case; calibrating on runoff and groundwater levels together constrains parameters much more than runoff alone, and motivated a model-structure change in one catchment.
- **Open work:** Extending multi-criteria calibration to other internal variables and catchments, and refining model structure where calibration reveals inconsistencies.
- **Issues:** Only two catchments; parameter equifinality remains when only runoff is used; groundwater data are point measurements compared with a lumped storage.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A novel deep learning neural network approach for predicting flash flood susceptibility: A case study at a high frequency tropical storm area.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2019.134413)
Bui et al. (2019), *Science of The Total Environment*. 371 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps flash flood susceptibility in a high-frequency tropical storm area of northwest Vietnam to aid mitigation and land-use planning.
- **Architecture:** Deep learning neural network (MLP with 3 hidden layers, 192 neurons, ReLU, Adam) with information-gain-ratio feature selection in a GIS framework.
- **Data:** GIS database of elevation, slope, curvature, aspect, stream density, NDVI, soil type, lithology and rainfall with flash flood locations.
- **Main result:** Classification accuracy 92.05%, positive predictive value 94.55%, negative predictive value 89.55%, better than a shallow MLP and SVM.
- **Open work:** Transferability to other regions and dynamic rainfall-triggered susceptibility.
- **Issues:** Single region; static factors; spatial autocorrelation between training and validation points may inflate accuracy.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Statistical downscaling of GCM simulations to streamflow using relevance vector machine](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.advwatres.2007.07.005)
Ghosh et al. (2008), *Advances in Water Resources*. 370 citations.

- **Main goal:** Downscales general circulation model simulations to basin-scale streamflow to assess climate change impacts on hydrology.
- **Architecture:** Relevance vector machine (sparse Bayesian kernel regression), with PCA and fuzzy clustering of predictors, compared with a support vector machine.
- **Data:** Reanalysis predictors for training and CGCM2 GCM simulations, with observed streamflow of the Mahanadi River, India.
- **Main result:** The relevance vector machine performs comparably or better than SVM with fewer relevance vectors and projects decreasing streamflow in the basin.
- **Open work:** Multi-GCM uncertainty and other basins.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; single GCM and basin, stationarity assumption of downscaling.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [PRECIPITATION-RUNOFF MODELING USING ARTIFICIAL NEURAL NETWORKS AND CONCEPTUAL MODELS](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2000)5:2(156))
Tokar et al. (2000), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 365 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses whether artificial neural networks can model precipitation-runoff as well as conceptual hydrological models.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward artificial neural network (MLP) compared with conceptual rainfall-runoff models such as the Sacramento soil moisture accounting model.
- **Data:** Precipitation, temperature and streamflow records from three US watersheds (Fraser River, Colorado; Raccoon Creek, Iowa; Little Patuxent River, Maryland).
- **Main result:** The neural networks give comparable or better runoff simulations than the conceptual models.
- **Open work:** Combining physical understanding with neural networks and testing generalisation to other basins.
- **Issues:** Black-box model with limited physical interpretability; performance on extremes and outside the training range is uncertain.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Prediction of rainfall time series using modular artificial neural networks coupled with data-preprocessing techniques](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2010.05.040)
Wu et al. (2010), *Journal of Hydrology*. 365 citations.

- **Main goal:** Seeks an optimal data-driven model for monthly and daily rainfall forecasting by studying inputs, methods and preprocessing.
- **Architecture:** Modular artificial neural network (MANN) compared with ANN, K-nearest neighbours and linear regression, coupled with moving average, PCA or singular spectrum analysis preprocessing.
- **Data:** Four rainfall records from different regions: two monthly and two daily series.
- **Main result:** SSA preprocessing gives considerable gains while MA and PCA give slight gains; MANN coupled with SSA is best, especially for daily rainfall.
- **Open work:** Testing at more stations and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Single-step forecasts on few series; SSA applied to whole series can leak future information if not done carefully.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Groundwater Level Forecasting in a Shallow Aquifer Using Artificial Neural Network Approach](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11269-006-4007-z)
Nayak et al. (2006), *Water Resources Management*. 363 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts groundwater levels in a shallow unconfined aquifer to support water management.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward artificial neural network (MLP) trained with backpropagation, using past groundwater levels, rainfall and canal releases as inputs.
- **Data:** Observation-well groundwater levels with rainfall and canal release data from the Central Godavari Delta, Andhra Pradesh, India.
- **Main result:** The neural network forecasts groundwater levels with reasonable accuracy up to several months ahead.
- **Open work:** Extending to more wells, spatial forecasting and coupling with physically based groundwater models.
- **Issues:** Site-specific wells; data-driven model cannot represent aquifer physics or changing pumping regimes.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Rainfall–runoff modeling using artificial neural network coupled with singular spectrum analysis](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2011.01.017)
Wu et al. (2011), *Journal of Hydrology*. 363 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves rainfall-runoff modelling with data-driven methods by addressing lag effects in predictions.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (MLP) coupled with singular spectrum analysis of rainfall inputs, compared with plain ANN and linear regression.
- **Data:** Daily rainfall-runoff records from Chinese watersheds; exact catchments not reported here.
- **Main result:** SSA preprocessing substantially improves ANN performance and reduces the lag between predicted and observed flows.
- **Open work:** Multi-step forecasting and more catchments.
- **Issues:** Abstract not available; SSA decomposition on full records can leak future information.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Flood susceptibility mapping with machine learning, multi-criteria decision analysis and ensemble using Dempster Shafer Theory](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2020.125275)
Nachappa et al. (2020), *Journal of Hydrology*. 361 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps flood susceptibility for Salzburg, Austria, comparing multi-criteria decision analysis and machine learning.
- **Architecture:** Random forest and support vector machine versus AHP and ANP, with Dempster Shafer Theory ensembling.
- **Data:** Flood inventory and eleven conditioning factors including elevation, slope, TWI, SPI, NDVI, geology, rainfall and land cover.
- **Main result:** RF (AUC 87.8%) and SVM (87%) beat ANP (86.6%) and AHP (85.9%); DST raises accuracy; ensemble of all four reaches 89.3%.
- **Open work:** Transfer to other regions and dynamic factors.
- **Issues:** Small differences between models; single region; static susceptibility.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Assessment of input variables determination on the SVM model performance using PCA, Gamma test, and forward selection techniques for monthly stream flow prediction](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2011.02.021)
Noori et al. (2011), *Journal of Hydrology*. 360 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses how input-variable selection affects support vector machine performance for monthly streamflow prediction.
- **Architecture:** Support vector machine regression with inputs chosen by principal component analysis, Gamma test or forward selection.
- **Data:** Monthly streamflow and related hydrological records from a river in Iran; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** Input preselection reduces inputs and improves SVM performance over using all inputs; specific numbers not available here.
- **Open work:** Comparison with other learners and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Abstract not available; single basin; card relies on title and general knowledge.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Exploring a Long Short-Term Memory based Encoder-Decoder framework for multi-step-ahead flood forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2020.124631)
Kao et al. (2020), *Journal of Hydrology*. 360 citations.

- **Main goal:** Produces multi-step-ahead reservoir inflow forecasts for operational flood control.
- **Architecture:** LSTM-based encoder-decoder (LSTM-ED) compared with a feed-forward neural network encoder-decoder.
- **Data:** 12,216 hourly records from 23 typhoon events at Shihmen Reservoir, Taiwan; rainfall from ten gauges and inflow.
- **Main result:** LSTM-ED gives more reliable and accurate 1–6 h forecasts than FFNN-ED and captures rainfall-runoff dependence.
- **Open work:** Longer lead times and use of forecast rainfall.
- **Issues:** Single catchment and limited events; observed rainfall inputs only.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A Multivariate ANN-Wavelet Approach for Rainfall–Runoff Modeling](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11269-009-9414-5)
Nourani et al. (2009), *Water Resources Management*. 356 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves rainfall-runoff modelling by capturing multiscale features of the input time series.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid wavelet-ANN: discrete wavelet transform decomposes rainfall and runoff series into subseries that feed a multivariate artificial neural network (MLP).
- **Data:** Rainfall and runoff records from the Ligvanchai watershed near Tabriz, Iran.
- **Main result:** The wavelet-ANN model outperforms a plain neural network and a linear ARIMAX-type model, especially for peak flows.
- **Open work:** Choice of wavelet type and decomposition level and extension to other catchments.
- **Issues:** Single small watershed; wavelet decomposition can leak future information if not applied causally; extremes are few.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Identifying the essential flood conditioning factors for flood prone area mapping using machine learning techniques](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.catena.2018.12.011)
Tehrany et al. (2019), *CATENA*. 348 citations.

- **Main goal:** Identifies which conditioning factors matter for river flood susceptibility mapping.
- **Architecture:** Decision tree and support vector machine classifiers with multicollinearity and factor-importance analysis.
- **Data:** 2011 Brisbane flood; LiDAR-derived factors (DS1) and LiDAR plus geology, soil, land use, distances (DS2).
- **Main result:** Best AUC with LiDAR-only factors: SVM 85.52% and DT 88.47%; altitude, SPI and TRI are most influential; more factors do not guarantee accuracy.
- **Open work:** Testing with other events and regions.
- **Issues:** Single event and region; static factors.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Two hybrid Artificial Intelligence approaches for modeling rainfall–runoff process](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2011.03.002)
Nourani et al. (2011), *Journal of Hydrology*. 346 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models the rainfall-runoff process with hybrid AI approaches capturing multiscale features.
- **Architecture:** Wavelet-artificial neural network and wavelet-adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) hybrids.
- **Data:** Rainfall and runoff records from a watershed in Iran; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** Wavelet-based hybrids improve on plain ANN and ANFIS; specific values not reported here.
- **Open work:** Multi-step forecasting and other basins.
- **Issues:** Abstract not available; card based partly on general knowledge.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Groundwater level prediction using machine learning models: A comprehensive review](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2022.03.014)
Tao et al. (2022), *Neurocomputing*. 345 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews machine learning models for groundwater level prediction.
- **Architecture:** Review covering artificial neural networks, support vector machines, ANFIS, tree-based and deep learning models.
- **Data:** Published groundwater level prediction studies; no new data.
- **Main result:** Not reported in detail here; summarizes model use and performance trends.
- **Open work:** Better generalization and physical interpretability.
- **Issues:** Abstract not available; card based on title and general knowledge.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Flood Detection and Susceptibility Mapping Using Sentinel-1 Remote Sensing Data and a Machine Learning Approach: Hybrid Intelligence of Bagging Ensemble Based on K-Nearest Neighbor Classifier](https://doi.org/10.3390/rs12020266)
Shahabi et al. (2020), *Remote Sensing*. 345 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps flood susceptibility in the Haraz watershed, northern Iran.
- **Architecture:** Bagging ensemble with K-nearest neighbour base classifiers (coarse, cosine, cubic and weighted KNN).
- **Data:** Flood locations from Sentinel-1 SAR and 10 conditioning factors.
- **Main result:** Bagging-Cubic-KNN performs best, reducing overfitting and improving on Cubic-KNN (AUC 0.660).
- **Open work:** Wider application in flood-prone areas.
- **Issues:** Modest AUC values; single watershed.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Mapping flood susceptibility in mountainous areas on a national scale in China.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2017.10.037)
Zhao et al. (2018), *Science of The Total Environment*. 345 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps flood susceptibility in mountainous areas of China at national scale.
- **Architecture:** Random forest classifier with conditioning factor importance analysis.
- **Data:** National flood inventory and topographic, climate and land-use factors for China's mountainous areas; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** Random forest gives high predictive accuracy; specific values not reported here.
- **Open work:** Higher resolution and dynamic factors.
- **Issues:** Abstract not available; card partly based on general knowledge.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Neural-Network Models of Rainfall-Runoff Process](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)0733-9496(1995)121:6(499))
Smith et al. (1995), *Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management*. 343 citations.

- **Main goal:** Explores neural networks as rainfall-runoff models, predicting peak discharge and full hydrographs.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward backpropagation neural network (multilayer perceptron); hydrographs represented through Fourier series coefficients.
- **Data:** Synthetic rainfall-runoff data generated on a grid of cells representing a watershed.
- **Main result:** The network predicts peak discharge and timing and reconstructs hydrographs well for the synthetic cases.
- **Open work:** Application to real watersheds with observed data.
- **Issues:** Synthetic data only; idealized watershed representation.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Comparison of Several Flood Forecasting Models in Yangtze River](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2005)10:6(485))
Chau et al. (2005), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 342 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares data-driven flood forecasting models for a large river to identify accurate and practical options.
- **Architecture:** Compares linear regression, an artificial neural network (MLP), a genetic-algorithm-trained neural network and an adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS).
- **Data:** Water level or discharge records from stations in the middle reaches of the Yangtze River, China.
- **Main result:** The genetic-algorithm-based neural network and ANFIS outperform the linear model and standard neural network, with ANFIS needing fewer parameters.
- **Open work:** Testing longer lead times and other reaches and combining with hydrodynamic models.
- **Issues:** Single river reach; limited number of flood events; short lead times.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Deep learning rainfall-runoff predictions of extreme events](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-2021-423)
Frame et al. (2021), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 341 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether deep learning rainfall-runoff models remain reliable for extreme, high return-period events not seen in training.
- **Architecture:** LSTM recurrent neural network and a mass-conserving LSTM (MC-LSTM) variant architecturally constrained to conserve water mass.
- **Data:** CAMELS US basins with daily forcing and streamflow; benchmarks are the Sacramento conceptual model and the US National Water Model.
- **Main result:** LSTM and MC-LSTM remain relatively accurate for extreme events, even when extremes are excluded from training; adding mass-balance constraints reduced skill during extremes.
- **Open work:** Understanding why mass constraints hurt extremes and improving data-driven extrapolation.
- **Issues:** Limited to US basins and daily resolution; few truly extreme events available for evaluation.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A non-linear rainfall–runoff model using an artificial neural network](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-1694(98)00273-x)
Sajikumar et al. (1999), *Journal of Hydrology*. 340 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models monthly rainfall-runoff with limited data using neural networks.
- **Architecture:** Temporal backpropagation neural network (feedforward network with time-delay connections), compared with a Volterra-type functional series model.
- **Data:** Monthly rainfall and runoff from catchments including the River Lee (UK) and the Thuthapuzha (Kerala, India).
- **Main result:** The neural network models rainfall-runoff well even with short calibration records and outperforms the functional series model.
- **Open work:** Daily scale and more catchments.
- **Issues:** Monthly resolution; few catchments; black-box structure.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Synergic Use of Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 Images for Operational Soil Moisture Mapping at High Spatial Resolution over Agricultural Areas](https://doi.org/10.3390/rs9121292)
Hajj et al. (2017), *Remote Sensing*. 340 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops an operational approach to map soil moisture at high spatial resolution over agricultural areas, for both bare and vegetated soils.
- **Architecture:** Neural network inversion of Sentinel-1 SAR backscatter combined with Sentinel-2 NDVI; network type beyond a generic neural network is not specified in the abstract.
- **Data:** Sentinel-1 VV and VH backscatter and Sentinel-2 NDVI; networks trained on synthetic databases and validated with real in situ databases.
- **Main result:** Soil moisture accuracy about 5 vol%; VV alone outperforms VH, VV+VH is similar to VV, and a priori soil moisture information improves accuracy.
- **Open work:** Extending to dense vegetation (NDVI above 0.75) and rough surfaces, and to other regions and land covers.
- **Issues:** Valid only for NDVI below 0.75 and works best for moderate roughness; relies on synthetic training data from backscatter models.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Spatial prediction of flood susceptibility using random-forest and boosted-tree models in Seoul metropolitan city, Korea](https://doi.org/10.1080/19475705.2017.1308971)
Lee et al. (2017), *Geomatics, Natural Hazards and Risk*. 339 citations.

- **Main goal:** Produces flood susceptibility maps for the Seoul metropolitan area to support flood-risk management under increasing flood frequency.
- **Architecture:** Random forest and boosted regression tree models, in regression and classification modes, within a GIS environment.
- **Data:** Flooded-area inventory (2010 for training, 2011 for validation) and 12 factors from topography, geology, soil and land-use datasets.
- **Main result:** Random forest validation accuracies of 78.8% (regression) and 79.2% (classification) versus 77.6% and 77.3% for boosted trees; distance to river, geology and DEM are most important.
- **Open work:** Incorporating rainfall and drainage network data and testing over more flood years.
- **Issues:** Static susceptibility only, two flood years, single city, and modest accuracies.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Drought forecasting using artificial neural networks and time series of drought indices](https://doi.org/10.1002/joc.1498)
Morid et al. (2007), *International Journal of Climatology*. 338 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts drought indices months ahead to support drought early warning.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward artificial neural network (MLP) predicting the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) and Effective Drought Index (EDI) from past rainfall, index values and climate indices such as SOI and NAO.
- **Data:** Rainfall records from stations in Tehran Province, Iran, with SOI and NAO indices.
- **Main result:** The neural networks forecast drought indices with useful skill at lead times up to about 12 months, with EDI better predicted than SPI.
- **Open work:** Including more large-scale climate predictors and extending to other regions.
- **Issues:** Limited station set; skill decreases with lead time; relatively few drought events.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Novel forecasting approaches using combination of machine learning and statistical models for flood susceptibility mapping.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2018.03.089)
Shafizadeh-Moghadam et al. (2018), *Journal of Environmental Management*. 337 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares individual machine learning and statistical models and their ensembles for flood susceptibility mapping, aiming to reduce model uncertainty.
- **Architecture:** Eight models (artificial neural network, CART, FDA, GLM, GAM, boosted regression trees, MARS, MaxEnt) and seven ensemble combinations such as committee averaging, mean, median and weighted mean.
- **Data:** 201 flood events and 10,000 random non-occurrence points in the Haraz watershed, Mazandaran province, Iran.
- **Main result:** Boosted regression trees reach AUROC 0.975 and GLM 0.642; the median ensemble (EMmedian) is best at 0.976.
- **Open work:** Testing ensembles in other watersheds and with independent flood events.
- **Issues:** Single watershed, random background points, and high AUC that may reflect spatial autocorrelation rather than true generalization.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Research on Particle Swarm Optimization in LSTM Neural Networks for Rainfall-Runoff Simulation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2022.127553)
Xu et al. (2022), *Journal of Hydrology*. 336 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves LSTM rainfall-runoff simulation by optimizing its hyperparameters automatically.
- **Architecture:** LSTM neural network whose hyperparameters are tuned by particle swarm optimization (PSO-LSTM), as stated in the title.

Panahi et al. (2020), *Journal of Hydrology*. 334 citations.

Sivakumar et al. (2002), *Journal of Hydrology*. 332 citations.

Bui et al. (2016), *Journal of Hydrology*. 332 citations.

### [Global Reconstruction of Naturalized River Flows at 2.94 Million Reaches](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019wr025287)
Lin et al. (2019), *Water Resources Research*. 326 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reconstructs naturalized daily river discharge globally at reach level, including small streams, for hydrology and the SWOT mission.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates global terrestrial evapotranspiration estimates from remote sensing, machine learning and land surface models, since ET cannot be measured directly globally.

Bowden et al. (2002), *Water Resources Research*. 325 citations.

### [Drought assessment and monitoring through blending of multi-sensor indices using machine learning approaches for different climate regions](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agrformet.2015.10.011)
Park et al. (2016), *Agricultural and Forest Meteorology*. 324 citations.

- **Main goal:** Monitors drought by blending multiple satellite drought indices with machine learning for different climate regions.
