- **Main result:** LSTM gives better low-flow forecasts than the comparison methods.
- **Open work:** Adding meteorological inputs and longer horizons.
- **Issues:** Single basin, univariate inputs and no uncertainty quantification.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Flood susceptibility mapping using convolutional neural network frameworks](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2019.124482)
Wang et al. (2020), *Journal of Hydrology*. 296 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses flood susceptibility in Shangyou County, China, to help mitigate and manage floods.
- **Architecture:** Convolutional neural network frameworks for classification and feature extraction with three data representations, compared with support vector machine.
- **Data:** 13 flood triggering factors and historical flood events in Shangyou County, China.
- **Main result:** CNN classifiers score 0.022–0.054 higher AUC than SVM, and CNN feature extraction improves SVM by 0.021–0.051 AUC.
- **Open work:** Applying the frameworks to other regions.
- **Issues:** Single county; spatial autocorrelation may inflate scores.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Streamflow and rainfall forecasting by two long short-term memory-based models](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2019.124296)
Ni et al. (2020), *Journal of Hydrology*. 294 citations.

- **Main goal:** Monthly streamflow and rainfall forecasting for water resources planning and management.
- **Architecture:** Two LSTM-based hybrids: wavelet-LSTM (à trous wavelet decomposition) and convolutional LSTM (CNN feature extraction plus LSTM), compared with MLP and LSTM.
- **Data:** Two streamflow and two rainfall monthly datasets; sites not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** LSTM is applicable to time series prediction, but WLSTM and CLSTM are superior alternatives.
- **Open work:** Testing longer lead times and adding exogenous predictors.
- **Issues:** No quantitative values in the abstract; monthly series are short.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A Ranking of Hydrological Signatures Based on Their Predictability in Space](https://doi.org/10.1029/2018wr022606)
Addor et al. (2018), *Water Resources Research*. 292 citations.

- **Main goal:** Ranks 15 common hydrological signatures by their predictability in space to guide signature selection for catchment classification and model calibration.
- **Architecture:** Random forest regression of signatures from catchment attributes, benchmarked against Sacramento Soil Moisture Accounting model simulations and spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I).
- **Data:** CAMELS dataset of 600+ U.S. catchments with climate, topography, land cover, soil and geology attributes and streamflow.
- **Main result:** The three approaches give similar rankings; signatures with noisy spatial patterns are poorly simulated, weakly related to attributes and sensitive to discharge uncertainty.
- **Open work:** Better understanding of signature drivers and better characterization of discharge uncertainties to increase signature value.
- **Issues:** Restricted to U.S. catchments in CAMELS; random forests capture correlation, not causal drivers.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [ESTIMATION AND FORECASTING OF DAILY SUSPENDED SEDIMENT DATA BY MULTI-LAYER PERCEPTRONS](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.advwatres.2003.10.003)
Cigizoglu (2004), *Advances in Water Resources*. 291 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates and forecasts daily suspended sediment concentrations, which are costly to measure.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural network compared with sediment rating curves and multiple linear regression.
- **Data:** Daily streamflow and suspended sediment data from rivers in the USA.
- **Main result:** The MLP estimates and forecasts suspended sediment better than rating curves and regression.
- **Open work:** Adding rainfall and other inputs and testing on more rivers.
- **Issues:** Limited extrapolation for extreme sediment events; few rivers.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Caravan - A global community dataset for large-sample hydrology](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-023-01975-w)
Kratzert et al. (2023), *Scientific Data*. 290 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides a globally standardized large-sample hydrology dataset, since existing regional CAMELS datasets differ in format and content and hinder global studies.
- **Architecture:** Benchmark dataset and open-source software: harmonizes seven CAMELS-style datasets and provides cloud-based (Google Earth Engine) code to extract forcings and catchment attributes for new basins. Not an ML model itself.
- **Data:** 6830 catchments with streamflow, ERA5-Land meteorological forcing and static attributes (HydroATLAS geophysical, sociological and climatological attributes) aggregated from CAMELS (US, GB, BR, CL, AUS), LamaH-CE and HYSETS.
- **Main result:** Delivers a consistent global dataset of forcing, streamflow and attributes plus tooling that lets the community add catchments, supporting global training of models such as LSTMs.
- **Open work:** Community extension to under-represented regions (Africa, Asia), additional forcing products and variables, and use as a standard benchmark for global hydrological ML.
- **Issues:** Reanalysis-based forcing (ERA5-Land) is coarser and more biased than local station products; geographic coverage is skewed to North America and Europe; streamflow quality varies by source.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Short-Term Water Demand Forecast Modelling at IIT Kanpur Using Artificial Neural Networks](https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1014415503476)
Jain et al. (2001), *Water Resources Management*. 289 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts short-term water demand for a campus water supply system.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (MLP) compared with regression and time series models.
- **Data:** Weekly water demand, rainfall and maximum air temperature data at IIT Kanpur, India.
- **Main result:** The neural networks forecast water demand better than regression and time series models; demand depends mainly on past demand rather than climate inputs.
- **Open work:** Testing for daily or hourly demand and other cities.
- **Issues:** Small single system; short record.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Surface Water Mapping by Deep Learning](https://doi.org/10.1109/jstars.2017.2735443)
Isikdogan et al. (2017), *IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Applied Earth Observations and Remote Sensing*. 289 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps surface water from multispectral satellite imagery and separates it from land, snow, ice, clouds and shadows.
- **Architecture:** DeepWaterMap, a fully convolutional neural network (CNN) for per-pixel water segmentation.
- **Data:** Landsat multispectral imagery with reference water masks from existing global inland water datasets.
- **Main result:** The CNN produces accurate surface water maps and distinguishes water from snow, ice, clouds and shadows better than index-based approaches.
- **Open work:** Applying to other sensors and to temporal water dynamics at global scale.
- **Issues:** Accuracy depends on the quality of the reference labels; turbid or small water bodies remain difficult.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Flash-flood susceptibility mapping based on XGBoost, random forest and boosted regression trees](https://doi.org/10.1080/10106049.2021.1920636)
Abedi et al. (2021), *Geocarto International*. 289 citations.

- **Main goal:** Produces a flash-flood susceptibility map for the Bâsca Chiojdului River Basin in Romania to support disaster management.
- **Architecture:** Classification and regression tree (CART) and tree ensembles: random forest, boosted regression trees and XGBoost.
- **Data:** 962 flash-flood locations from orthophotomaps and field surveys with conditioning factors such as slope, LULC, soil groups, lithology, TWI, TPI and SPI.
- **Main result:** Random forest achieves the highest AUC (0.956), followed by BRT (0.899), XGBoost (0.892) and CART (0.868); slope is the most important factor.
- **Open work:** Transfer to other basins and inclusion of rainfall and dynamic factors.
- **Issues:** Single basin; static susceptibility only, no temporal prediction; inventory from orthophotos may be incomplete.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Multivariate modelling of water resources time series using artificial neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1080/02626669509491401)
Raman et al. (1995), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 288 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models and synthesizes multivariate water resources time series such as reservoir inflows with artificial neural networks.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward multilayer perceptron trained with backpropagation, compared with a multivariate autoregressive statistical model.
- **Data:** Monthly inflow series to two reservoirs in India.
- **Main result:** The neural network models fit and forecast the multivariate series better than the autoregressive model.
- **Open work:** Application to more sites and longer forecast horizons.
- **Issues:** Short records and few series; no uncertainty quantification and limited testing on independent periods.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A hybrid model coupled with singular spectrum analysis for daily rainfall prediction](https://doi.org/10.2166/hydro.2010.032)
Chau et al. (2010), *Journal of Hydroinformatics*. 288 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves daily rainfall prediction by combining data preprocessing with machine learning models.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid model coupling singular spectrum analysis with artificial neural network (MLP) and support vector regression components.
- **Data:** Daily rainfall series from rain gauges in China; exact stations not confirmed here.
- **Main result:** SSA preprocessing is reported to improve rainfall prediction over models without it; numbers not reported here.
- **Open work:** Extending to longer lead times and to more stations and climates.
- **Issues:** Abstract missing; decomposition on full series can leak future information; details not verified.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Two decades of anarchy? Emerging themes and outstanding challenges for neural network river forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1177/0309133312444943)
Abrahart et al. (2012), *Progress in Physical Geography: Earth and Environment*. 287 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews two decades of neural network rainfall-runoff and streamflow modelling ('river forecasting') to identify emerging themes and outstanding challenges.
- **Architecture:** Review of artificial neural network (mostly MLP) river forecasting, covering input selection, physical interpretation, modular designs, ensembles and hybridization with conventional hydrological models.
- **Data:** Literature review; no new data. Discusses the need for agreed benchmark data sets for intermodel comparison.
- **Main result:** The field is established but fragmented; it needs consistent protocols for inputs, interpretation and benchmarking, and confidence intervals before operational use.
- **Open work:** Agreed benchmark data sets, better diagnostics, uncertainty characterization and a coordinated international research effort instead of isolated incremental studies.
- **Issues:** Predates the deep learning era (e.g., LSTMs), so recent architectures are not covered; perspective-driven rather than a systematic quantitative review.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Comparing neural network and autoregressive moving average techniques for the provision of continuous river flow forecasts in two contrasting catchments](https://doi.org/10.1002/1099-1085(20000815/30)14:11/12<2157::aid-hyp57>3.0.co;2-s)
Abrahart et al. (2000), *Hydrological Processes*. 287 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares neural network and ARMA models for continuous river flow forecasting in contrasting catchments.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (MLP) compared with autoregressive moving average (ARMA) time series models.
- **Data:** Hourly river flow records from the River Wye (Wales) and River Ouse (Yorkshire), UK.
- **Main result:** Neural networks perform as well as or better than ARMA models, with differences depending on catchment characteristics.
- **Open work:** Testing longer lead times and adding rainfall inputs.
- **Issues:** Two catchments; univariate flow inputs; short lead times.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A non-linear combination of the forecasts of rainfall-runoff models by the first-order Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy system](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-1694(01)00349-3)
Xiong et al. (2001), *Journal of Hydrology*. 287 citations.

- **Main goal:** Combines forecasts from several rainfall-runoff models to obtain better discharge forecasts.
- **Architecture:** First-order Takagi-Sugeno fuzzy system combining outputs of several rainfall-runoff models, compared with simple average, weighted average and neural network combination methods.
- **Data:** Daily rainfall-runoff data from multiple catchments worldwide.
- **Main result:** The Takagi-Sugeno fuzzy combination performs comparably to the neural network combination and better than simple averaging.
- **Open work:** Testing combinations under changing conditions and for longer horizons.
- **Issues:** Gains depend on diversity of member models; combination does not correct shared model biases.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Multi-time scale stream flow predictions: The support vector machines approach](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2005.06.001)
Asefa et al. (2006), *Journal of Hydrology*. 287 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts streamflow at multiple time scales (seasonal volumes and short-term hourly flows) to support water-management decisions in a semi-arid basin.
- **Architecture:** Support vector machine regression, chosen for its sparse, well-generalizing structure and compared with a neural network benchmark.
- **Data:** Streamflow and related hydrological records from the Sevier River basin, Utah; exact periods and inputs not stated here.
- **Main result:** Support vector machines give accurate predictions at both seasonal and hourly scales with compact models, performing comparably to or better than the neural network benchmark.
- **Open work:** Testing on other basins, adding uncertainty quantification and exploring kernel and input selection systematically.
- **Issues:** Single-basin application; no abstract available, so quantitative skill and comparison details are not reported here.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Evaluation of random forests and generalized regression neural networks for daily reference evapotranspiration modelling.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agwat.2017.08.003)
Feng et al. (2017), *Agricultural Water Management*. 286 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates machine learning models for estimating daily reference evapotranspiration, useful for irrigation scheduling where full meteorological data are lacking.
- **Architecture:** Random forest and generalized regression neural network (GRNN) compared with empirical ET0 equations.
- **Data:** Daily meteorological records from weather stations in China, with FAO-56 Penman-Monteith ET0 as reference; exact stations not confirmed here.
- **Main result:** Both machine learning models are reported to estimate ET0 satisfactorily, outperforming temperature-based empirical formulas; numbers not reported here.
- **Open work:** Testing generalization across climates and spatially between stations.
- **Issues:** Abstract missing; few stations; details of input combinations not verified.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Forecasting daily streamflow using hybrid ANN models](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2005.09.032)
Wang et al. (2006), *Journal of Hydrology*. 285 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves daily streamflow forecasting by accounting for the seasonal and regime-dependent behaviour of river flow.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid artificial neural network models: threshold-based ANN, cluster-based ANN using fuzzy C-means, and periodic ANN, compared with a standard MLP neural network.
- **Data:** Daily streamflow records from the upper Yellow River (Tangnaihai station), China.
- **Main result:** Hybrid models outperform a single global ANN, with the periodic ANN giving the best daily forecasts.
- **Open work:** Adding exogenous inputs such as precipitation and temperature and testing on other rivers.
- **Issues:** Univariate flow inputs at a single station; performance in extreme floods and transferability are not established.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Short‐term flood forecasting with a neurofuzzy model](https://doi.org/10.1029/2004wr003562)
Nayak et al. (2005), *Water Resources Research*. 285 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops a short-term flood forecasting model that combines the learning ability of neural networks with interpretable fuzzy rules.
- **Architecture:** Neurofuzzy model (adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system type), compared with neural network and conventional approaches.
- **Data:** Hourly river flow and rainfall data from an Indian river basin; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** The neurofuzzy model forecasts flood hydrographs with good accuracy at short lead times and preserves the statistical properties of the flows.
- **Open work:** Extending lead times, handling peak-flow underestimation and testing in other basins.
- **Issues:** No abstract available; accuracy at longer leads and for the largest peaks is not reported here.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Estimating Actual Evapotranspiration from Limited Climatic Data Using Neural Computing Technique](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)0733-9437(2003)129:3(214))
Sudheer et al. (2003), *Journal of Irrigation and Drainage Engineering*. 284 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates actual crop evapotranspiration when only limited climatic variables are available, avoiding costly lysimeter measurements.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network; the network type is not specified here.
- **Data:** Limited climatic data and lysimeter-measured actual evapotranspiration from an Indian site; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** The neural network estimates actual evapotranspiration from few climatic inputs with accuracy comparable to or better than conventional methods.
- **Open work:** Validation at other sites and crops and analysis of input importance.
- **Issues:** Single-site data; no abstract available, so error statistics and the exact inputs are not reported here.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Data preprocessing for river flow forecasting using neural networks: Wavelet transforms and data partitioning](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pce.2006.03.020)
Cannas et al. (2006), *Physics and Chemistry of the Earth, Parts A/B/C*. 282 citations.

- **Main goal:** Studies how data preprocessing affects neural-network river flow forecasting.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer perceptron neural networks with inputs preprocessed by discrete wavelet transforms and with different data-partitioning schemes.
- **Data:** River flow records from the Tirso basin, Sardinia, Italy.
- **Main result:** Wavelet-decomposed inputs and continuous data partitioning improve forecast accuracy over networks trained on raw flows.
- **Open work:** Generalizing preprocessing guidelines across basins and forecast horizons.
- **Issues:** Single basin; wavelet decomposition of the whole series can leak future information if not done causally.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Local and global factors controlling water‐energy balances within the Budyko framework](https://doi.org/10.1002/2013gl058324)
Xu et al. (2013), *Geophysical Research Letters*. 282 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts the water-energy partitioning parameter of the Budyko framework to assess global water availability.
- **Architecture:** Neural network (MLP) predicting Fu's equation parameter from local (slope, NDVI) and global (geolocation) factors.
- **Data:** 224 small U.S. basins and 32 large global basins; predictions for ~36,600 basins checked against a satellite-based ET product.
- **Main result:** Predicted mean annual ET agrees with the independent satellite ET product (R2 = 0.72).
- **Open work:** Adding more controlling factors and assessing changes under climate change.
- **Issues:** Validation against a satellite product with its own errors; mean annual scale only.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Daily water level forecasting using wavelet decomposition and artificial intelligence techniques](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2014.11.050)
Seo et al. (2015), *Journal of Hydrology*. 280 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts daily river water levels to support flood and water resources management.
- **Architecture:** Wavelet decomposition combined with artificial intelligence models such as artificial neural networks and ANFIS.
- **Data:** Daily water level records from river gauging stations; exact sites not confirmed here.
- **Main result:** Wavelet-based hybrids are reported to outperform the corresponding single models; numbers not reported here.
- **Open work:** Extending to longer lead times and other basins.
- **Issues:** Abstract missing; wavelet decomposition can leak future information if not done causally.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [A counterpropagation fuzzy-neural network modeling approach to real time streamflow prediction](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-1694(01)00350-x)
Chang et al. (2001), *Journal of Hydrology*. 278 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides real-time streamflow prediction for flood warning with a fast-learning hybrid network.
- **Architecture:** Counterpropagation fuzzy-neural network combining a counterpropagation neural network with fuzzy inference.
- **Data:** Hourly rainfall and streamflow from a river basin in Taiwan; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** The counterpropagation fuzzy-neural network learns quickly and gives accurate one- to few-hour-ahead streamflow predictions.
- **Open work:** Extending lead time and testing on more flood events and basins.
- **Issues:** Limited events and single basin; no abstract available, so quantitative skill is not reported here.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [A novel hybrid approach based on a swarm intelligence optimized extreme learning machine for flash flood susceptibility mapping](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.catena.2019.04.009)
Bui et al. (2019), *CATENA*. 278 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts flash-flood susceptibility in a tropical typhoon-prone area of Northwest Vietnam.
- **Architecture:** Extreme learning machine (single-hidden-layer neural network) optimized with particle swarm optimization (PSO-ELM), compared with MLP, SVM and C4.5 decision tree.
- **Data:** Geospatial database of 654 flash flood locations and 12 factors including elevation, slope, NDVI, soil, lithology and rainfall.
- **Main result:** PSO-ELM achieves kappa 0.801, RMSE 0.281, MAE 0.079, R2 0.829 and AUC 0.954, outperforming the benchmarks.
- **Open work:** Testing in other regions and adding dynamic rainfall information.
- **Issues:** Single study area; static susceptibility, not event forecasting.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Flood estimation at ungauged sites using artificial neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2005.07.032)
Dawson et al. (2006), *Journal of Hydrology*. 276 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates T-year flood events and the index flood at ungauged catchments, where gauge-based flood frequency analysis is not possible.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural networks (type not specified in the abstract), compared with multiple regression and the FEH empirical model.
- **Data:** Catchment descriptors and annual maximum flood data for 850 UK catchments from the Flood Estimation Handbook (FEH) dataset.
- **Main result:** ANNs give improved flood estimates over multiple regression models; spatial patterns in residuals show geographical factors influence performance.
- **Open work:** Incorporating geographical information to reduce spatially structured residuals and quantifying estimate uncertainty.
- **Issues:** Residuals show spatial bias; no uncertainty on the estimates; results tied to UK catchment descriptors.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Surface water extent dynamics from three decades of seasonally continuous Landsat time series at subcontinental scale in a semi-arid region](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2016.02.034)
Tulbure et al. (2016), *Remote Sensing of Environment*. 274 citations.

- **Main goal:** Quantifies three decades of surface water extent dynamics in a semi-arid region at subcontinental scale.
- **Architecture:** Supervised classification of seasonally continuous Landsat time series, using a random forest classifier.
- **Data:** Landsat TM/ETM+ time series over roughly 25 years covering the Murray-Darling Basin, Australia.
- **Main result:** Produces seasonal surface water maps showing strong variability linked to drought and flood periods; accuracy figures not reported here.
- **Open work:** Linking water dynamics to climate drivers and extending with newer sensors.
- **Issues:** Abstract missing; cloud and Landsat 7 gaps limit continuity; small water bodies hard to detect.

### [Daily streamflow forecasting by machine learning methods with weather and climate inputs](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2011.10.039)
Rasouli et al. (2012), *Journal of Hydrology*. 273 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts daily streamflow 1-7 days ahead in a small mountainous watershed to assess whether nonlinear machine learning beats linear regression when using weather and climate inputs.
- **Architecture:** Bayesian neural network, support vector regression and Gaussian process regression, compared with multiple linear regression.
- **Data:** Local meteorological observations, NWP (NCEP GFS reforecast) outputs and large-scale climate indices as predictors; streamflow in the Stave River basin, British Columbia, Canada.
- **Main result:** Nonlinear methods generally outperform linear regression at short lead times; GFS outputs help most at short leads and climate indices add some value at longer leads.
- **Open work:** Testing other basins and ensemble NWP inputs, and probabilistic forecasting.
- **Issues:** Single basin; skill drops quickly with lead time; numbers not verified here because the abstract is unavailable.

### [Flood susceptibility modelling using novel hybrid approach of reduced-error pruning trees with bagging and random subspace ensembles](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2019.05.089)
Chen et al. (2019), *Journal of Hydrology*. 273 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps flood susceptibility with GIS and ensemble machine learning to locate flood-prone areas.
- **Architecture:** Reduced-error pruning tree (REPTree, a decision tree) used alone and inside bagging (Bag-REPTree) and random subspace (RS-REPTree) ensembles; inputs chosen by correlation attribute evaluation.
- **Data:** Flood inventory of 363 locations with 13 conditioning factors (altitude, slope, aspect, curvature, SPI, STI, TWI, distance to rivers, NDVI, soil, land use, lithology, rainfall); study area not named in the abstract.
- **Main result:** RS-REPTree is best (AUC 0.949 training, 0.907 validation), followed by Bag-REPTree and single REPTree, showing ensembles help.
- **Open work:** Compare with other ensemble learners and test transfer to other basins and dynamic flood drivers.
- **Issues:** Static susceptibility only (no timing or depth); random point-based validation may be spatially autocorrelated; single study area.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Modeling of daily pan evaporation in sub tropical climates using ANN, LS-SVR, Fuzzy Logic, and ANFIS](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eswa.2014.02.047)
Goyal et al. (2014), *Expert Systems with Applications*. 272 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models daily pan evaporation in subtropical climates from meteorological variables, as a proxy for evaporative demand in water management.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of artificial neural network, least-squares support vector regression (LS-SVR), fuzzy logic and adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) models, with empirical evaporation formulas as reference.
- **Data:** Daily meteorological and pan evaporation records from subtropical station(s) in India; exact stations and period not reported here.
- **Main result:** Machine learning models reproduce daily pan evaporation better than the empirical methods, with LS-SVR and fuzzy logic among the best performers.
- **Open work:** Test across more stations and climates and with reduced input sets.
- **Issues:** Station-based study with limited spatial generality; pan evaporation measurements carry their own errors; no abstract available to confirm details.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Estimation of reference evapotranspiration in Brazil with limited meteorological data using ANN and SVM – A new approach](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2019.03.028)
Ferreira et al. (2019), *Journal of Hydrology*. 272 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates daily reference evapotranspiration across Brazil when only temperature, or temperature and humidity, are available instead of full FAO-56 Penman-Monteith inputs.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (MLP) and support vector machine regression, with K-means clustering of stations into climatic groups and lagged meteorological inputs, compared with empirical ET0 equations.
- **Data:** Daily data from 203 weather stations across Brazil; FAO-56 Penman-Monteith ET0 as target.
- **Main result:** ANN and SVM beat calibrated empirical equations; clustering and previous-day inputs help. An ANN with four previous days of data is recommended for both input sets.
- **Open work:** Test with reanalysis or gridded inputs for ungauged areas and assess transfer to other countries.
- **Issues:** Target is a computed FAO-56 value rather than measured ET; gains vary by region; skill numbers not given in the abstract.

### [Short‐term municipal water demand forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.5763)
Bougadis et al. (2005), *Hydrological Processes*. 269 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts short-term (weekly peak) municipal water demand to support operation of water supply systems.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network compared with regression and time-series models.
- **Data:** Municipal water demand and climatic data for a Canadian city (Ottawa); period not reported here.
- **Main result:** The neural network models give more accurate short-term demand forecasts than regression and time-series models.
- **Open work:** Daily or hourly forecasting and including socio-economic drivers.
- **Issues:** Single city; no abstract available, so error statistics are not reported here.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Predicting Standardized Streamflow index for hydrological drought using machine learning models](https://doi.org/10.1080/19942060.2020.1715844)
Shamshirband et al. (2020), *Engineering Applications of Computational Fluid Mechanics*. 269 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts hydrological drought indices to support drought monitoring and water management.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of support vector regression, gene expression programming and M5 model trees for predicting SPI, SSI and SPEI.
- **Data:** Precipitation, evapotranspiration and runoff-based drought index series; basin and period not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** SPI is predicted most accurately; for SSI the M5 model tree is best with correlation coefficient 0.82 and RMSE 0.82.
- **Open work:** Test longer lead times and include climate indices and other basins.
- **Issues:** Abstract gives little on data, lead time or validation design; skill for SSI is moderate.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Drought forecasting in eastern Australia using multivariate adaptive regression spline, least square support vector machine and M5Tree model](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.atmosres.2016.10.004)
Deo et al. (2017), *Atmospheric Research*. 268 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts drought conditions in eastern Australia to support agricultural and water resource planning.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of multivariate adaptive regression splines (MARS), least-squares support vector machine (LSSVM) and M5Tree model trees.

- **Open work:** Extend to longer lead times and to more sites and hybrid or ensemble methods.
- **Issues:** No abstract available; data, lead time and results could not be confirmed. Station-based models may not generalize.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Flood Susceptibility Assessment in Bangladesh Using Machine Learning and Multi-criteria Decision Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1007/s41748-019-00123-y)
Rahman et al. (2019), *Earth Systems and Environment*. 266 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses flood susceptibility across Bangladesh, a highly flood-prone country, by combining machine learning and multi-criteria decision analysis.
- **Architecture:** Machine learning classifiers combined with multi-criteria decision analysis; the specific model types are not specified here.
- **Data:** Flood inventory and geospatial conditioning factors for Bangladesh; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** Produces flood susceptibility maps for Bangladesh; quantitative results not available here.

- **Issues:** No abstract available; methods and results could not be confirmed. Static susceptibility mapping ignores flood timing and magnitude.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Machine learning algorithms for modeling groundwater level changes in agricultural regions of the U.S.](https://doi.org/10.1002/2016wr019933)
Sahoo et al. (2017), *Water Resources Research*. 265 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts seasonal groundwater level change and quantifies the relative importance of climate, pumping and surface-water drivers in agricultural aquifers without expensive physical models.
- **Architecture:** Ensemble framework combining spectral analysis, input selection by mutual information, genetic algorithms and lag analysis, and a multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural network, with uncertainty analysis.
- **Data:** Well observations in the High Plains aquifer and the Mississippi River Valley alluvial aquifer, USA, with climate, irrigation demand and streamflow predictors; testing period 2003–2012.
- **Main result:** Irrigation demand is the dominant driver at most wells; held-out observations correlate with R > 0.8 at 88% (HPA) and 83% (MRVA) of wells; cumulative level-change error is under 2 m over most of the area.
- **Open work:** Apply the framework to other aquifers and to scenario projections of water availability under changing climate and management.
- **Issues:** Purely statistical so physical consistency is not guaranteed; relies on proxy pumping/irrigation data; well-by-well models may not transfer to unmonitored locations.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Developing reservoir monthly inflow forecasts using artificial intelligence and climate phenomenon information](https://doi.org/10.1002/2017wr020482)
Yang et al. (2017), *Water Resources Research*. 264 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts monthly reservoir inflows for water management by combining artificial intelligence methods with large-scale climate phenomenon information (climate indices).
- **Architecture:** Machine learning regression models using climate-phenomenon predictors; the model set is not reported in the available metadata.
- **Data:** Not reported in the available metadata; title implies historical reservoir inflow records with climate indices (e.g., ENSO-related) as predictors.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the available metadata; the title suggests climate-index information improves monthly inflow forecasts.
- **Open work:** Extend to longer lead times and probabilistic forecasts usable for reservoir operation decisions.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable, so data, region and quantitative skill could not be verified; monthly data give small samples, and teleconnection-based predictability varies by region and season.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Machine learning methods for empirical streamflow simulation: a comparison of model accuracy, interpretability, and uncertainty in seasonal watersheds](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-20-2611-2016)
Shortridge et al. (2016), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 264 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares machine learning methods for monthly streamflow simulation not only on accuracy but also on interpretability and uncertainty, which matter for planning and management.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of multiple regression and machine learning methods: generalized additive models, multivariate adaptive regression splines, artificial neural networks (MLP), random forests and M5 cubist models.
- **Data:** Monthly streamflow and climate data for five highly seasonal rivers in the Ethiopian highlands (Blue Nile region); compared with physical models developed for the region.
- **Main result:** Data-driven models reduce errors relative to regional physical models, with relative ranking varying by basin; random forests and GAMs aid interpretation, but GAMs and MARS become highly variable under high temperatures.
- **Open work:** Evaluate robustness of empirical models under climate change and extreme conditions before using them for planning.
- **Issues:** Monthly data in few basins limit generality; extrapolation under unprecedented climate (high temperatures) is unreliable; empirical models lack process representation.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Improving Streamflow Prediction in the WRF-Hydro Model with LSTM Networks](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2021.127297)
Cho et al. (2021), *Journal of Hydrology*. 264 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves streamflow predictions of the physically based WRF-Hydro model, which carry systematic errors, by combining it with deep learning.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks combined with WRF-Hydro simulations, e.g., to correct or post-process simulated streamflow.
- **Data:** WRF-Hydro simulations and observed streamflow for a study basin; basin and period are not given here.
- **Main result:** Combining LSTM with WRF-Hydro improves streamflow prediction relative to WRF-Hydro alone.
- **Open work:** Testing in more basins and coupling strategies, and adding uncertainty quantification.
- **Issues:** No abstract available; coupling design, basin and skill numbers are not verified here.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Improved annual rainfall-runoff forecasting using PSO-SVM model based on EEMD](https://doi.org/10.2166/hydro.2013.134)
Wang et al. (2013), *Journal of Hydroinformatics*. 264 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts annual rainfall-runoff, where short records and nonstationarity hinder prediction.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid of ensemble empirical mode decomposition with a support vector machine whose parameters are tuned by particle swarm optimization (PSO-SVM).
- **Data:** Annual runoff and rainfall series for a Chinese basin; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** The EEMD-based PSO-SVM is reported to outperform models without decomposition; numbers not available here.
- **Open work:** Test on more basins and with climate indices as predictors.
- **Issues:** No abstract available; details unconfirmed. Annual series give very few samples for training.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Differentiable, Learnable, Regionalized Process‐Based Models With Multiphysical Outputs can Approach State‐Of‐The‐Art Hydrologic Prediction Accuracy](https://doi.org/10.1029/2022wr032404)
Feng et al. (2022), *Water Resources Research*. 263 citations.

- **Main goal:** Shows that differentiable, learnable process-based hydrologic models can approach LSTM accuracy for streamflow while remaining interpretable and predicting untrained physical variables.
- **Architecture:** Differentiable (δ) model: the HBV conceptual hydrologic model implemented in a differentiable programming framework with embedded neural networks (LSTM/MLP) that regionalize parameters and enhance or replace process modules.
- **Data:** 671 CAMELS basins across the contiguous USA with Daymet and a second forcing dataset (Maurer/NLDAS); simulated evapotranspiration and baseflow compared with alternative estimates.
- **Main result:** Median Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.732 versus 0.748 for a state-of-the-art LSTM with Daymet (0.715 vs 0.722 with another forcing), while also outputting soil and groundwater storage, snowpack, ET and baseflow.
- **Open work:** Apply to models with more process complexity, constrain with multi-variable observations, and use the framework to learn physics from big data.
- **Issues:** Still slightly below LSTM for streamflow; untrained internal states are only loosely validated; evaluated on CAMELS basins with limited human influence.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Application of the Artificial Neural Network model for prediction of monthly Standardized Precipitation and Evapotranspiration Index using hydrometeorological parameters and climate indices in eastern Australia](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.atmosres.2015.03.018)
Deo et al. (2015), *Atmospheric Research*. 263 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts monthly Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) in eastern Australia for drought assessment.

- **Main result:** The ANN predicts monthly SPEI well; specific scores not available here.
- **Open work:** Compare with other learners and extend to forecasting at longer leads.
- **Issues:** No abstract available; details unconfirmed. Station-based models may not generalize.

### [River suspended sediment modelling using the CART model: A comparative study of machine learning techniques.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2017.09.293)
Choubin et al. (2018), *Science of The Total Environment*. 262 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models river suspended sediment load, important for reservoir and watershed management.
- **Architecture:** Classification and regression tree (CART, a decision tree), compared with other machine learning techniques.
- **Data:** River discharge and sediment observations; basin and period not reported here.
- **Main result:** CART is reported to perform competitively or best among the compared methods; numbers not available here.
- **Open work:** Test ensemble tree methods and other basins.
- **Issues:** No abstract available; data and results unconfirmed. Sediment rating data are sparse and noisy.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Streamflow prediction using an integrated methodology based on convolutional neural network and long short-term memory networks](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-96751-4)
Ghimire et al. (2021), *Scientific Reports*. 262 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts hourly streamflow for water resources planning, hydropower, agriculture and flood control.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid CNN-LSTM (convolutional layers extract features, LSTM predicts), compared with CNN, LSTM, deep neural network and conventional AI and ensemble models.

### [Monthly streamflow forecasting using Gaussian Process Regression](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2014.01.023)
Sun et al. (2014), *Journal of Hydrology*. 261 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides probabilistic monthly streamflow forecasts for water resource management, using a nonparametric Bayesian method that yields predictive uncertainty.

### [HESS Opinions: Incubating deep-learning-powered hydrologic science advances as a community](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-22-5639-2018)
Shen et al. (2018), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 261 citations.

- **Main goal:** Argues that deep learning can open a complementary route to knowledge discovery in hydrologic science and outlines how the community can foster it.
- **Architecture:** Opinion/perspective paper on deep learning in hydrology: competing data-consistent hypotheses from DL, interpretation methods, and integration with process-based models.
- **Data:** No new data; discusses data limitations, heterogeneity and the need to share data and baseline models.
- **Main result:** Hydrology is ripe for DL breakthroughs, but progress needs coordinated community effort, process-DL integration, shared data and baselines, and open competitions.
- **Open work:** Building shared datasets, baseline models and competitions, interpretable DL, and grassroots DL education in hydrology.
- **Issues:** Perspective without quantitative evaluation; recommendations are not tested.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Self‐organizing linear output map (SOLO): An artificial neural network suitable for hydrologic modeling and analysis](https://doi.org/10.1029/2001wr000795)
Hsu et al. (2002), *Water Resources Research*. 261 citations.

- **Main goal:** Overcomes training difficulties of conventional neural networks for hydrologic prediction while giving insight into underlying processes.
- **Architecture:** Self-organizing linear output map (SOLO): a self-organizing map classification layer combined with local linear regression outputs.
- **Data:** Classic rainfall-runoff forecasting case (Leaf River basin, Mississippi, daily data).
- **Main result:** SOLO estimates structure and parameters rapidly and precisely and performs competitively against multilayer feedforward ANNs, linear time-series and conceptual rainfall-runoff models.
- **Open work:** Applying SOLO to other hydrologic variables and exploiting its interpretability for process studies.
- **Issues:** Demonstrated on a single classic basin; no uncertainty estimates.

### [Drought Forecasting Using a Hybrid Stochastic and Neural Network Model](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2007)12:6(626))
Mishra et al. (2007), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 260 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts drought conditions at several lead times to support drought preparedness.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid model combining a linear stochastic ARIMA model with an artificial neural network.
- **Data:** Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) series derived from rainfall in the Kansabati River basin, India.
- **Main result:** The hybrid stochastic-neural model forecasts SPI more accurately than either ARIMA or ANN alone, especially at longer leads.

- **Issues:** Single basin and SPI-only inputs; skill decreases with lead time.

Zhao et al. (2019), *Science of The Total Environment*. 260 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps urban flood susceptibility in Beijing when flood inventories are limited.

- **Main result:** WELLSVM uses unlabeled spatial data well and outperforms all compared models.

- **Issues:** Static susceptibility; numbers not given in the abstract; inventory incompleteness.

### [Long lead-time daily and monthly streamflow forecasting using machine learning methods](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2020.125376)
Cheng et al. (2020), *Journal of Hydrology*. 259 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses long lead-time daily and monthly streamflow forecasting with machine learning for water resources planning, where systematic short- versus long-term comparisons are scarce.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (MLP) and long short-term memory (LSTM) network, both run recursively by feeding one-step-ahead forecasts back as inputs.
- **Data:** Rainfall and runoff data from the Nan and Ping River Basins, Thailand, 1974-2014.
- **Main result:** Both models give accurate daily forecasts up to 20 days ahead; LSTM is better at long-lead daily forecasts but worse for multi-monthly forecasts due to small monthly training sets; time lag and epoch count are key settings.
- **Open work:** Larger training sets for monthly forecasting, additional predictors and uncertainty quantification.
- **Issues:** Recursive forecasting accumulates errors; two basins only; monthly data too short for LSTM; no probabilistic output.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Evaluating urban flood risk using hybrid method of TOPSIS and machine learning](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijdrr.2021.102614)
Rafiei-Sardooi et al. (2021), *International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction*. 259 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps urban flood risk in Jiroft, Iran, by combining machine-learning flood hazard maps with a socio-economic vulnerability analysis to support flood management in data-limited cities.
- **Architecture:** Support vector machine, random forest and boosted regression tree for hazard mapping, combined with the TOPSIS multi-criteria decision method for vulnerability.
- **Data:** 218 flood inundation points with conditioning factors (elevation, slope, rainfall, distances to streets, rivers and drainage, drainage density, land cover, curve number) and socio-economic indicators.
- **Main result:** Random forest gives the most accurate hazard map; urban drainage density and distance to drainage are the most important factors; high population density areas are most vulnerable.
- **Open work:** Incorporating hydrodynamic modelling and dynamic rainfall scenarios, and testing the framework in other cities.
- **Issues:** Single small city with few inventory points; static susceptibility rather than event-based inundation; vulnerability weights are subjective.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Global water use efficiency saturation due to increased vapor pressure deficit](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adf5041)
Li et al. (2023), *Science*. 258 citations.

- **Main goal:** Examines whether global ecosystem water use efficiency has kept increasing with rising CO2, given the interacting effects of climate change on carbon uptake and evapotranspiration.
- **Architecture:** Machine-learning upscaling of eddy-covariance fluxes to global gross primary production and evapotranspiration estimates; the specific learner is not specified in the abstract.
- **Data:** Global FLUXNET eddy-covariance observations upscaled with gridded drivers; analysis covers roughly 1982–2016.
- **Main result:** Global ecosystem water use efficiency rose until about 2000 but has not increased since 2001, because a higher vapor pressure deficit depressed photosynthesis and enhanced evapotranspiration.
- **Open work:** Assessing how projected VPD increases will alter coupling of terrestrial carbon and water cycles and constraining process models with these findings.
- **Issues:** Upscaled products inherit sparse flux-site coverage and machine-learning extrapolation errors, and may underrepresent CO2 fertilization trends.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Prediction of droughts over Pakistan using machine learning algorithms](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.advwatres.2020.103562)
Khan et al. (2020), *Advances in Water Resources*. 256 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops seasonal drought prediction models for Pakistan to support early warning for vulnerable communities.
- **Architecture:** Support vector machine, artificial neural network (MLP) and k-nearest neighbour models, with recursive feature elimination for predictor selection.
- **Data:** SPEI-based moderate, severe and extreme drought for the Rabi and Kharif seasons; predictors from NCEP/NCAR reanalysis.
- **Main result:** SVM best captures temporal and spatial drought characteristics; KNN performs worst; relative humidity, temperature and wind over the Mediterranean, Caspian, Indian Ocean and Arabian Sea are key predictors.
- **Open work:** Using climate model projections for future drought, and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Trained on reanalysis predictors and inherits its biases; skill numbers not reported in the abstract; limited sample of drought events.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Estimation, forecasting and extrapolation of river flows by artificial neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1623/hysj.48.3.349.45288)

- **Issues:** Poor extrapolation beyond observed ranges; no abstract available, so error figures are not reported here.

Padrón et al. (2020), *Nature Geoscience*. 255 citations.

### [Flash-Flood Susceptibility Assessment Using Multi-Criteria Decision Making and Machine Learning Supported by Remote Sensing and GIS Techniques](https://doi.org/10.3390/rs12010106)
Costache et al. (2019), *Remote Sensing*. 253 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves flood susceptibility mapping by replacing single train-test splits, which bias results, with multi-run resampling of training and validation data.
- **Architecture:** Generalized additive model (GAM), boosted regression trees (BRT) and multivariate adaptive regression splines (MARS), each combined with random subsampling or bootstrapping over 10 runs and averaged.
- **Data:** Flood inventory and conditioning factors for Ardabil Province on the Caspian Sea margin, Iran; MLP and SVM used as benchmarks.
- **Main result:** Bootstrapping beats random subsampling; BT-GAM performs best (AUC 0.98, TSS 0.93, COR 0.91), ahead of BT-MARS (AUC 0.97) and BT-BRT (AUC 0.95), outperforming standalone models.
- **Open work:** Testing transferability to other regions and flood types, and quantifying spread across resampling runs as uncertainty.
- **Issues:** Single study region; susceptibility validated against an inventory of past floods only; very high AUC may reflect spatial autocorrelation between training and test points.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Flood forecasting with machine learning models in an operational framework](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-2021-554)
Nevo et al. (2021), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 245 citations.

- **Main goal:** Describes Google's operational riverine flood forecasting and warning system, aiming to deliver accurate real-time flood alerts for large gauged rivers.
- **Architecture:** Operational system with four subsystems; stage forecasting uses Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and linear models, and inundation uses a Thresholding model and a new machine-learning Manifold model as an alternative to hydraulic modeling.
- **Data:** Historical river stage gauge data and inundation information for flood-prone rivers in India and Bangladesh; operational evaluation during the 2021 monsoon season.
- **Main result:** All models meet operational performance thresholds; LSTM beats the linear model; Thresholding and Manifold are similar for extent. In 2021 the system covered 287,000 km² and over 350M people, sending more than 100M alerts.
- **Open work:** Extend coverage to more flood-prone and ungauged locations and improve modeling skill and accuracy.
- **Issues:** Limited to large gauged rivers; evaluation on historical data with operational-metric framing rather than independent benchmarks; inundation depth validation is limited.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [River Flow Forecasting using Recurrent Neural Networks](https://doi.org/10.1023/b:warm.0000024727.94701.12)
Kumar et al. (2004), *Water Resources Management*. 245 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts monthly river flows for reservoir operation.

- **Data:** Monthly river flow records from a river in India (Hemavathi); details not reported here.
- **Main result:** The recurrent network forecasts monthly flows better than the feedforward network.
- **Open work:** Extending to longer horizons and other rivers.
- **Issues:** No abstract available; single river and error figures are not reported here.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Daily streamflow prediction using optimally pruned extreme learning machine](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2019.123981)
Adnan et al. (2019), *Journal of Hydrology*. 245 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts daily streamflow for flood warning, navigation and reservoir operation using a fast heuristic learning method.

- **Data:** Daily streamflow and hydro-climatic data at Fujiangqiao and Shehang stations on the Fujiang River, China.
- **Main result:** OP-ELM is best upstream and ANFIS-PSO downstream for prediction; in estimation OP-ELM reduces ANFIS-PSO error by 12%, and local data improve downstream estimates.
- **Open work:** Applying OP-ELM to other basins, longer lead times and with additional predictors.
- **Issues:** Two stations on one river; one-day-ahead setting; no uncertainty quantification or extreme-event analysis.
- *Basis: abstract*

### A 1 km daily soil moisture dataset over China using in situ measurement and machine learning
Li et al. (2022), *Venue not recorded*. 244 citations.

- **Main goal:** Produces a high-resolution daily soil moisture dataset over China because existing satellite and model products are coarse or biased.
- **Architecture:** Random forest regression mapping meteorological forcing, vegetation, land cover, terrain and soil properties to in situ soil moisture at multiple depths.
- **Data:** In situ soil moisture from China Meteorological Administration stations (about 1,700) with ERA5-Land forcing, MODIS LAI, land cover, DEM and soil property maps; 1 km daily, 2000–2020 (SMCI1.0).
- **Main result:** The dataset reproduces station soil moisture with correlation near 0.9 and ubRMSE around 0.04–0.05 cm3/cm3 in cross-validation, improving on ERA5-Land and satellite products.
- **Open work:** Extending coverage beyond station-dense regions and adding uncertainty estimates.
- **Issues:** Accuracy degrades where stations are sparse (western China); random forest may smooth extremes; inherits ERA5-Land forcing errors.

- **Main result:** The model predicts drought with good accuracy and the XAI analysis identifies the most influential predictors.

### [Comparison of Multivariate Regression and Artificial Neural Networks for Peak Urban Water-Demand Forecasting: Evaluation of Different ANN Learning Algorithms](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)he.1943-5584.0000245)
Adamowski et al. (2010), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 243 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts peak weekly urban water demand to support utility operations, comparing neural networks with regression.
- **Architecture:** Multiple linear regression versus feed-forward artificial neural networks trained with Levenberg-Marquardt, resilient backpropagation and conjugate gradient algorithms.

### [GRUN: an observation-based global gridded runoff dataset from 1902 to 2014](https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-11-1655-2019)
Ghiggi et al. (2019), *Earth System Science Data*. 242 citations.

- **Main goal:** Builds a long observation-based global runoff record to study past freshwater variability in data-sparse regions.

- **Data:** In situ streamflow from small catchments (GSIM) with GSWP3 reanalysis forcing; global 0.5° monthly runoff 1902–2014, compared with 13 global hydrological models.

### [Intelligent control for modelling of real‐time reservoir operation](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.226)
Chang et al. (2001), *Hydrological Processes*. 241 citations.

### [Prediction of Water Level and Water Quality Using a CNN-LSTM Combined Deep Learning Approach](https://doi.org/10.3390/w12123399)
Baek et al. (2020), *Water*. 241 citations.

- **Main goal:** Simulates river water level and water quality to support water management in a regulated basin.
- **Architecture:** Combined deep learning approach: a convolutional neural network (CNN) for water level and LSTM for total nitrogen, total phosphorus and total organic carbon.
- **Data:** Nakdong River basin, Korea: WAMIS water level, real-time water quality, KMA rainfall radar images and estuary barrage operation; calibration Jan 2016–Mar 2017, validation Mar–Nov 2017.
- **Main result:** Both CNN and LSTM reach 'very good' performance with Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency above 0.75 and capture pollutant temporal variations.

### [Physics Guided RNNs for Modeling Dynamical Systems: A Case Study in Simulating Lake Temperature Profiles](https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9781611975673.63)
Jia et al. (2018), *SDM*. 241 citations.

- **Main goal:** Combines physics-based models with recurrent networks to model physical processes accurately, consistently with physical laws and with scarce observations.
- **Architecture:** Physics-guided recurrent neural network (PGRNN, LSTM-based) with a density-depth physical constraint in the loss and pre-training on simulations from a process-based lake model.
- **Data:** Observed and General Lake Model (GLM)-simulated temperature profiles for lakes such as Lake Mendota, Wisconsin.
- **Main result:** PGRNN improves accuracy over the physical model, produces physically consistent outputs and generalizes better than a standard RNN; pre-training and density constraints both help.

### [A hybrid approach to monthly streamflow forecasting: Integrating hydrological model outputs into a Bayesian artificial neural network](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2016.06.026)
Humphrey et al. (2016), *Journal of Hydrology*. 238 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves monthly streamflow forecasting by combining a conceptual hydrological model with a data-driven model, to exploit both physical knowledge and statistical learning.

- **Main result:** The hybrid gives better monthly forecasts and uncertainty estimates than either the conceptual model or the Bayesian ANN alone.

### [Generating surface soil moisture at 30 m spatial resolution using both data fusion and machine learning toward better water resources management at the field scale](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2021.112301)
Abowarda et al. (2021), *Remote Sensing of Environment*. 238 citations.

- **Main goal:** Generates spatiotemporally continuous surface soil moisture at 30 m for field-scale water management, beyond coarse microwave products.

- **Data:** MODIS, Landsat, CLDAS, ESA CCI v4.4, SMAP Level-4 soil moisture, precipitation, soil texture and in situ sites on the North China Plain.

Alp et al. (2007), *Environmental Modelling & Software*. 237 citations.

- **Main goal:** Simulates suspended sediment load in a river from hydrometeorological data, since sediment transport is hard to describe physically and rating curves are often inaccurate.
- **Architecture:** Compares two artificial neural network types: a feedforward backpropagation MLP and a radial basis function (RBF) network, using rainfall and flow as inputs.
- **Data:** Daily rainfall, river flow and suspended sediment records from a river basin in the USA (Juniata River basin); exact periods not reported here.
- **Main result:** Both neural networks simulate sediment load satisfactorily and outperform conventional approaches such as sediment rating curves and regression; the RBF network trains without iterative weight optimization.
- **Open work:** Testing on more basins, longer lead times and extreme sediment events, and hybridizing with physically based sediment models.
- **Issues:** Single-basin daily data; peak sediment events are few and tend to be underestimated; no uncertainty quantification; abstract unavailable so details rely on recollection.

### [River Stage Forecasting in Bangladesh: Neural Network Approach](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)0887-3801(2000)14:1(1))
Liong et al. (2000), *Journal of Computing in Civil Engineering*. 237 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts river stages in Bangladesh several days ahead to support flood warning in a large, flood-prone delta river system.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward neural network (MLP) trained with backpropagation, using water levels at upstream gauging stations as inputs; sensitivity analysis is used to reduce the number of input stations.
- **Data:** Daily water level records from gauging stations on the Bangladesh river network (Dhaka region forecast point); exact periods not reported here.
- **Main result:** The network forecasts stages with high accuracy at short lead times, with accuracy decreasing for longer horizons up to about a week; few key upstream stations suffice as inputs.
- **Open work:** Including rainfall and upstream transboundary information, and extending to multiple forecast points and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Single forecast location and station-based inputs only; performance degrades with lead time; no probabilistic output; abstract unavailable.

### [A robust method for non-stationary streamflow prediction based on improved EMD-SVM model](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2018.11.015)
Meng et al. (2019), *Journal of Hydrology*. 237 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves monthly streamflow prediction for strongly non-stationary series to support water resources management.

- **Main result:** ANN performs worst; M-EMDSVM beats EMD-SVM for strongly non-stationary series and matches it for weakly non-stationary series.

### [Machine learning for hydrologic sciences: An introductory overview](https://doi.org/10.1002/wat2.1533)
Xu et al. (2021), *WIREs Water*. 236 citations.

- **Data:** Literature review; no new data.
- **Main result:** Summarizes applications in pattern/event detection, approximation of hydrologic variables (e.g., rainfall-runoff), relationship mining, parameterization, surrogate modelling and bias correction.

Chang et al. (2014), *Journal of Hydrology*. 235 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts urban water levels multiple steps ahead in real time to support flood control.

- **Open work:** Extending to more stations and integrating into control systems.
- **Issues:** Single site; error accumulates over steps; no abstract to confirm numbers.

### [Soil moisture determines the recovery time of ecosystems from drought](https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.16620)
Yao et al. (2023), *Global Change Biology*. 235 citations.

- **Main goal:** Identifies global patterns of terrestrial ecosystem recovery time after drought and the environmental factors that control it, which are poorly understood.

Pradhan et al. (2023), *Geoscience Frontiers*. 235 citations.

Jain et al. (2004), *Water Resources Research*. 233 citations.

Amitrano et al. (2024), *Remote Sensing*. 233 citations.

Tikhamarine et al. (2020), *Journal of Hydrology*. 233 citations.

### [Estimating daily reference evapotranspiration based on limited meteorological data using deep learning and classical machine learning methods](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2020.125286)
Chen et al. (2020), *Journal of Hydrology*. 232 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates deep learning for estimating daily reference evapotranspiration (ETo) from limited meteorological inputs and tests transferability beyond training stations.

### [Physics‐Constrained Machine Learning of Evapotranspiration](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019gl085291)
Zhao et al. (2019), *Geophysical Research Letters*. 232 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates ecosystem evapotranspiration (latent heat flux) while conserving the surface energy budget, to improve generalization of machine learning models.

- **Data:** Eddy covariance flux observations at 82 tower sites (FLUXNET).

- **Main result:** LSTM and EA-LSTM reach median NSE of 0.88 and 0.86, outperforming the conceptual models, with largest gains in north-east Scotland and south-east England.
- **Open work:** Add inputs describing groundwater, abstractions and percolation; use spatial performance patterns to refine conceptual models.
- **Issues:** South-east England remains hard to model because the LSTMs cannot learn groundwater processes and human abstractions from standard meteorological inputs.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Improved streamflow forecasting using self-organizing radial basis function artificial neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2004.03.027)
Moradkhani et al. (2004), *Journal of Hydrology*. 218 citations.

- **Main goal:** Explores one-step-ahead daily streamflow forecasting, a challenging task central to water resources system control.
- **Architecture:** Self-Organizing Radial Basis (SORB) function network: a Gaussian radial basis function architecture combined with a self-organizing feature map (SOM); compared with a multilayer feedforward network (MLP), SOLO and linear regression.
- **Data:** Daily streamflow from the semi-arid Salt River basin, Arizona; cross-validation compared with split-sample testing.
- **Main result:** SORB outperforms the MLP and SOLO networks for daily streamflow; linear regression is unreliable; cross-validation confirms the nonlinear input-output relationship.
- **Open work:** Extending to multi-step forecasts and other basins.
- **Issues:** Single basin; one-step-ahead only; deterministic forecasts.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Neural network river forecasting through baseflow separation and binary-coded swarm optimization](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2015.08.008)
Taormina et al. (2015), *Journal of Hydrology*. 218 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improve neural network river flow forecasting by separating baseflow and optimising input selection.

- **Main result:** Not reported in the abstract; the title implies baseflow separation and swarm-based input selection improve forecasts over standard ANNs.

### [Flash Flood Susceptibility Modeling Using New Approaches of Hybrid and Ensemble Tree-Based Machine Learning Algorithms](https://doi.org/10.3390/rs12213568)

- **Issues:** Single watershed; moderate AUC; susceptibility maps are static and depend on the flood inventory and absence sampling.

Rezaeianzadeh et al. (2013), *Neural Computing and Applications*. 217 citations.

### [Flood forecasting using support vector machines](https://doi.org/10.2166/hydro.2007.027)

### [Monthly runoff time series prediction by variational mode decomposition and support vector machine based on quantum-behaved particle swarm optimization](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2020.124627)
Feng et al. (2020), *Journal of Hydrology*. 216 citations.

### [Hybrid forecasting: blending climate predictions with AI models](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-27-1865-2023)
Slater et al. (2023), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 215 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews hybrid hydroclimatic forecasting that blends dynamical weather/climate model predictions with statistical or AI methods to improve forecast skill.
- **Architecture:** Review of hybrid forecasting systems that use machine learning and statistical post-processing to integrate outputs of numerical weather prediction, climate, land, hydrology and Earth system models.
- **Data:** Review of literature covering subseasonal-to-decadal predictions of rainfall, temperature, streamflow, floods, droughts, tropical cyclones and atmospheric rivers.
- **Main result:** Hybrid systems can reduce dynamical model biases, avoid running costly land models, and combine sources of predictability across horizons, and are attracting growing attention.
- **Open work:** Physically explainable results, assimilating human influences, new ensemble techniques, seamless short-to-long lead prediction, land/ocean/ice initial conditions, spatial variability and operational uptake.

Nourani et al. (2008), *Hydrological Processes*. 215 citations.

Shu et al. (2008), *Journal of Hydrology*. 215 citations.

Ibrahim et al. (2021), *Alexandria Engineering Journal*. 213 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews hybrid artificial intelligence and optimization models for hydrological streamflow forecasting, motivated by reservoir operation needs.

### [Estimation and forecasting of daily suspended sediment data using wavelet–neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2008.06.013)
Partal et al. (2008), *Journal of Hydrology*. 212 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates and forecasts daily suspended sediment load using wavelet decomposition to improve neural network performance.

### [Addressing the incorrect usage of wavelet-based hydrological and water resources forecasting models for real-world applications with best practices and a new forecasting framework](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2018.05.003)
Quilty et al. (2018), *Journal of Hydrology*. 212 citations.

- **Data:** Urban water demand data from Montreal, Canada.
- **Main result:** Common DWT-MRA and MODWT-MRA set-ups use future data and overstate skill; WDDFF gives realistic forecasts and beats random walk, linear regression, ELM and Volterra benchmarks.

Mondini et al. (2023), *Nature Communications*. 209 citations.

Saggi et al. (2019), *Computers and Electronics in Agriculture*. 209 citations.

Gebrehiwot et al. (2019), *Sensors*. 209 citations.

Wunsch et al. (2021), *Nature Communications*. 208 citations.

Löwe et al. (2021), *Journal of Hydrology*. 208 citations.

Khu et al. (2001), *JAWRA Journal of the American Water Resources Association*. 205 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops genetic programming as a data-driven tool for real-time runoff forecasting, both as a stand-alone forecaster and as an error-updating scheme for a conceptual rainfall-runoff model.

- **Data:** Rainfall and runoff records from the Orgeval catchment in France; exact periods not reported here.
- **Main result:** Genetic programming gives accurate short-lead runoff forecasts and, as an updating scheme, improves the conceptual model's real-time predictions.
- **Open work:** Test on more catchments and longer lead times, and compare with other updating schemes such as neural networks or Kalman filtering.
- **Issues:** Single small catchment; skill decays with lead time; evolved expressions can be hard to interpret physically.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Evolving neural network using real coded genetic algorithm for daily rainfall-runoff forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eswa.2008.05.024)
Sedki et al. (2009), *Expert Systems with Applications*. 205 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves daily rainfall-runoff forecasting by training a neural network with a real-coded genetic algorithm instead of gradient-based backpropagation.

- **Data:** Daily rainfall and runoff series from a semi-arid catchment in Morocco; exact record length not reported here.
- **Main result:** The genetic-algorithm-trained network forecasts daily runoff more accurately than the backpropagation-trained network, especially avoiding poor local minima.
- **Open work:** Extend to multi-step forecasting, other catchments, and hybrid evolutionary-gradient training.
- **Issues:** Single catchment; genetic training is computationally costly; no uncertainty quantification.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Predicting groundwater level changes using GRACE data](https://doi.org/10.1002/wrcr.20421)
Sun (2013), *Water Resources Research*. 205 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether GRACE satellite gravimetry can be used to predict groundwater level changes at individual wells, where in-situ monitoring is sparse.

- **Open work:** Downscaling GRACE signals more rigorously and extending to more aquifers and to GRACE Follow-On data.
- **Issues:** GRACE has coarse spatial resolution (hundreds of km) relative to single wells; short GRACE record; performance varies by well. Abstract not available, so details are from memory.

### [Evaluating the performance of random forest for large-scale flood discharge simulation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2020.125531)
Schoppa et al. (2020), *Journal of Hydrology*. 204 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates whether random forest can serve as a low-cost alternative to conceptual hydrological models for large-scale daily flood discharge simulation across heterogeneous catchments.

### [Evaluating Different Machine Learning Methods for Upscaling Evapotranspiration from Flux Towers to the Regional Scale](https://doi.org/10.1029/2018jd028447)
Xu et al. (2018), *Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres*. 203 citations.

- **Main goal:** Upscales evapotranspiration from flux towers to the regional scale, where in situ measurements have limited coverage.

- **Data:** Eddy covariance ET at 36 flux tower sites (65 site-years) in the Heihe River Basin; regional daily 1 km estimates for 2012–2016.
- **Main result:** ANN, Cubist, RF and SVM perform almost identically and slightly better than the deep belief network; RF has the lowest regional relative uncertainty (three-cornered hat).

Konapala et al. (2020), *Environmental Research Letters*. 202 citations.

- **Open work:** Applying delta models to regional and global simulations, improving low-flow processes, and assimilating multi-source observations for climate impact studies.

- **Architecture:** Deep neural network (fully connected DNN) for flood susceptibility combined with Analytic Hierarchy Process multi-criteria decision analysis; compared with Bagging and Decorate ensembles of Forest by Penalizing Attributes.
- **Data:** 847 past flood locations in Quang Nam province, Vietnam, with conditioning factors for training and testing.
- **Main result:** The DNN-MCDA integration produces accurate flood risk maps; performance validated with ROC curves and standard statistics.
- **Open work:** Applying to other regions and incorporating dynamic hydrological drivers.
- **Issues:** No quantitative metrics in the abstract; AHP weights are subjective; single province.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Deep Learning Data-Intelligence Model Based on Adjusted Forecasting Window Scale: Application in Daily Streamflow Simulation](https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2020.2974406)
Fu et al. (2020), *IEEE Access*. 153 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses long short-term memory networks for daily streamflow forecasting in a tropical river and how data choices affect performance.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) network compared with a classic backpropagation neural network (MLP).
- **Data:** Historical daily streamflow of the Kelantan River, north-east Peninsular Malaysia.
- **Main result:** LSTM outperforms the backpropagation network, performing well in steady dry-season flows and capturing rapidly fluctuating rainy-season flows; no metrics are given in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Adding meteorological inputs and testing on other basins and longer horizons.
- **Issues:** Single catchment; streamflow-only inputs; quantitative results not reported in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [The potential of different ANN techniques in evapotranspiration modelling](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.6837)
Kisi (2008), *Hydrological Processes*. 153 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates several artificial neural network types for modelling reference evapotranspiration.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer perceptron, radial basis function and generalized regression neural networks compared with empirical evapotranspiration equations.
- **Data:** Daily climatic data from California Irrigation Management Information System (CIMIS) stations.
- **Main result:** The neural networks reproduce Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration better than empirical formulas, with differences among network types.
- **Open work:** Testing in other climates and with reduced inputs.
- **Issues:** Target is a computed reference ET; few stations.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [A 21-year dataset (2000–2020) of gap-free global daily surface soil moisture at 1-km grid resolution](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-023-01991-w)
Zheng et al. (2023), *Scientific Data*. 153 citations.

- **Main goal:** Produces a long-term global gap-free surface soil moisture dataset at fine resolution, overcoming satellite gaps and coarse spatial resolution.
- **Architecture:** Benchmark dataset produced by gap-filling ESA-CCI soil moisture with ERA5 and downscaling to 1 km with a random forest.
- **Data:** ESA-CCI combined soil moisture at 0.25 degree, ERA5 soil moisture, International Soil Moisture Network in situ data and optical remote sensing; 2000-2020.
- **Main result:** The 1-km product has correlation 0.89 and unbiased RMSE 0.045 m3/m3 in cross-validation; claimed only long-term global gap-free 1-km dataset.
- **Open work:** Extending in time and to deeper soil layers, and validation in sparsely monitored regions.
- **Issues:** Gap-filling inherits ERA5 biases; in situ validation is sparse in many regions; cross-validation may overstate accuracy.
