### [A note on leveraging synergy in multiple meteorological data sets with deep learning for rainfall–runoff modeling](https://doi.org/10.31223/osf.io/pjm5a)
Kratzert et al. (2020), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 152 citations.

- **Main goal:** Shows that a deep learning rainfall-runoff model can exploit multiple meteorological forcing products together rather than relying on a single product.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory network (LSTM) taking several precipitation and meteorological forcing products simultaneously as input.
- **Data:** CAMELS basins in the continental US with forcings from NLDAS, Maurer and Daymet.
- **Main result:** Combining forcing products in a single LSTM significantly improves streamflow simulation accuracy over any individual product; the LSTM blends precipitation products differently by location and by hydrograph part.
- **Open work:** Extending to more forcing products and regions, and to operational forecasting with forecast inputs.
- **Issues:** US-only with gridded products that are themselves correlated; benefit relies on all products being available at prediction time.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Flood frequency analysis at ungauged sites using artificial neural networks in canonical correlation analysis physiographic space](https://doi.org/10.1029/2006wr005142)
Shu et al. (2007), *Water Resources Research*. 152 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates flood quantiles at ungauged sites, a key need for design where no streamflow records exist.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network regional model operating in the canonical correlation analysis (CCA) physiographic space, compared with other regional flood frequency approaches.
- **Data:** Flood quantiles and physiographic/climatic catchment attributes for gauging stations in Quebec, Canada.
- **Main result:** The ANN in CCA space gives more accurate flood quantile estimates than standard CCA-based regionalization.
- **Open work:** Combining with other region-of-influence methods and quantifying uncertainty.
- **Issues:** Jackknife evaluation on one region; flood quantiles themselves are uncertain at sites with short records.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Application of Several Data-Driven Techniques for Predicting Groundwater Level](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11269-012-0194-y)
Shirmohammadi et al. (2012), *Water Resources Management*. 152 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts groundwater levels with several data-driven techniques to support groundwater resources management where physically based models are data-demanding.
- **Architecture:** Several data-driven techniques compared; the specific model types are not specified here.
- **Data:** Groundwater level observations; aquifer and period not reported here.
- **Main result:** The title implies a comparison of several data-driven techniques for groundwater level prediction; which performs best is not reported here.
- **Open work:** Testing at more wells and aquifers and at longer prediction horizons would follow naturally.
- **Issues:** No abstract available; model types, data and metrics cannot be confirmed, so this card is general.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [A mixed approach for urban flood prediction using Machine Learning and GIS](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijdrr.2021.102154)
Motta et al. (2021), *International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction*. 152 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts urban flood occurrence with machine learning and GIS, giving city managers a tool for resilience planning as extreme weather and urbanization increase.
- **Architecture:** Machine learning classifiers, of which random forest performs best, combined with GIS hot spot analysis into a flood risk index.
- **Data:** Observed urban flood history and weather conditions for a city; details not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Random forest reaches Matthews correlation 0.77 and accuracy 0.96; combined with hot spots into a flood risk index.
- **Open work:** Integrating real-time weather forecasts and testing transfer to other cities would follow naturally.
- **Issues:** Single city; with rare flood events, accuracy of 0.96 can be inflated by class imbalance; the city and data are not named in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Exploring complex water stress–gross primary production relationships: Impact of climatic drivers, main effects, and interactive effects](https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.16201)
Wang et al. (2022), *Global Change Biology*. 152 citations.

- **Main goal:** Disentangles the roles of vapor pressure deficit and soil water content in limiting gross primary production, including climatic confounding and their interaction, to inform vegetation models.
- **Architecture:** Extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) models interpreted with SHAP main and interaction values, combined with statistical analyses that remove the effect of main climatic drivers.
- **Data:** Eddy-covariance site observations from the global FLUXNET2015 dataset across plant functional types, about a decade of records per site.
- **Main result:** VPD is more important than SWC for water stress across most plant functional types once climatic drivers are removed; VPD-SWC interaction reverses sign with soil moisture and VPD stress shows a threshold; no significant CO2 alleviation found.
- **Open work:** Use the identified VPD and SWC limitations and thresholds to improve water-stress formulations in dynamic global vegetation models; revisit CO2 effects with longer records.
- **Issues:** Records of about ten years are too short to detect CO2 effects; SHAP attributions are associative, not causal; site-level results may not scale uniformly.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Forecast of rainfall distribution based on fixed sliding window long short-term memory](https://doi.org/10.1080/19942060.2021.2009374)
Chen et al. (2022), *Engineering Applications of Computational Fluid Mechanics*. 152 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts monthly rainfall with a model that has memory of past values, addressing uncertainty of memoryless data-mining approaches.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) network with fixed sliding input windows to select optimal lags, compared against a random forest model.
- **Data:** Monthly rainfall 1980–2020 from two meteorological stations in Turkey (Rize and Konya) with contrasting climates.
- **Main result:** LSTM outperforms random forest at both stations, improving RMSE by 12.2–14.9%, RSR by 12.3–14.8%, R by 9.4–13.5% and NSE by 32.9–33.2%.
- **Open work:** Test the approach under other climates and at more stations, and add exogenous climate predictors.
- **Issues:** Only two stations and univariate monthly series; single benchmark model; no uncertainty quantification or extreme-event analysis.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Widespread and complex drought effects on vegetation physiology inferred from space](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-40226-9)
Li et al. (2023), *Nature Communications*. 152 citations.

- **Main goal:** Isolates vegetation physiological responses to drought (photosynthesis, evaporation, water content) from structural changes at large scales using satellite data.
- **Architecture:** Machine learning technique used to separate physiological from structural responses; the model type is not specified in the abstract. Results are checked against a soil–plant–atmosphere continuum model coupled with radiative transfer.
- **Data:** Remotely sensed proxies of photosynthesis, evaporation and vegetation water content, plus hydro-meteorological drivers; process-model simulations for comparison.
- **Main result:** Functional declines under drought are largely driven by downregulated stomatal conductance and light use efficiency, strongest in water-limited regions; spatial patterns are controlled mainly by aridity.
- **Open work:** Use the isolated physiological responses to constrain ecosystem feedbacks in land surface and climate models.
- **Issues:** Attribution relies on satellite proxies with their own retrieval uncertainties; separating physiology from structure is model-dependent.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A comprehensive study of deep learning for soil moisture prediction](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-28-917-2024)
Wang et al. (2024), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 151 citations.

- **Main goal:** Systematically compares deep learning architectures for soil moisture prediction to identify network design principles and understand how models use data.
- **Architecture:** Ten deep learning structures (three basic feature extractors such as LSTM, CNN-type and MLP-type networks, plus seven hybrids including feature-attention LSTM and GAN-based LSTM), interpreted with SHAP and t-SNE; three classical ML baselines.
- **Data:** Soil moisture observations across different soil textures and depths with meteorological drivers; specific sites and products not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** LSTM's temporal modelling suits soil moisture forecasting; feature-attention LSTM and GAN-LSTM further improve accuracy, showing benefits of attention and adversarial training. Code for 13 models is open source.
- **Open work:** Applying the design principles to other hydrology problems and testing transfer across regions.
- **Issues:** Site and dataset details are not given in the abstract; skill gains are modest and interpretability analyses are qualitative.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Experimental investigation of the predictive capabilities of data driven modeling techniques in hydrology - Part 2: Application](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-14-1943-2010)
Elshorbagy et al. (2009), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 151 citations.

- **Main goal:** Systematically compares data-driven modelling techniques across hydrological problems to guide technique selection.
- **Architecture:** Benchmark of neural networks (ANN), genetic programming, evolutionary polynomial regression, support vector machines, M5 model trees, k-nearest neighbours and multiple linear regression, with the Gamma test for guidance.
- **Data:** Five case studies: half-hourly actual evapotranspiration, daily peat and till soil moisture, and two daily rainfall-runoff data sets, each resampled into 12 realizations.
- **Main result:** Genetic programming is most successful overall; ANNs are sub-optimal for evapotranspiration and rainfall-runoff; M5 suits linear data; k-nn performs well in linear and nonlinear cases; SVM is kernel-sensitive.
- **Open work:** Extending the experiment to more data sets and better guidance for model choice from data characteristics.
- **Issues:** Results depend on the five data sets and tuning choices; random resampling ignores temporal dependence.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Wavelet-entropy data pre-processing approach for ANN-based groundwater level modeling](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2015.02.048)
Nourani et al. (2015), *Journal of Hydrology*. 151 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves groundwater level modelling with artificial neural networks by selecting informative wavelet-decomposed inputs.
- **Architecture:** Wavelet transform combined with an entropy-based measure to select dominant subseries as inputs to a feed-forward artificial neural network (ANN).
- **Data:** Hydro-meteorological and groundwater level time series from observation wells, reportedly in the Ardabil plain, Iran; period not reported here.
- **Main result:** The wavelet-entropy preprocessed ANN is reported to outperform ANN models with conventional inputs; specific metrics not available here.
- **Open work:** Extend the input selection approach to other aquifers and multi-step forecasting.
- **Issues:** Results tied to one aquifer; wavelet preprocessing risks boundary effects and look-ahead leakage; details unverified without abstract.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A physically based and machine learning hybrid approach for accurate rainfall-runoff modeling during extreme typhoon events](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.asoc.2016.12.052)
Young et al. (2017), *Applied Soft Computing*. 151 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves rainfall-runoff simulation during extreme typhoon events by combining a physically based hydrological model with machine learning.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid approach coupling a physically based rainfall-runoff model (HEC-HMS) with machine learning models (support vector machine and artificial neural network) that refine its runoff output.
- **Data:** Hourly rainfall and runoff for typhoon events in a watershed in Taiwan; event counts not reported here.
- **Main result:** The hybrid model is reported to simulate typhoon runoff more accurately than the physically based or machine learning models alone.
- **Open work:** Extend to real-time forecasting with rainfall forecasts and to other basins.
- **Issues:** Limited number of extreme events; site-specific calibration; details partly from knowledge, abstract not available.

Wen et al. (2015), *Water Resources Management*. 150 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models daily reference evapotranspiration in extreme arid regions where climatic data are limited.

- **Main result:** SVM models with limited inputs such as temperature and radiation are reported to estimate ET0 well and outperform ANN and empirical methods.
- **Open work:** Test transferability to other arid sites and with fewer inputs.

### [A comparison of numerical and machine-learning modeling of soil water content with limited input data](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2016.11.007)
Karandish et al. (2016), *Journal of Hydrology*. 150 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares numerical and machine learning modelling of soil water content when input data are limited.

Chen et al. (2006), *Journal of Hydrology*. 149 citations.

Wu et al. (2005), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 149 citations.

### [Mapping the spatial and temporal variability of flood hazard affected by climate and land-use changes in the future.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2021.113551)
Janizadeh et al. (2021), *Journal of Environmental Management*. 149 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps current and future flood hazard under climate and land-use change to support flood management.

- **Issues:** Single GCM; static susceptibility mapping, not hydrodynamic; small inventory; moderate AUC.

### [Forecasting Groundwater Table in a Flood Prone Coastal City with Long Short-term Memory and Recurrent Neural Networks](https://doi.org/10.3390/w11051098)
Bowes et al. (2019), *Water*. 148 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts groundwater table response to storms in a flood-prone coastal city, where shallow groundwater amplifies flooding under sea level rise.

Parasuraman et al. (2007), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 148 citations.

Maity et al. (2010), *Hydrological Processes*. 148 citations.

Ch et al. (2013), *Neurocomputing*. 148 citations.

### [Gaussian process emulation of spatio-temporal outputs of a 2D inland flood model.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.watres.2022.119100)
Donnelly et al. (2022), *Water Research*. 148 citations.

Abrahart et al. (2002), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 147 citations.

### [On the relevance of using artificial neural networks for estimating soil moisture content](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2008.08.012)
Elshorbagy et al. (2008), *Journal of Hydrology*. 147 citations.

Hundecha et al. (2001), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 147 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops a rainfall-runoff model based on fuzzy logic for simulating catchment discharge.

Isik et al. (2013), *Journal of Hydrology*. 147 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models the effects of land use and land cover change on daily streamflow.

- **Issues:** Details unverified without abstract.

### [Nearest‐neighbor methods for nonparametric rainfall‐runoff forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1029/wr023i007p01300)
Karlsson et al. (1987), *Water Resources Research*. 146 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops nonparametric forecasting of streamflow from rainfall without specifying a physical or parametric model.
- **Architecture:** Nearest-neighbour (k-nearest neighbour) nonparametric regression for rainfall-runoff forecasting.
- **Data:** Historical rainfall and runoff records from river basins; specific catchments not reported here.

### [Bayesian neural network for rainfall‐runoff modeling](https://doi.org/10.1029/2005wr003971)
Khan et al. (2006), *Water Resources Research*. 146 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides rainfall-runoff predictions with quantified uncertainty, which standard deterministic neural networks do not give.
- **Architecture:** Bayesian neural network: a multilayer perceptron (MLP) trained with Bayesian learning so that weights have posterior distributions and predictions carry confidence intervals.
- **Data:** Daily precipitation, temperature and streamflow from a Canadian catchment; exact record lengths are not reported here.
- **Main result:** The Bayesian neural network gives forecasts comparable to or better than a standard ANN and a conceptual hydrological model, while also providing predictive uncertainty bounds.

### [Flood Risk Mapping by Remote Sensing Data and Random Forest Technique](https://doi.org/10.3390/w13213115)
Farhadi et al. (2021), *Water*. 146 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps flood risk and identifies the most influential flood-conditioning factors in the Galikesh River basin, northern Iran.
- **Architecture:** Random forest used to rank the importance of 11 flood risk indices and produce the flood hazard map, with GIS-based index normalization.
- **Data:** Landsat 8 imagery and SRTM DEM processed in Google Earth Engine to derive 11 indices (elevation, slope, aspect, land use, NDVI, NDWI, TWI, river distance, waterway density, soil texture, maximum one-day precipitation).
- **Main result:** Waterway and river density, river distance, maximum one-day precipitation and elevation explain about 68.3% of total flood risk; about 21% and 18% of the basin fall in high and highest risk classes.
- **Open work:** Validation against observed flood inventories and transfer to other basins would strengthen the mapping.
- **Issues:** Single small basin; validation of the hazard map against independent flood events is not detailed in the abstract.

### [Flood Detection in Urban Areas Using Satellite Imagery and Machine Learning](https://doi.org/10.3390/w14071140)
Tanim et al. (2022), *Water*. 146 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops rapid urban flood detection from satellite imagery to support timely flood management in San Diego, California.
- **Architecture:** Supervised random forest, support vector machine and maximum likelihood classifiers compared with a new unsupervised change-detection framework combining Otsu thresholding, fuzzy rules and iso-clustering.
- **Data:** Sentinel-1 SAR imagery with ground truth from police road-closure reports for the City of San Diego.
- **Main result:** F1 scores are 0.67 (RF), 0.85 (SVM), 0.79 (MLC) and 0.85 (change detection); the unsupervised method matches the best accuracy (0.87) with the least data and computation.
- **Open work:** Application to other cities and to nuisance flooding is suggested.
- **Issues:** Ground truth from road-closure reports is sparse and indirect; SAR flood detection in dense urban areas suffers from layover and shadow effects.

### [Evapotranspiration estimation using four different machine learning approaches in different terrestrial ecosystems](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compag.2018.03.010)
Dou et al. (2018), *Computers and Electronics in Agriculture*. 146 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates evapotranspiration in different terrestrial ecosystems with machine learning as an alternative to physically based models.

- **Data:** Eddy covariance flux and meteorological measurements from sites across different ecosystems; specific sites not reported here.
- **Main result:** The models estimate ET well across ecosystems, with differences in performance among methods; exact metrics not reported here.
- **Open work:** Extension to more ecosystems and gap-filling or upscaling applications is a natural next step.
- **Issues:** Site-based evaluation may not generalize; eddy covariance energy-balance closure errors propagate into targets.

### [Daily Streamflow Forecasting in Mountainous Catchment Using XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost](https://doi.org/10.3390/hydrology9120226)
Szczepanek (2022), *Hydrology*. 146 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares gradient boosting models for daily streamflow forecasting in a mountainous catchment.
- **Architecture:** Gradient boosting decision trees: XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost, with default and tuned hyperparameters.
- **Data:** Daily precipitation, upstream gauge runoff and two preceding days of observations for a mountainous catchment; at least 12 years of training data.
- **Main result:** All models reach NSE 0.85–0.89 and RMSE 6.8–7.8 m3/s; CatBoost is best with default settings and LightGBM after tuning; hyperparameter effects exceed between-model differences.

- **Issues:** Single catchment; one-day-ahead forecasts using upstream observations limit applicability to ungauged settings.

### [Comparison of Machine Learning Algorithms for Flood Susceptibility Mapping](https://doi.org/10.3390/rs15010192)
Seydi et al. (2022), *Remote Sensing*. 146 citations.

- **Main goal:** Produces reliable flood susceptibility maps for flood management in Iranian basins.

- **Data:** 21 flood-conditioning factors with flood inventories from satellite imagery, historical reports and field data in the Karun and Gorganrud basins, Iran.

- **Main goal:** Provides near-real-time forecasts of satellite-based surface soil moisture, using recent observations to correct a data-driven model.

### [A High‐Resolution Global Map of Soil Hydraulic Properties Produced by a Hierarchical Parameterization of a Physically Based Water Retention Model](https://doi.org/10.1029/2018wr023539)
Zhang et al. (2018), *Water Resources Research*. 145 citations.

### [Prediction of Flow Based on a CNN-LSTM Combined Deep Learning Approach](https://doi.org/10.3390/w14060993)

- **Issues:** Demonstrated mainly on one basin's annual flows; resampling-based methods depend on record length and stationarity.

- **Main result:** SVM-based models give more accurate hourly inflow forecasts than the neural network benchmark, and adding typhoon characteristics improves longer-lead forecasts.
- **Open work:** Extension to longer lead times and use of quantitative precipitation forecasts.
- **Issues:** Limited number of typhoon events; deterministic forecasts without uncertainty.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Comparison of Artificial Neural Network and regression models for sediment loss prediction from Banha watershed in India](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agwat.2005.02.001)
Sarangi et al. (2005), *Agricultural Water Management*. 125 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts sediment loss from an Indian watershed and compares artificial neural networks with regression models.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (feedforward MLP) compared with regression models for sediment loss prediction.
- **Data:** Rainfall, runoff and sediment observations from the Banha watershed in India; period not reported in the available metadata.
- **Main result:** The neural network predicts sediment loss more accurately than the regression models, according to the authors.
- **Open work:** Including geomorphological and land-use inputs and testing on other watersheds.
- **Issues:** Small single-watershed dataset; limited events for training and validation.

### [Wavelet regression model for short-term streamflow forecasting.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2010.06.013)
Kisi (2010), *Journal of Hydrology*. 125 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves short-term (daily) streamflow forecasting by exploiting multi-scale information in past flows.

- **Data:** Daily streamflow records from river gauging stations; specific basins and periods not reported here.
- **Main result:** The wavelet regression model is reported to outperform the single ANN and AR benchmarks for one-day-ahead flow forecasts.
- **Open work:** Extending to longer lead times and to other basins and climate regimes.
- **Issues:** Uses only antecedent flows; wavelet decomposition over the full series can leak future information if not done causally; single-site evaluation.

### [A Stacking Ensemble Model of Various Machine Learning Models for Daily Runoff Forecasting](https://doi.org/10.3390/w15071265)
Lu et al. (2023), *Water*. 125 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves accuracy and stability of daily runoff (reservoir inflow) prediction for water resource management and flood control.

- **Data:** Daily inflow to the Fuchun River Reservoir, Qiantang River basin, China; predictor details and period not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Versus XGBoost and weighted-average ensembles, NSE rises 10.2% and 8.5%, RMSE drops 18.5% and 16.4%, MAE drops 28.2% and 18.7%; significant by Friedman and Nemenyi tests.
- **Open work:** Applying to other basins, longer lead times and probabilistic forecasting.
- **Issues:** Single reservoir; lead time and inputs unclear; no uncertainty quantification or extreme-flood analysis.

### [Artificial neural networks in drought prediction in the 21st century-A scientometric analysis](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.asoc.2021.108080)
Dikshit et al. (2021), *Applied Soft Computing*. 124 citations.

- **Data:** Literature database of published studies on ANN drought prediction; details of corpus not reported here.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the available metadata.
- **Open work:** Not reported; likely calls for explainable, hybrid and multi-index drought models.
- **Issues:** No abstract available; corpus selection and coverage could not be verified.

### [Evaluation of global optimization methods for conceptual rainfall-runoff model calibration](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0273-1223(97)00461-7)
Cooper et al. (1997), *Water Science and Technology*. 124 citations.

### [Geomorphology-based artificial neural networks (GANNs) for estimation of direct runoff over watersheds](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-1694(02)00313-x)
Zhang et al. (2003), *Journal of Hydrology*. 124 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates direct runoff over watersheds by embedding geomorphologic information into neural network structure to make it more physically interpretable.
- **Architecture:** Geomorphology-based artificial neural networks (GANNs) whose structure follows the geomorphologic instantaneous unit hydrograph concept, linking network weights to flow paths.

### [River flow forecasting with artificial neural networks using satellite observed precipitation pre-processed with flow length and travel time information: case study of the Ganges river basin](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-13-1607-2009)
Akhtar et al. (2009), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 124 citations.

- **Main goal:** Incorporates spatially distributed satellite precipitation into ANN river flow forecasting for a large basin without full distributed hydrological modelling.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (ANN) models with rainfall preprocessed using flow length and travel time information, compared across different hydrological preprocessing schemes.
- **Data:** Satellite-observed (remotely sensed) precipitation and local streamflow measurements for the Ganges river basin.
- **Main result:** ANN forecasts discharge 3 days ahead with acceptable accuracy, where pre-processed rainfall has marginal influence; at 7–10 days it adds noticeable value though overall performance deteriorates.

### [Statistical downscaling of river flows](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2010.02.030)
Tisseuil et al. (2010), *Journal of Hydrology*. 124 citations.

- **Main goal:** Downscales large-scale atmospheric circulation to local river flows to assess hydrological impacts of climate.

- **Data:** Large-scale reanalysis predictors (NCEP) and daily flows at French river gauging stations.
- **Main result:** Nonlinear methods (GAM, boosted trees, MLP) generally outperform the linear GLM in reproducing observed flows.

- **Issues:** Statistical downscaling assumes stationary predictor–flow relationships under climate change; inherits reanalysis biases.

Jalalkamali et al. (2015), *International Journal of Environmental Science and Technology*. 124 citations.

Çıtakoğlu et al. (2013), *Water Resources Management*. 124 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates monthly mean reference evapotranspiration (ET0) across Turkey where full meteorological data are limited.

### [Modeling reference evapotranspiration with calculated targets. Assessment and implications](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agwat.2014.10.028)
Martí et al. (2015), *Agricultural Water Management*. 124 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses the consequences of training and testing data-driven ET0 models with calculated FAO56-PM targets instead of lysimeter measurements.
- **Architecture:** Gene expression programming (GEP) symbolic regression models, compared with FAO56 Penman–Monteith and calibrated Hargreaves equations; non-deep method.
- **Data:** Lysimeter measurements and calculated ET0 targets at stations (Spain), with two input combinations and k-fold testing including cross-station evaluation.
- **Main result:** GEP trained on lysimeter targets beats HG and FAO56-PM locally, but loses accuracy cross-station; models trained on calculated targets degrade markedly against lysimeter benchmarks.

### [Comparative applications of data-driven models representing water table fluctuations](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2019.02.051)
Jeong et al. (2018), *Journal of Hydrology*. 123 citations.

- **Issues:** Only two wells; quantitative metrics are not reported in the abstract; site-specific results.

Pramanik et al. (2009), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 119 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts river flow at a downstream location from upstream flows, comparing two data-driven approaches for operational flow forecasting.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward artificial neural network (ANN) compared with an adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS).
- **Data:** Daily flow records from gauging stations in the Mahanadi River system, India.
- **Main result:** ANFIS gives somewhat better flow predictions than the ANN, with both performing acceptably. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Adding rainfall and catchment inputs and testing on extreme flood events.
- **Issues:** Single river system; limited treatment of high flows and no uncertainty quantification.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Groundwater Level Modeling with Machine Learning: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis](https://doi.org/10.3390/w14060949)
Ahmadi et al. (2022), *Water*. 119 citations.

- **Main goal:** Systematically reviews machine learning for groundwater monitoring and prediction and quantifies model accuracy through meta-analysis.
- **Architecture:** Review and meta-analysis of regression machine learning models (feed-forward artificial neural networks, support vector machines, tree ensembles and others) for groundwater.
- **Data:** 197 peer-reviewed articles from 2010–2020 across 28 countries, following the Center for Evidence-Based Conservation protocol.
- **Main result:** Feed-forward ANNs are most used and most accurate, but performance depends more on input information than model choice; about 10–12 years of monthly data are needed.
- **Open work:** Merging deep learning with physics-based models and new data such as InSAR to raise spatiotemporal resolution.
- **Issues:** Meta-analysis across heterogeneous studies with differing metrics and sites; publication bias toward successful applications.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Modeling of monthly rainfall and runoff of Urmia lake basin using “feed-forward neural network” and “time series analysis” model](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wri.2014.10.003)
Farajzadeh et al. (2014), *Water Resources and Industry*. 119 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts monthly rainfall and the resulting runoff into Urmia Lake, Iran, whose declining level causes ecological problems, to support water management.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward neural network (MLP) compared with an ARIMA time-series model; runoff derived from forecast rainfall with a runoff coefficient regime.
- **Data:** Monthly rainfall and runoff for the Urmia lake basin over 39 years; 6-year test period, with forecasts for 2012–2017.
- **Main result:** Feed-forward NN rainfall estimates are close to ARIMA, with correlation 0.62 and RMSE 12.43 mm over the 6-year test period.
- **Open work:** Including climate predictors and testing physically based runoff models would improve multi-year projections.
- **Issues:** Modest correlation; multi-year extrapolation from past rainfall alone and a fixed runoff coefficient ignore climate and land-use change.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Machine-learning methods for stream water temperature prediction](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-25-2951-2021)
Feigl et al. (2021), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 118 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops and benchmarks machine learning models for daily river water temperature prediction to support water management under climate change.
- **Architecture:** Six models: stepwise linear regression, random forest, XGBoost, feed-forward neural networks (MLP) and two recurrent neural networks, tuned by Bayesian optimization, versus linear regression and air2stream.
- **Data:** 10 Austrian catchments (200 to 96,000 km2) with daily air temperature, runoff, precipitation and global radiation.
- **Main result:** Mean RMSE of 0.55 °C versus 1.55 °C for linear regression and 0.98 °C for air2stream; FNN and XGBoost each best in 4 of 10 catchments, RNNs best in the largest.
- **Open work:** Regional multi-catchment models and applications to future climate; R package wateRtemp released.
- **Issues:** High sensitivity to hyperparameters (FNN RMSE standard deviation 1.60 °C); single-catchment models; Austrian setting only.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A novel approach to parameter uncertainty analysis of hydrological models using neural networks](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-13-1235-2009)
Shrestha et al. (2009), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 118 citations.

- **Main goal:** Replaces time-consuming Monte Carlo parameter uncertainty analysis of hydrological models with a fast emulator usable in real time.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (MLP) trained to map model inputs to uncertainty descriptors (prediction quantiles) derived from Monte Carlo realizations.
- **Data:** Monte Carlo simulations of the lumped conceptual HBV model for the Brue catchment, United Kingdom.
- **Main result:** The ANN reproduces Monte Carlo prediction intervals reasonably accurately on verification data.
- **Open work:** Applying the emulator to complex distributed models and to real-time forecasting with short lead times.
- **Issues:** Only parametric uncertainty is considered; single catchment and model; the emulator inherits the Monte Carlo setup assumptions.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Application of fuzzy logic to forecast seasonal runoff](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.1359)
Mahabir et al. (2003), *Hydrological Processes*. 118 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts seasonal spring runoff volumes in snowmelt-dominated basins where regression methods are unreliable.
- **Architecture:** Fuzzy logic (rule-based fuzzy inference) model using snowpack, soil moisture and precipitation indices.
- **Data:** Historical seasonal runoff and snow and climate indices for basins in Alberta, Canada.
- **Main result:** The fuzzy model categorises runoff (e.g. low, average, high) more reliably than regression-based forecasts.
- **Open work:** Extending to more basins and integrating climate signals into the rule base.
- **Issues:** Coarse categorical output; rule base partly expert-defined; short records.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Application of BP Neural Network Algorithm in Traditional Hydrological Model for Flood Forecasting](https://doi.org/10.3390/w9010048)
Wang et al. (2017), *Water*. 118 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves flood forecasting by combining a data-driven error correction with a traditional hydrological model.
- **Architecture:** Improved backpropagation neural network (MLP) coupled to the semi-distributed Xinanjiang (XAJ) model to update flow forecast errors without losing lead time.
- **Data:** A real flood forecasting case study basin in China; data details not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** The method significantly increases flood forecast accuracy, and its global correction outperforms second-order autoregressive real-time correction.
- **Open work:** Testing across more basins and events and quantifying forecast uncertainty.
- **Issues:** Single case study; no numbers reported in the abstract, and error correction depends on observed flows being available in real time.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A Comprehensive Survey of Machine Learning Methodologies with Emphasis in Water Resources Management](https://doi.org/10.3390/app132212147)
Drogkoula et al. (2023), *Applied Sciences*. 118 citations.

- **Main goal:** Surveys machine learning methods and their applications in water resources management amid climate change and resource pressures.
- **Architecture:** Review of ML algorithm taxonomy (supervised prediction, clustering, reinforcement learning) mapped to water management tasks.
- **Data:** Literature on irrigation optimization, water quality monitoring, flood forecasting and water demand forecasting using remote sensing, sensors and social media data.
- **Main result:** Provides a comparative mapping of ML methods to water management tasks and a tabulation of representative studies.
- **Open work:** Addressing data heterogeneity, stakeholder education and cost barriers to wider AI adoption.
- **Issues:** Broad narrative survey without systematic search protocol or quantitative synthesis.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Comparing various artificial neural network types for water temperature prediction in rivers](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2015.07.044)
Piotrowski et al. (2015), *Journal of Hydrology*. 118 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares neural network types for predicting river water temperature, which matters for aquatic ecosystems and water use.
- **Architecture:** Several artificial neural network types, including multilayer perceptron (MLP) and other variants, compared with simpler models.
- **Data:** Observed river water temperature with meteorological and hydrological inputs; specific rivers and periods not reported here.
- **Main result:** The study ranks the network types by prediction skill; the specific ranking and error values are not available without the abstract.
- **Open work:** Assessment under climate change scenarios and in other river types.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; findings may be specific to the studied catchments and inputs.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Performance Evaluation of Artificial Neural Networks for Runoff Prediction](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2000)5:4(424))
Elshorbagy et al. (2000), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 117 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates how well artificial neural networks predict runoff and how their performance should be assessed.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward artificial neural networks compared with regression-based alternatives.
- **Data:** Streamflow and hydrometeorological records from a Canadian basin (Red River, Manitoba).
- **Main result:** ANNs predict runoff competitively, and the study highlights the need for multiple performance measures. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Better evaluation criteria for peak flows and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Single basin; standard performance measures may hide poor peak-flow performance.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Forecasting of hydrologic time series with ridge regression in feature space](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2006.07.003)
Yu et al. (2007), *Journal of Hydrology*. 117 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts hydrologic time series with a kernel method that is faster to train than support vector regression.
- **Architecture:** Kernel ridge regression in feature space combined with phase-space (chaos-based) reconstruction of the time series.
- **Data:** Daily river flow series from benchmark catchments. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Ridge regression in feature space matches support vector machine accuracy at lower computational cost. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Automated selection of embedding and kernel parameters and tests on more catchments.
- **Issues:** Results depend on embedding and kernel choices; univariate inputs only.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Division-based rainfall-runoff simulations with BP neural networks and Xinanjiang model](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2008.12.032)
Ju et al. (2009), *Neurocomputing*. 117 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves rainfall-runoff simulation by combining a conceptual model with neural networks applied to divided parts of the flow regime.
- **Architecture:** Back-propagation (BP) neural networks combined with the Xinanjiang conceptual model in a division-based scheme.
- **Data:** Rainfall and runoff records from a Chinese catchment. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** The division-based hybrid improves simulations over a single model. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Testing other division criteria and catchments.
- **Issues:** Single-catchment evidence; division thresholds are subjective.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Forecasting flows in Apalachicola River using neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.1492)
Huang et al. (2004), *Hydrological Processes*. 117 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts river flows in the Apalachicola River, Florida, with data-driven models to support water management.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward artificial neural networks using upstream flows and antecedent observations.
- **Data:** Daily streamflow records from gauging stations on the Apalachicola River system.
- **Main result:** Neural networks forecast flows accurately at short lead times. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Including rainfall forecasts and extending lead times.
- **Issues:** Single river; skill expected to decline at longer leads and for extreme flows.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [A Neural Networks Approach for Deriving Irrigation Reservoir Operating Rules](https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1015563820136)
Cancelliere et al. (2002), *Water Resources Management*. 117 citations.

- **Main goal:** Derives monthly operating rules for an irrigation reservoir that approximate optimal release policies.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network trained on optimal releases from dynamic programming to form operating rules.
- **Data:** Inflow, storage and demand data for an irrigation reservoir in Sicily, Italy, with optimised releases as targets.
- **Main result:** ANN-based rules reproduce optimal releases better than linear rules and reduce irrigation shortages in simulation.
- **Open work:** Extending to multireservoir systems and including inflow forecasts.
- **Issues:** Depends on deterministic optimisation of historical inflows; single reservoir.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Spatial Downscaling of GRACE Data Based on XGBoost Model for Improved Understanding of Hydrological Droughts in the Indus Basin Irrigation System (IBIS)](https://doi.org/10.3390/rs15040873)
Ali et al. (2023), *Remote Sensing*. 117 citations.

- **Main goal:** Downscales GRACE terrestrial water storage to monitor hydrological droughts in the Indus Basin Irrigation System at finer resolution.
- **Architecture:** Extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) compared with an artificial neural network for downscaling; partial least squares regression for drought–climate links.
- **Data:** GRACE TWSA downscaled from 1° to 0.25° with hydroclimatic predictors; compared with SPEI and sc-PDSI drought indices.
- **Main result:** XGBoost outperforms the ANN (NSE 0.99, R 0.99, RMSE 5.22 mm, MAE 2.75 mm); eight drought episodes detected, and potential evaporation is the second strongest driver after precipitation.
- **Open work:** Validation of downscaled storage against independent in situ groundwater data.
- **Issues:** Near-perfect scores are against GRACE-derived values, not independent fine-scale truth; downscaled detail is limited by predictor information.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Hydrologically Informed Machine Learning for Rainfall‐Runoff Modeling: A Genetic Programming‐Based Toolkit for Automatic Model Induction](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019wr026933)
Chadalawada et al. (2020), *Water Resources Research*. 116 citations.

- **Main goal:** Automates the construction of physically meaningful rainfall-runoff models from flexible modelling frameworks, avoiding time-consuming manual trial of configurations.
- **Architecture:** Genetic programming (evolutionary computation) model induction toolkit (ML-RR-MI) that searches SUPERFLEX and FUSE building blocks to build lumped conceptual models.
- **Data:** Rainfall-runoff data for the Blackwater River basin, Alabama, USA.
- **Main result:** Evolved model configurations are consistent with fieldwork and previous research findings; quantitative skill is not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Extending to semi-distributed models (later done in MIKA-SHA) and other building-block libraries.
- **Issues:** Single basin; computational cost of the search; no comparison with deep learning in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Challenges in Applying Machine Learning Models for Hydrological Inference: A Case Study for Flooding Events Across Germany](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019wr025924)
Schmidt et al. (2020), *Water Resources Research*. 116 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether machine learning models can be used for hydrological inference, not just prediction, using flood events across Germany.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural networks (MLP) and random forest compared with multiple linear regression, interpreted using permuted feature importance.
- **Data:** Large dataset of flood events across Germany with catchment and event predictors.
- **Main result:** ML models beat linear regression and reflect basic hydrological principles, but feature importances differ across algorithms, revealing equifinality that hampers inference.
- **Open work:** Using multiple algorithms and interpretation methods within cross-validation when doing ML-based inference.
- **Issues:** Inference conclusions depend on chosen algorithms; correlated predictors complicate importance estimates.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Modelling groundwater levels in an urban coastal aquifer using artificial neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.6686)
Krishna et al. (2008), *Hydrological Processes*. 116 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models groundwater levels in an urban coastal aquifer to support groundwater management under pumping and seawater intrusion risk.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward artificial neural networks trained with back-propagation variants (e.g. Levenberg-Marquardt).
- **Data:** Observed groundwater levels, rainfall and related records from wells in a coastal city aquifer in India.
- **Main result:** Neural networks reproduce observed groundwater level fluctuations well. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Adding pumping data and longer forecasts for management scenarios.
- **Issues:** Few wells and short records; no physical constraints on groundwater dynamics.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [A split-step particle swarm optimization algorithm in river stage forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2007.09.004)
Chau (2007), *Journal of Hydrology*. 116 citations.

- **Main goal:** Speeds up and improves training of neural networks used for river stage forecasting.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward neural network trained by a split-step particle swarm optimization algorithm (PSO followed by Levenberg-Marquardt).
- **Data:** Water level records from the Shing Mun River, Hong Kong.
- **Main result:** The split-step PSO trains faster and gives more accurate stage forecasts than standard back-propagation or PSO alone.
- **Open work:** Applying the hybrid training to other hydrological problems and lead times.
- **Issues:** Single river; gains depend on optimiser settings.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A non-linear neural network technique for updating of river flow forecasts](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-5-577-2001)
Shamseldin et al. (2001), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 116 citations.

- **Main goal:** Updates conceptual model river flow forecasts using recent errors to improve real-time accuracy.
- **Architecture:** Non-linear auto-regressive exogenous-input (NARX) updating procedure built on a multilayer neural network, compared with linear ARX updating.
- **Data:** Daily discharge forecasts from the SMAR conceptual model on five catchments with different climatic conditions.
- **Main result:** The NARX neural network updating procedure outperforms the linear ARX procedure.
- **Open work:** Testing at sub-daily time steps and with other conceptual models.
- **Issues:** Daily data only; updating limited to output correction rather than model states.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Forward and inverse modeling of water flow in unsaturated soils with discontinuous hydraulic conductivities using physics-informed neural networks with domain decomposition](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-26-4469-2022)
Bandai et al. (2022), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 116 citations.

- **Main goal:** Solves forward and inverse problems of unsaturated soil water flow (Richardson–Richards equation) without requiring precisely prescribed boundary conditions.
- **Architecture:** Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) with adaptive activation functions and domain decomposition (separate networks per soil layer).
- **Data:** Analytical and numerical reference solutions for homogeneous and layered soils, and sparse synthetic soil moisture measurements.
- **Main result:** PINN solutions match traditional numerical methods, correctly simulate layered soils with discontinuous conductivity, and recover water fluxes from sparse data.
- **Open work:** Improving robustness to initialization and computational speed, and applying to field data.
- **Issues:** PINNs are sensitive to network initialization and much slower than traditional numerical solvers; tests are largely synthetic.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Pan evaporation modeling using six different heuristic computing methods in different climates of China](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2016.11.059)
Wang et al. (2017), *Journal of Hydrology*. 116 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates pan evaporation across different climate zones of China, important for water balance and irrigation planning.
- **Architecture:** Six heuristic methods including multilayer perceptron (MLP), generalized regression neural network, fuzzy genetic, least squares support vector regression, MARS and adaptive neuro-fuzzy models, compared with empirical equations.
- **Data:** Daily meteorological data and pan evaporation from stations across different climates of China.
- **Main result:** Heuristic ML methods generally outperform empirical formulas, with neural-network-type models among the best; skill varies by climate region.
- **Open work:** Testing spatial transferability and use of fewer inputs at ungauged stations.
- **Issues:** Station-based results may not transfer to other regions; no uncertainty analysis.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Rapid Prediction Model for Urban Floods Based on a Light Gradient Boosting Machine Approach and Hydrological–Hydraulic Model](https://doi.org/10.1007/s13753-023-00465-2)
Xu et al. (2023), *International Journal of Disaster Risk Science*. 116 citations.

- **Main goal:** Enables rapid real-time urban flood prediction in coastal cities, where physically based models are too slow.
- **Architecture:** Light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM) trained on outputs of a PCSWMM hydrological–hydraulic model, tuned by grid search and K-fold cross-validation; compared with random forest, XGBoost and KNN.
- **Data:** Simulated inundation from PCSWMM driven by rainfall and tide level scenarios for Haidian Island, Hainan, China.
- **Main result:** LightGBM achieves NSE 0.9896 on the test set and outperforms random forest, XGBoost and KNN; tide level variables dominate inundation depth.
- **Open work:** Validation with observed flood events and extension to other coastal cities.
- **Issues:** Trained and tested on simulator outputs, so it inherits PCSWMM biases; site-specific model.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A Comparative Study of Daily Pan Evaporation Estimation Using ANN, Regression and Climate Based Models](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11269-009-9514-2)
Shirsath et al. (2010), *Water Resources Management*. 116 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates daily pan evaporation, a key input for irrigation and water balance, comparing data-driven and climate-based approaches.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (MLP-type ANN) compared with multiple regression and conventional climate-based evaporation models.
- **Data:** Daily meteorological observations and measured pan evaporation from a station; location and period are not reported here.
- **Main result:** Not reported here; the study ranks ANN, regression and climate-based models for daily pan evaporation estimation.
- **Open work:** Test transferability to other stations and climates and compare with newer ML methods.
- **Issues:** Likely single-site data with limited record length; no abstract available to confirm metrics or validation design.

### [Optimizing neural networks for river flow forecasting – Evolutionary Computation methods versus the Levenberg–Marquardt approach](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2011.06.019)
Piotrowski et al. (2011), *Journal of Hydrology*. 116 citations.

- **Main goal:** Investigates how best to train neural networks for river flow forecasting, comparing evolutionary computation optimizers with gradient-based training.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural networks trained with several evolutionary computation algorithms (e.g. differential evolution, particle swarm) versus the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm.
- **Data:** Observed river flow and related hydrological time series from a catchment; details are not reported here.
- **Main result:** Not reported here; the study compares the forecasting skill and efficiency of evolutionary versus Levenberg–Marquardt training.
- **Open work:** Assess training strategies for deeper networks and multiple catchments.
- **Issues:** Conclusions depend on the chosen catchment, network sizes and optimizer settings; no abstract available to confirm results.

### [Artificial neural networks for streamflow prediction](https://doi.org/10.1080/00221680209499899)
Dolling et al. (2002), *Journal of Hydraulic Research*. 115 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts streamflow with artificial neural networks as an alternative to conceptual and statistical models.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward artificial neural networks.
- **Data:** Streamflow and hydrometeorological records from a mountain basin. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Neural networks give accurate streamflow predictions. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Testing on more basins and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Limited data; no uncertainty quantification.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Evaluation of artificial neural network techniques for flow forecasting in the River Yangtze, China](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-6-619-2002)
Dawson et al. (2002), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 115 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates neural networks for six-hourly flow forecasting on the River Yangtze and compares them with conventional statistical techniques.

Nanda et al. (2016), *Journal of Hydrology*. 115 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops a real-time flood forecasting model driven by satellite rainfall to support warning in data-scarce basins.

### [Graph neural network for groundwater level forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2022.128792)
Bai et al. (2023), *Journal of Hydrology*. 115 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts groundwater levels across a well network by exploiting spatial dependencies between wells.

### [Simulation of river stage using artificial neural network and MIKE 11 hydrodynamic model](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cageo.2009.07.012)
Panda et al. (2010), *Computers & Geosciences*. 115 citations.

### [Reconstruction of GRACE Total Water Storage Through Automated Machine Learning](https://doi.org/10.1029/2020wr028666)
Sun et al. (2020), *Water Resources Research*. 114 citations.

- **Main goal:** Fills the roughly 1-year gap between GRACE and GRACE-FO total water storage records to maintain data continuity.

- **Data:** GRACE/GRACE-FO total water storage anomalies over CONUS with meteorological and climatic predictors.

Koya et al. (2023), *arXiv*. 114 citations.

- **Architecture:** Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT), combining LSTM recurrence with attention, compared with LSTM and transformer models.

### [Application of adaptive fuzzy rule-based models for reconstruction of missing precipitation events](https://doi.org/10.1080/02626660009492339)
Abebe et al. (2000), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 114 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reconstructs missing precipitation records from neighbouring gauges to complete hydrological datasets.

- **Issues:** Performance depends on correlation between gauges; rule generation is data-hungry.

### [Retrieving surface roughness and soil moisture from synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data using neural networks](https://doi.org/10.5589/m02-066)
Baghdadi et al. (2002), *Canadian Journal of Remote Sensing*. 114 citations.

- **Main goal:** Retrieves surface roughness and soil moisture from SAR backscatter for bare agricultural soils.

### [Neural network modelling of non-linear hydrological relationships](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-11-1563-2007)

Xiong et al. (2002), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 108 citations.

- **Open work:** Extend to longer lead times and other catchments.
- **Issues:** Single-basin study; performance on extreme floods not quantified.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Generalisation for neural networks through data sampling and training procedures, with applications to streamflow predictions](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-8-940-2004)
Anctil et al. (2004), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 97 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares generalisation techniques for neural network streamflow models to give practitioners guidelines for building models that infer behaviour beyond the training data.
- **Architecture:** Multi-layer perceptron neural networks trained by Levenberg-Marquardt, with five generalisation approaches: stop training, Bayesian regularisation, stacking, bagging and boosting.
- **Data:** Streamflow modelling in six catchments with diverse hydrological behaviours.
- **Main result:** All approaches beat standard networks; stacking, bagging and boosting improve most, stacking slightly best but inconsistent across catchments.
- **Open work:** Authors recommend combining stop training or Bayesian regularisation with bagging or boosting; further testing in other catchments remains.
- **Issues:** Gains from stacking are small and catchment-dependent; ensemble methods increase computational cost.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Knowledge Extraction from Trained Neural Network River Flow Models](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2005)10:4(264))
Sudheer (2005), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 97 citations.

- **Main goal:** Extracts physically interpretable knowledge from trained neural network river flow models to address their black-box nature.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward neural network (MLP) river flow models analysed with sensitivity and input-contribution techniques.
- **Data:** River flow and rainfall records from a catchment; details not reported in the available information.
- **Main result:** The analysis shows the trained networks capture physically plausible relations between inputs and flow.
- **Open work:** Develop general interpretability methods for hydrological neural networks.
- **Issues:** Interpretation techniques are approximate and case-specific.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Optimal tree-based release rules for real-time flood control operations on a multipurpose multireservoir system.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2008.11.038)
Wei et al. (2009), *Journal of Hydrology*. 97 citations.

- **Main goal:** Derives real-time reservoir release rules for flood control in a multipurpose multireservoir system.
- **Architecture:** Decision tree models learning release rules from optimal releases computed by an optimization model.
- **Data:** Historical typhoon flood events and multireservoir operation data from a river basin in Taiwan.
- **Main result:** Tree-based release rules approximate optimal operations and reduce flood peaks compared with conventional rules.
- **Open work:** Incorporate forecast uncertainty in inflows and test on new events.
- **Issues:** Limited number of flood events for rule learning; performance depends on optimization targets.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Predicting groundwater level using traditional and deep machine learning algorithms](https://doi.org/10.3389/fenvs.2024.1291327)
Feng et al. (2024), *Frontiers in Environmental Science*. 97 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts groundwater level in Izeh City, Khuzestan, Iran, to support water resource management under scarcity.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of convolutional neural network (CNN), recurrent neural network (RNN), support vector machine (SVM), decision tree, random forest and generative adversarial network (GAN).
- **Data:** Local records of groundwater extraction rate, rainfall rate and river flow rate as inputs for Izeh City.
- **Main result:** CNN performs best with RMSE 0.0558 and R2 0.9948 and no outlier predictions; river flow and extraction are the most influential inputs.
- **Open work:** Adding more input variables and applying the approach to other water-scarce regions.
- **Issues:** Single site with three inputs; extremely high R2 suggests possible overfitting or leakage; GAN use for regression is unusual.
- *Basis: abstract*

Mehr et al. (2015), *International Journal of Environmental Science and Technology*. 97 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts monthly streamflow at a downstream station from upstream station records, useful where only successive gauges are available.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of different artificial neural network (ANN) algorithms for successive-station streamflow prediction.
- **Data:** Monthly streamflow records from successive gauging stations on a river; details are not reported here.
- **Main result:** Relative performance of the ANN algorithms is reported in the paper; values are not available here.
- **Open work:** Adding climatic inputs and testing on more river systems.
- **Issues:** Few stations; monthly data only; no uncertainty quantification.

### [Fractional snow cover mapping through artificial neural network analysis of MODIS surface reflectance](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2011.07.018)
Dobreva et al. (2011), *Remote Sensing of Environment*. 97 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps fractional snow cover at sub-pixel level from MODIS, improving on binary snow maps in mixed pixels.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network regression from MODIS surface reflectance to fractional snow cover.
- **Data:** MODIS surface reflectance with fractional snow cover reference derived from higher-resolution Landsat imagery.
- **Main result:** The neural network estimates fractional snow cover with accuracy comparable to or better than index-based approaches.
- **Open work:** Testing across more land cover types, seasons and regions.
- **Issues:** Reference data from Landsat are limited in time; forest canopy and illumination effects remain challenging.

### [Forecasting of meteorological drought using Wavelet-ANFIS hybrid model for different time steps (case study: southeastern part of east Azerbaijan province, Iran)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11069-013-0716-9)
Shirmohammadi et al. (2013), *Natural Hazards*. 97 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts meteorological drought at several time steps in southeastern East Azerbaijan, Iran.

### [Continental-scale streamflow modeling of basins with reservoirs: Towards a coherent deep-learning-based strategy](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2021.126455)
Ouyang et al. (2021), *Journal of Hydrology*. 96 citations.

- **Main goal:** Determines which dam-influenced basins can be modeled by deep learning for continental-scale daily streamflow prediction using readily available information.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks trained on basin groups defined by reservoir degree of regulation (dor), purpose and diversion, in a divide-and-conquer strategy.
- **Data:** 3,557 basins over the contiguous United States (83% dammed), extending reference-basin datasets with reservoir attributes (e.g. GAGES-II-type information).
- **Main result:** Training on all basins gives median NSE 0.74; pooled training yields median NSE 0.73, 0.78 and 0.71 for zero-, small- and large-dor basins; reference-trained models transfer poorly and migrating models between dor groups fails.
- **Open work:** Separately modeling reservoirs for irrigation, fire protection, hydropower and flood control, and explicit representation of large-dor reservoirs.
- **Issues:** Large-dor basins with irrigation dams remain poorly simulated; no explicit reservoir operation data; dammed basins must be in the training set.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A graph neural network (GNN) approach to basin-scale river network learning: the role of physics-based connectivity and data fusion](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-26-5163-2022)
Sun et al. (2022), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 96 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops a fast basin-scale river network model for streamflow forecasting, since high-resolution vector-based river network models are computationally demanding.
- **Architecture:** Multistage physics-guided graph neural network (GNN) pretrained to emulate a vector-based river routing model, fine-tuned on gauge observations, with graph-based data fusion for bias correction and graph coarsening for scalability.
- **Data:** Outputs of a high-resolution vector-based river network model and streamflow gauge observations in a snow-dominated western US watershed and a larger basin.
- **Main result:** The GNN surrogate reproduces the process model with median KGE above 0.97; data fusion improves KGE by up to 50% at cross-validation gauges; coarsened graphs give comparable skill at a fraction of training cost.
- **Open work:** Scaling to continental river networks and determining the degree of physical realism needed in large-scale GNN river models.
- **Issues:** Surrogate inherits biases of the process-based model; tested in a limited number of basins; forecasting skill under extremes not detailed.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Intelligent control for modeling of real‐time reservoir operation, part II: artificial neural network with operating rule curves](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.5582)
Chang et al. (2005), *Hydrological Processes*. 96 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models real-time reservoir operation decisions by learning from operating rule curves.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (specific type not specified in the available information) incorporating reservoir operating rule curves; part II of a study on intelligent control.
- **Data:** Reservoir operation records from a reservoir in Taiwan.
- **Main result:** The neural network with rule curves reproduces operator decisions and improves operation performance.
- **Open work:** Combine with inflow forecasts and multi-objective optimization.
- **Issues:** Single reservoir; learned rules reflect historical operating practice.

### [Monthly runoff simulation: Comparing and combining conceptual and neural network models](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2005.08.007)
Nilsson et al. (2006), *Journal of Hydrology*. 96 citations.

- **Main result:** Combining the conceptual model with a neural network performs best, better than either model alone.
- **Open work:** Extend hybrid approaches to daily scales and other climates.
- **Issues:** Small number of catchments; neural networks extrapolate poorly beyond training range.

### [Rainfall‐runoff modelling using artificial neural networks technique: a Blue Nile catchment case study](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.5932)
Antar et al. (2006), *Hydrological Processes*. 96 citations.

- **Main goal:** Applies neural networks to rainfall-runoff modelling of the Blue Nile catchment where data are scarce.

- **Data:** Rainfall and discharge records for the Blue Nile catchment.
- **Main result:** The neural network simulates runoff with good accuracy for the case study.
- **Open work:** Improve rainfall inputs and test for climate change scenarios.
- **Issues:** Sparse data; single-catchment study.

### [Comparison of Artificial Intelligence Techniques for river flow forecasting](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-12-123-2008)
Firat (2008), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 96 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares artificial intelligence methods for daily river flow forecasting to identify the most suitable approach.

- **Main result:** ANFIS outperforms GRNN and FFNN models and provides high accuracy and reliability for daily river flow forecasting.

Kornelsen et al. (2014), *Water Resources Research*. 96 citations.

- **Data:** In situ soil moisture observations; sites and period are not reported here.
- **Main result:** Data-driven models estimate root-zone soil moisture with useful skill; values are not available here.

- **Issues:** Site-specific training; transfer to ungauged locations uncertain.

### [Runoff forecasting by artificial neural network and conventional model](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aej.2012.01.005)
Ghumman et al. (2011), *Alexandria Engineering Journal*. 96 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops a rainfall-runoff model suited to short and low-quality datasets in a Pakistani watershed.

### [Machine-learning- and deep-learning-based streamflow prediction in a hilly catchment for future scenarios using CMIP6 GCM data](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-27-1047-2023)
Singh et al. (2023), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 95 citations.

- **Main goal:** Projects future streamflow in the Himalayan Sutlej River basin under climate change for water resource planning.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of Gaussian linear regression, generalized additive model, MARS, artificial neural network (MLP), random forest and a 1D convolutional neural network; random forest selected for projections.
- **Data:** Daily data 1979–2009 at Kasol for training; bias-corrected CMIP6 output from six GCMs downscaled to 0.25° under SSP245 and SSP585 for 2041–2070 and 2071–2100.
- **Main result:** Random forest performs best (test R2 0.78, NSE 0.71, KGE 0.82); mean annual streamflow rises about 0.8–1.4%, monsoon flow increases ~10–13%, while pre-monsoon and winter flows decline (winter ~-22%).
- **Open work:** Incorporating glacier and snowmelt dynamics and land-use change, and assessing downstream agricultural water impacts.
- **Issues:** Statistical models trained on historical relationships may not hold under future climate; GCM and downscaling uncertainty; glacier retreat not explicitly modeled.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Surrogate optimization of deep neural networks for groundwater predictions](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10898-020-00912-0)
Müller et al. (2019), *Journal of Global Optimization*. 95 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provide accurate, cheap groundwater level predictions for water managers who cannot run complex mechanistic models, and find good hyperparameters efficiently.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of four deep learning models including MLP, LSTM and convolutional neural network (CNN), with hyperparameters tuned by two surrogate-model-based optimizers and random sampling.
- **Data:** Groundwater level observations in Butte County, California, with streamflow, precipitation and ambient temperature as predictors.
- **Main result:** Optimized models reach RMSE of 2 m or less; the simple MLP outperforms LSTM and CNN in accuracy and time-to-solution.
- **Open work:** Testing on more wells and regions, longer horizons, and additional predictors such as pumping.
- **Issues:** Single study area; small data may favour simple networks, and no uncertainty quantification is reported.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Flood Prediction and Uncertainty Estimation Using Deep Learning](https://doi.org/10.3390/w12030884)
Gude et al. (2020), *Water*. 95 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predict river gauge height for flood forecasting with finer time steps and an estimate of prediction uncertainty.

- **Data:** Gauge height observations for the Meramec River at Valley Park, Missouri.
- **Main result:** The deep learning model is more accurate than the physical and statistical models in use and provides forecasts every 15 minutes instead of 6 hours; data sub-selection regularizes better than dropout.

- **Issues:** Single gauge site; few extreme floods to validate on, and gains over operational models are not quantified in the abstract.

### [Use of Radial Basis Function Type Artificial Neural Networks for Runoff Simulation](https://doi.org/10.1111/0885-9507.00089)
Jayawardena et al. (1998), *Computer-Aided Civil and Infrastructure Engineering*. 95 citations.

- **Main goal:** Investigates radial basis function neural networks for simulating runoff discharge from a small catchment.

He et al. (2023), *Water Research*. 95 citations.

### [A spatial–temporal graph deep learning model for urban flood nowcasting leveraging heterogeneous community features](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-32548-x)
Farahmand et al. (2021), *Scientific Reports*. 94 citations.

- **Main goal:** Nowcasts urban flood inundation during extreme weather events by combining physics-based and human-sensed data to improve situational awareness.

- **Data:** Arithmetic tasks, traffic forecasting, a pendulum, and a large hydrology benchmark (CAMELS-US rainfall-runoff).
- **Main result:** Sets a new state of the art for neural arithmetic units and for peak-flow prediction in the hydrology benchmark; its states correlate with real-world processes.
- **Open work:** Handling non-conserved fluxes and unobserved sinks, and extension to spatially distributed systems.
- **Issues:** Strict mass conservation can hurt when data have biases or unmeasured losses such as evapotranspiration; overall streamflow skill is not clearly above a standard LSTM.

- **Issues:** Single-basin case study; improvements described largely qualitatively in the abstract; computational cost of DA within WRF not discussed.

### [The suitability of a seasonal ensemble hybrid framework including data-driven approaches for hydrological forecasting](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-27-501-2023)
Hauswirth et al. (2023), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 27 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether a hybrid framework that drives data-driven hydrological models with seasonal reforecasts can give fast, flexible seasonal forecasts of discharge and surface water levels in the Netherlands.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid framework: five machine learning models of increasing complexity trained on historical observations, then forced with dynamical seasonal reforecasts; the individual model families are not named in the abstract.
- **Data:** Historical observations of discharge, precipitation, evaporation and sea level for Dutch stations; hindcasts forced with EFAS and ECMWF SEAS5 seasonal reforecasts; evaluated with ACC, CRPSS and BSS against climatology.
- **Main result:** Outperforms climatological reference by roughly 60 % for discharge and 80 % for surface water level; skill at one month lead for all initializations, extending to 2 to 3 months in spring through snowmelt; model differences become minor in hindcast mode.
- **Open work:** Adapting the framework to water managers' needs, for example inside model-predictive control, and improving the seasonal forcing inputs.
- **Issues:** Skill is limited by seasonal forecast uncertainty; models trained on observations but run on reforecast forcing, introducing input distribution shift; national single-country focus.

### [Hydrological Projections in the Third Pole Using Artificial Intelligence and an Observation‐Constrained Cryosphere‐Hydrology Model](https://doi.org/10.1029/2023ef004222)
Long et al. (2024), *Earth's Future*. 21 citations.

Liao et al. (2025), *Water Resources Research*. 21 citations.

Wang et al. (2024), *Water Resources Research*. 20 citations.

### [Interrogating process deficiencies in large-scale hydrologic models with interpretable machine learning](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-29-4457-2025)

He et al. (2024), *Water Resources Research*. 17 citations.

- **Main goal:** Corrects orographic quantitative precipitation estimate (QPE) errors in headwater basins to improve flood simulation and nowcasting.

### [An explainable deep learning model based on hydrological principles for flood simulation and forecasting](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-29-7217-2025)
Xiang et al. (2025), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 12 citations.

### [Global Flood Projection and Socioeconomic Implications Under a Deep Learning Framework](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024wr037139)
Kang et al. (2025), *Water Resources Research*. 12 citations.

- **Main goal:** Projects global changes in bivariate flood risk (peak and volume) and their socioeconomic exposure under climate change, and identifies drivers of streamflow change.

- **Data:** Bias-corrected outputs of 20 CMIP6 global climate models under four SSPs; global catchment streamflow; population and GDP exposure data.
- **Main result:** Under SSP3-7.0 the median joint return period of a 50-year flood falls to about 27.6 years, exposing 186 trillion USD and 4 billion people; downwelling shortwave radiation is the dominant driver of daily streamflow changes.

- **Issues:** Long model chain propagates GCM, bias-correction and hydrological model uncertainty; ML model extrapolates beyond training climate; exposure estimates are scenario-dependent.

- *Basis: abstract*

- **Main goal:** Forecasts global river discharge and floods while exploiting spatial connections across river networks, beyond local-scale deep learning models.

- **Data:** Long-term reanalysis data for pretraining (GloFAS-type discharge reanalysis), ECMWF HRES meteorological forecasts; global 0.05° grid, up to 7-day lead time.
- **Main result:** Provides reliable discharge predictions across flood return periods, including extreme floods, and lead times, surpassing both AI- and physics-based models.
- **Open work:** Extend lead times, add uncertainty quantification and evaluate operationally against gauged observations worldwide.
- **Issues:** Training on reanalysis targets inherits its biases; deterministic forecasts; quantitative gains not given in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Effective Deep Learning Seasonal Prediction Model for Summer Drought Over China](https://doi.org/10.1029/2023ef004409)
Liu et al. (2024), *Earth's Future*. 10 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves seasonal prediction of summer drought, measured by consecutive dry days (CDD), over China.
