- **Architecture:** Gradient boosting trees combined with three probabilistic methods: conformalized quantile regression, natural gradient boosting and conditional diffusion models; baselines are power curve, wake model and variational Gaussian process regression.
- **Data:** Four years of production data for all Belgian offshore wind farms with an ensemble of weather forecasts from multiple providers.
- **Main result:** Tree-based models clearly reduce MAE over deterministic baselines; the conditional diffusion model is best, improving MAE by 5% and CRPS by 12% over the GP baseline; using multiple weather forecasts improves point accuracy by 17% on average.
- **Open work:** Extend to longer horizons, other farm types and spatio-temporal dependence across farms.
- **Issues:** Single region; four years of data; performance depends on the available weather providers.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Climate change impacts on solar energy generation in the continental United States, forecasts from deep learning](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envsoft.2025.106535)
Nichols et al. (2025), *Environmental Modelling & Software*. 3 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses climate change impacts on solar energy generation across the continental United States using deep learning, as implied by the title.
- **Architecture:** Deep learning model (family not known) used to project solar generation; abstract not available.
- **Data:** Not reported (abstract missing); likely climate model projections over the continental US.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Likely needs multi-model uncertainty quantification and validation against observed generation.
- **Issues:** Abstract missing; projections depend on climate model biases and the learned mapping's validity under future climate.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [SolarSeer: Ultrafast and accurate 24-hour solar irradiance forecasts outperforming numerical weather prediction across the USA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03590)
Bai et al. (2025), *arXiv*. 3 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides fast 24-hour solar irradiance forecasting across CONUS without the cost of NWP data assimilation and PDE solving.
- **Architecture:** SolarSeer, an end-to-end large deep learning model mapping historical satellite observations to future cloud cover and irradiance. Network family not reported in the abstract.
- **Data:** Historical satellite observations over CONUS; evaluation against HRRR, reanalysis data and 1,800 ground stations.
- **Main result:** Over 1,500 times faster than NWP, producing 5 km 24-hour forecasts in under 3 s; RMSE reduced by 27.28% vs HRRR on reanalysis and 15.35% across stations.
- **Open work:** Extend to probabilistic forecasts and longer horizons and other regions.
- **Issues:** Satellite-only inputs may miss synoptic evolution beyond 24 h; deterministic.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Predicting Australian energy demand variability using weather data and machine learning](https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/ad9b3b)
Richardson et al. (2024), *Environmental Research Letters*. 2 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates long-term weather-driven variability of Australian energy demand, since demand records are short.
- **Architecture:** Machine learning regression models (type not specified in the abstract) using reanalysis weather predictors.
- **Data:** Daily demand 2010–2019 for Australian National Electricity Market states; reanalysis weather variables as predictors (product not named in the abstract); demand reconstructed for 1959–2022.
- **Main result:** Median errors 2–4% on held-out years; extreme-demand probability varies from half to twice across decades and up to 7 times when conditioned on ENSO phase.
- **Open work:** Include future climate projections and demand trends.
- **Issues:** Assumes the 2010s weather–demand relationship holds across 1959–2022, ignoring changes in technology, population and rooftop solar; inherits reanalysis biases.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Bridging CORDEX and CMIP6: machine learning downscaling for wind and solar energy droughts in central Europe](https://doi.org/10.1088/3049-4753/aea998)
Effenberger et al. (2025), *Machine Learning: Earth*. 2 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides regional climate information for renewable energy planning by emulating CORDEX regional climate models with machine learning, focusing on wind and solar energy droughts.
- **Architecture:** Machine learning emulators (two models; families not stated in the abstract) mapping GCM to RCM fields.
- **Data:** CMIP5 and CORDEX for training; CMIP6 for application; Central Europe.
- **Main result:** The emulator reproduces RCM data with sufficient accuracy and gives plausible results for unseen CMIP6 simulations; the number of low-wind, low-solar energy drought days in Central Europe is likely to decrease.
- **Open work:** Extend to other regions, variables and impact metrics, and use emulators to enlarge downscaled ensembles.
- **Issues:** Transfer to CMIP6 cannot be verified directly; emulator inherits RCM biases.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Combination of Deterministic and Probabilistic Meteorological Models to enhance Wind Farm Power Forecasts](https://doi.org/10.1088/1742-6596/75/1/012050)
Bremen (2007), *Journal of Physics: Conference Series*. 2 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves day-ahead wind farm power forecasts by combining deterministic and probabilistic numerical weather prediction models.
- **Architecture:** Neural network for model output statistics of each NWP model and for the aggregated power curve, combined via linear weighting or principal component regression; ensemble spread used for uncertainty.
- **Data:** ECMWF and HIRLAM forecasts and ECMWF ensemble predictions with power data from the Middelgrunden offshore wind farm.
- **Main result:** Combining two NWP models beats the best single model, cutting normalized day-ahead RMSE by 1% versus ECMWF (6% relative); low ensemble spread tends to go with low forecast error.
- **Open work:** More sophisticated combination methods for lead times beyond 24 h and use of ensemble spread for probabilistic power forecasts.
- **Issues:** Single wind farm; modest gains; spread-skill relation shown only with simple contingency diagrams.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Machine Learning‐Based Denoising of Surface Solar Irradiance Simulated With Monte Carlo Ray Tracing](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024jh000515)
Reeze et al. (2024), *Journal of Geophysical Research: Machine Learning and Computation*. 1 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reduces the cost of Monte Carlo ray-traced surface solar irradiance in cloud-resolving models, which needs large sampling budgets to converge.
- **Architecture:** Denoising autoencoder (convolutional) mapping noisy to well-converged irradiance fields.
- **Data:** Pairs of noisy and well-converged Monte Carlo ray-traced irradiance fields for an ensemble of simulated cumulus cloud fields and solar angles.
- **Main result:** Denoising diffuse irradiance from 1 sample per pixel is ten times faster and twice as accurate as 128 samples; adding liquid water path and solar angles halves errors.
- **Open work:** Improve generalization across resolutions and cloud types; couple online.
- **Issues:** Errors at cloud shadow edges for direct irradiance; trained on cumulus only.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Fourier Geometric Wind Power Forecasting with Numerical Weather Prediction](https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3818905)
Piao et al. (2026), *Proceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining V.2*. 0 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves short-term wind power forecasting by combining turbine SCADA data with gridded numerical weather prediction forecasts.
- **Architecture:** Multimodal network with scalar/vector feature decomposition, a geometric encoder giving rotation-invariant wind vector features, and a Fourier Neural Operator for global frequency-domain convolutions.
- **Data:** Historical SCADA data and gridded NWP forecasts for three real-world wind farms; NWP source and period not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on all three wind farms; code released.
- **Open work:** Extend to more farms, probabilistic forecasts and longer horizons.
- **Issues:** Only three farms; quantitative gains not stated in the abstract; dependence on NWP quality.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Global drought impacts on hydropower integrating physically-based and machine learning modelling](https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/ae7b62)
Shah et al. (2026), *Environmental Research Letters*. 0 citations.

- **Main goal:** Quantifies historical drought impacts on global hydropower generation at plant level.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid framework coupling physically based hydropower potential simulations with machine learning trained on observed generation, for run-of-river and storage plants; ML family not specified in the abstract.
- **Data:** Physically based hydropower potential simulations and observed plant-level generation, monthly, global, 1982–2022.
- **Main result:** Drought reduces global hydropower generation by about 11% relative to the long-term average, with larger declines in western and eastern North America, southeastern South America, the Mediterranean and East Asia.
- **Open work:** Develop monitoring tools for climate-extreme impacts on hydropower and support water–energy nexus policy.
- **Issues:** Described as an initial step; observed generation data are uneven across regions; reservoir operations are inferred rather than modeled explicitly.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Integrating Weather Foundation Model and Satellite to Enable Fine-Grained Solar Irradiance Forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3818436)
Ma et al. (2026), *Proceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining V.2*. 0 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides day-ahead, kilometer-scale solar irradiance forecasts for grid integration, which NWP lacks in resolution and satellite extrapolation in lead time.
- **Architecture:** Baguan-solar, a two-stage multimodal deep learning framework fusing forecasts from the Baguan weather foundation model (transformer) with geostationary satellite imagery; first forecasts cloud cover, then irradiance.
- **Data:** Baguan forecasts and high-resolution geostationary satellite imagery over East Asia; CLDAS used as ground truth.
- **Main result:** Reduces RMSE by 16.08% versus strong baselines including ECMWF IFS, vanilla Baguan and SolarSeer, better resolving cloud transients; operational in an eastern Chinese province since July 2025.
- **Open work:** Extend to other regions and probabilistic irradiance forecasts.
- **Issues:** Evaluated against CLDAS analysis rather than ground pyranometers; regional; deterministic only.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Advanced predictor selection for post-processing of global horizontal irradiance forecasts with stepwise machine learning regression](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.solener.2026.114521)
Markovics et al. (2026), *Solar Energy*. 0 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves post-processing of global horizontal irradiance forecasts by selecting the most informative predictors.
- **Architecture:** Stepwise machine learning regression for predictor selection in GHI forecast post-processing; specific models not available (abstract missing).
- **Data:** Not reported; likely NWP-based GHI forecasts with ground measurements, but details unknown.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the abstract (abstract unavailable).
- **Open work:** Not reported; testing predictor selection across sites and NWP models follows naturally.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable, so data, methods and results cannot be verified.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Characterization and forecasting of national-scale solar power ramp events](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26596)
Lanzilao et al. (2026), *arXiv*. 0 citations.

- **Main goal:** Characterizes national-scale solar power ramp events and evaluates how well forecasting models predict them.
- **Architecture:** Statistical ramp metrics plus evaluation of deep learning and physics-based nowcasts: SolarSTEPS, SHADECast (diffusion-based), IrradianceNet (ConvLSTM) and IFS-ENS.
- **Data:** Two years of 15-min PV production from 6434 stations at national scale; IFS-ENS forecasts as physics-based baseline; nowcast inputs not detailed in the abstract.
- **Main result:** SHADECast is most reliable, with CRPS 10.8% lower than SolarSTEPS at 2-h lead, but forecast RMSE rises by up to 50% during ramps.
- **Open work:** Develop improved high-resolution spatiotemporal models targeting ramp prediction.
- **Issues:** Two years only; single country; models struggle on ramp dynamics.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A Novel Wind Power Forecast Model: Statistical Hybrid Wind Power Forecast Technique (SHWIP)](https://doi.org/10.1109/tii.2015.2396011)
Özkan et al. (2015), *IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics*. 0 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves wind power forecasting with a hybrid statistical technique (SHWIP).
- **Architecture:** Statistical hybrid wind power forecast technique combining numerical weather prediction inputs with data-driven statistical modelling; component model types are not specified in the record.
- **Data:** Wind power production data from wind farms and NWP forecasts; details not reported.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the record.
- **Open work:** Test across more wind farms and add probabilistic outputs.
- **Issues:** Depends on NWP forecast quality; site-specific tuning. No abstract available; details of data, validation and skill cannot be confirmed from the record.
- *Basis: assessment*

<a id="agriculture"></a>
## Climate & water for agriculture

### [Crop yield prediction using machine learning: A systematic literature review](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compag.2020.105709)
Klompenburg et al. (2020), *Computers and Electronics in Agriculture*. 1,604 citations.

- **Main goal:** Systematically reviews which machine learning algorithms and input features are used for crop yield prediction.
- **Architecture:** Systematic literature review of machine learning and deep learning for crop yield prediction, covering artificial neural networks, CNN, LSTM, deep neural networks and others.
- **Data:** 567 studies retrieved from six databases, 50 ML studies selected, plus 30 deep learning studies from an additional search.
- **Main result:** Temperature, rainfall and soil type are the most used features; artificial neural networks are the most applied ML method, and CNN is the most used deep learning algorithm, followed by LSTM and DNN.
- **Open work:** Provides suggestions for further research on algorithms and features for crop yield prediction.
- **Issues:** Review based on a limited sample of studies; does not quantitatively compare model performance across studies.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Machine learning approaches for crop yield prediction and nitrogen status estimation in precision agriculture: A review](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compag.2018.05.012)
Chlingaryan et al. (2018), *Computers and Electronics in Agriculture*. 1,357 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews machine learning for crop yield prediction and nitrogen status estimation from remote sensing, to support precision agriculture decisions.
- **Architecture:** Review of machine learning techniques (neural networks, regression trees, support vector machines and others) applied to remotely sensed data over the last 15 years.
- **Data:** Literature covering remote sensing platforms (satellite, airborne, ground sensors) used for yield and nitrogen estimation; no new dataset.
- **Main result:** Concludes that advances in sensing and machine learning will provide cost-effective solutions for crop and environment state estimation and decision making.
- **Open work:** Targeted sensor use, fusion of sensor modalities with expert knowledge, and hybrid systems combining machine learning and signal processing.
- **Issues:** Qualitative review without a quantitative meta-analysis; predates deep learning adoption in agriculture.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Global predictions of primary soil salinization under changing climate in the 21st century](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-26907-3)
Hassani et al. (2021), *Nature Communications*. 890 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts how climate change will affect naturally occurring soil salinization in the world's drylands through 2100.
- **Architecture:** Data-driven machine learning models predicting soil salinity from climatic and environmental covariates; specific model type not specified in the abstract.
- **Data:** Global soil salinity measurements and climate projections to 2100; datasets not named in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Identifies salinization hotspots in South America, southern and western Australia, Mexico, the southwest US and South Africa, and decreases in the northwest US, Horn of Africa, Eastern Europe and Central Asia.
- **Open work:** Including secondary (human-induced) salinization and irrigation effects.
- **Issues:** Projections inherit climate model uncertainty and sparse soil sampling; extrapolation to future climates beyond training conditions.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Crop Yield Prediction Using Deep Neural Networks](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2019.00621)
Khaki et al. (2019), *Frontiers in Plant Science*. 836 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts maize hybrid yield from genotype and environment (weather and soil) data, as part of the 2018 Syngenta Crop Challenge.
- **Architecture:** Deep neural network (deep feedforward MLP with residual connections) for yield, with a separate model to predict weather, plus DNN-based feature selection.
- **Data:** Syngenta Crop Challenge 2018 data: genotypes and yields of 2,267 maize hybrids at 2,247 locations, 2008-2016, with weather and soil data; 2017 yields as target.
- **Main result:** RMSE is 12% of average yield using predicted weather and 11% with perfect weather, outperforming Lasso, shallow neural networks and regression trees; environment matters more than genotype.
- **Open work:** Improving weather prediction for the growing season and better interpretability of genotype-by-environment interactions.
- **Issues:** Single competition dataset; results depend on weather predictions; limited interpretability of the deep network.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Random Forests for Global and Regional Crop Yield Predictions](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0156571)
Jeong et al. (2016), *PLOS ONE*. 796 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates random forests for predicting crop yield responses to climate and biophysical variables at global and regional scales.
- **Architecture:** Random forest regression compared with multiple linear regression as a benchmark.
- **Data:** Gridded global wheat yield, US county maize grain yield over thirty years, and potato and maize silage yields from the US northeastern seaboard, with climate and biophysical predictors.
- **Main result:** Random forest RMSE ranges 6-14% of mean observed yield versus 14-49% for multiple linear regression, outperforming the benchmark in all statistics.
- **Open work:** Testing under climate conditions outside the training range and for climate change impact projection.
- **Issues:** Random forests lose accuracy at extreme ends and for responses beyond the training data range, limiting extrapolation under future climate.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [The effects of climate extremes on global agricultural yields](https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/ab154b)
Vogel et al. (2019), *Environmental Research Letters*. 747 citations.

- **Main goal:** Quantifies how climate extremes affect global yields of maize, soybeans, rice and spring wheat to improve agricultural prediction and adaptation.
- **Architecture:** Random forest machine learning model relating growing-season mean climate and extreme indices to yield anomalies.
- **Data:** Global sub-national crop yield data, growing-season climate and climate-extreme indices, and irrigation information.
- **Main result:** Growing-season climate explains 20–49% of yield anomaly variance, 18–43% of which is due to extremes; temperature extremes matter more than precipitation; irrigation partly offsets heat effects.
- **Open work:** Using these hotspots in agricultural forecasting and adaptation planning; adding management and socioeconomic drivers.
- **Issues:** Statistical associations, not causal; much variance unexplained; yield data quality varies across regions.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A CNN-RNN Framework for Crop Yield Prediction](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2019.01750)
Khaki et al. (2019), *Frontiers in Plant Science*. 664 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts corn and soybean yields across the US Corn Belt from environment and management data.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid convolutional neural network and recurrent neural network (CNN-RNN), compared with random forest, deep fully connected networks and LASSO.
- **Data:** Historical yield, weather, soil and management data for 13 Corn Belt states; tested on 2016–2018.
- **Main result:** RMSE is 9% and 8% of mean corn and soybean yields, outperforming the other methods and generalizing to untested environments.
- **Open work:** Including genotype data and improved weather predictions in the model.
- **Issues:** County-level yields; performance depends on accurate weather inputs; limited interpretability.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Deep Gaussian Process for Crop Yield Prediction Based on Remote Sensing Data](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v31i1.11172)
You et al. (2017), *AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence*. 641 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts crop yield before harvest from inexpensive public remote sensing data to support agricultural monitoring and food security.
- **Architecture:** Convolutional neural network or LSTM trained on histograms of pixel values (dimensionality reduction), combined with a Gaussian process layer modelling spatio-temporal structure (deep Gaussian process).
- **Data:** Publicly available remote sensing data (MODIS surface reflectance and land surface temperature) with US county-level soybean yields.
- **Main result:** Outperforms competing techniques for county-level US soybean yield prediction; the Gaussian process component further improves accuracy.
- **Open work:** Extending to other crops and to data-scarce developing countries, where the method is aimed.
- **Issues:** Histogram representation discards spatial location within counties; evaluation limited to US soybean.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A bitter cup: climate change profile of global production of Arabica and Robusta coffee](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-014-1306-x)
Bunn et al. (2015), *Climatic Change*. 576 citations.

- **Main goal:** Projects current and future global climatic suitability for Arabica and Robusta coffee to inform long-term adaptation of the coffee supply chain.
- **Architecture:** Species distribution modelling with machine learning algorithms fitted to occurrence data, combined over several parameter settings into a multi-model ensemble; specific algorithms are not named in the abstract.
- **Data:** Database of geo-referenced coffee production locations with current climate and future climate projections across emission scenarios.
- **Main result:** Global area suitable for coffee falls by about 50% across emission scenarios, with largest losses at low latitudes and altitudes, including Brazil and Vietnam; some East African and Asian areas gain.
- **Open work:** Assess adaptation options, shifting regions and links with forest conservation; refine with yield and management data.
- **Issues:** Suitability is not yield; correlative niche models ignore CO2 effects, adaptation and non-climatic constraints; projections inherit GCM uncertainty.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Integrating satellite and climate data to predict wheat yield in Australia using machine learning approaches](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agrformet.2019.03.010)
Cai et al. (2018), *Agricultural and Forest Meteorology*. 543 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts wheat yield across Australia and quantifies the relative contributions of climate and satellite data, comparing regression with machine learning.
- **Architecture:** LASSO regression benchmark compared with support vector machine, random forest and neural network (MLP) models.
- **Data:** Wheat yields at statistical division level, 2000-2014; climate data plus MODIS EVI and solar-induced fluorescence from GOME-2 and SCIAMACHY.
- **Main result:** Machine learning outperforms LASSO; combined climate and satellite data reach R2 ~0.75; EVI beats noisy SIF; optimal prediction about two months before maturity.
- **Open work:** Extension to other crops and regions and use of higher-resolution SIF products.
- **Issues:** Coarse spatial units and a short 15-year record; SIF input is noisy and coarse.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Machine learning methods for crop yield prediction and climate change impact assessment in agriculture](https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aae159)
Crane-Droesch (2018), *Environmental Research Letters*. 436 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models the weather-yield relationship for crops to project climate change impacts on agriculture more accurately than classical statistical methods.
- **Architecture:** Semiparametric deep neural network combining a nonparametric neural network (MLP) with parametric terms and fixed effects for cross-sectional heterogeneity.
- **Data:** US Midwest corn yield data with weather variables; climate change scenarios from a suite of climate models.
- **Main result:** Outperforms classical statistical methods and fully nonparametric neural networks on held-out years; projects large negative climate impacts on corn yield, but less severe than classical methods, especially in the warmest regions and scenarios.
- **Open work:** Applying to other crops and regions and incorporating adaptation.
- **Issues:** Projections extrapolate beyond observed climate; limited to US Midwest corn; does not account for future adaptation.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Coupling machine learning and crop modeling improves crop yield prediction in the US Corn Belt](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-80820-1)
Shahhosseini et al. (2020), *Scientific Reports*. 419 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether coupling a process-based crop model with machine learning improves corn yield predictions in the US Corn Belt.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid approach: APSIM crop model simulation outputs as input features to linear regression, LASSO, LightGBM, random forest and XGBoost, plus six ensemble models.
- **Data:** US Corn Belt county corn yields with weather and soil data, plus APSIM-simulated variables (e.g., drought stress, water table depth).
- **Main result:** Adding APSIM variables reduces RMSE by 7-20%; soil-moisture-related variables, average drought stress and water table depth are most influential.
- **Open work:** More hydrological inputs and further hybrid designs for operational yield forecasting.
- **Issues:** Requires running a calibrated crop model; confined to the US Corn Belt.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A Review of Precision Irrigation Water-Saving Technology under Changing Climate for Enhancing Water Use Efficiency, Crop Yield, and Environmental Footprints](https://doi.org/10.3390/agriculture14071141)
Lakhiar et al. (2024), *Agriculture*. 364 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews precision irrigation water-saving systems for improving water use efficiency and crop yield under climate change.
- **Architecture:** Review of precision irrigation systems covering monitoring and control, architecture, communication technologies and the role of artificial intelligence.
- **Data:** Previously published studies on precision irrigation; no new data.
- **Main result:** Concludes that precision irrigation systems will play a critical role in sustainable water management as scarcity intensifies.
- **Open work:** Wider adoption, lower-cost sensing and AI-driven irrigation control.
- **Issues:** Narrative review with brief literature search; AI coverage is one component rather than the focus.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Satellite-based soybean yield forecast: Integrating machine learning and weather data for improving crop yield prediction in southern Brazil](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agrformet.2019.107886)
Schwalbert et al. (2020), *Agricultural and Forest Meteorology*. 356 citations.

- **Main goal:** Produces in-season soybean yield forecasts in southern Brazil to support markets, policy and food security.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network compared with multivariate OLS linear regression and random forest.
- **Data:** Satellite NDVI, EVI and land surface temperature plus precipitation, masked with Rural Environment Registry field boundaries, and municipality yield data.
- **Main result:** Municipality-scale MAE of 0.24 Mg/ha at DOY 64; LSTM beats other methods except at DOY 16, where OLS is best; MAE grows to 0.42 Mg/ha for earlier forecasts.
- **Open work:** Earlier accurate forecasts and crop-specific masks.
- **Issues:** Non-crop-specific mask; accuracy degrades early in the season.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Crop Yield Prediction Using Deep Reinforcement Learning Model for Sustainable Agrarian Applications](https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2020.2992480)
Elavarasan et al. (2020), *IEEE Access*. 336 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts crop yield from environmental, soil, water and crop parameters with a framework that maps raw data directly to yield.
- **Architecture:** Deep reinforcement learning: a Deep Recurrent Q-Network combining a stacked recurrent neural network with Q-learning, with a linear layer mapping outputs to Q-values.
- **Data:** Environmental, soil, water and crop parameter data; specific dataset and region are not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Reported accuracy of 93.7%, outperforming existing models.
- **Open work:** Validating on independent regions and years and comparing with standard regression baselines.
- **Issues:** Unusual framing of regression as reinforcement learning, accuracy metric unclear for a continuous target, and data not described.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Integrating Multi-Source Data for Rice Yield Prediction across China using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Approaches](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agrformet.2020.108275)
Cao et al. (2021), *Agricultural and Forest Meteorology*. 331 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts county-level rice yield across China in a timely, scalable way to support food security under climate change.
- **Architecture:** LASSO regression, random forest and LSTM compared within Google Earth Engine.
- **Data:** Satellite vegetation indices (EVI) and solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF), meteorological indices and soil properties.
- **Main result:** LSTM R2 0.77–0.87 and random forest R2 0.76–0.82 beat LASSO (0.33–0.42); combining EVI and SIF helps slightly; optimal predictions come one to two months before maturity.
- **Open work:** Applying to other crops and data-sparse regions worldwide.
- **Issues:** County statistics as targets; modest gain from SIF; transferability outside China untested.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Machine learning for large-scale crop yield forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agsy.2020.103016)
Paudel et al. (2020), *Agricultural Systems*. 330 citations.

- **Main goal:** Builds a machine learning baseline for large-scale regional crop yield forecasting comparable to the operational MARS system.
- **Architecture:** Modular machine learning workflow with agronomically designed features from crop simulations, avoiding information leakage; specific algorithms compared are not named in the abstract.
- **Data:** MCYFS database: crop simulation outputs, weather, remote sensing and soil data for five crops in the Netherlands, Germany and France.
- **Main result:** Early-season NRMSE comparable to MCYFS in many cases (e.g., 7.87 vs 6.32 for Dutch soft wheat) but about twice as large for some crop-country pairs.
- **Open work:** Adding data sources, designing better features and testing more algorithms.
- **Issues:** Underperforms the operational system in several cases; regional yield statistics are short and noisy.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A Systematic Literature Review on Crop Yield Prediction with Deep Learning and Remote Sensing](https://doi.org/10.3390/rs14091990)
Muruganantham et al. (2022), *Remote Sensing*. 306 citations.

- **Main goal:** Identifies research gaps in deep learning and remote sensing for crop yield prediction and the role of vegetation indices and environmental factors.
- **Architecture:** Systematic literature review of deep learning approaches (LSTM, CNN and others) combined with remote sensing for crop yield prediction.
- **Data:** Studies published 2012–2022 from multiple databases; MODIS satellite data are the most common source.
- **Main result:** LSTM and CNN are the most used architectures, satellite remote sensing (especially MODIS) dominates, and vegetation indices are the most used features.
- **Open work:** Improving model accuracy, practical usefulness for farmers and policymakers, and interpretability of black-box models.
- **Issues:** Descriptive review without meta-analysis of reported accuracies; frequently used features do not work equally for all approaches.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Impact of extreme weather conditions on European crop production in 2018](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2019.0510)
Beillouin et al. (2020), *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences*. 290 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses how climate extremes affected the yields of nine crop species in Europe, focusing on the 2018 drought and heatwave.
- **Architecture:** Machine learning models relating regional yield anomalies to climate variables; specific model family not named in the abstract.
- **Data:** More than 82,000 regional yield records from 17 European countries since 1901, with climate data.
- **Main result:** Models explain up to 65% of historical yield anomalies; 2018 losses in Northern and Eastern Europe were tied to low rainfall plus heat, offset by high Southern European yields.
- **Open work:** Considering compound climate extremes more explicitly in yield-loss attribution.
- **Issues:** Statistical associations rather than process modelling; regional aggregation hides local management effects.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A Comprehensive Review of Crop Yield Prediction Using Machine Learning Approaches With Special Emphasis on Palm Oil Yield Prediction](https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2021.3075159)
Rashid et al. (2021), *IEEE Access*. 290 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews machine learning for crop yield prediction with emphasis on palm oil yield.
- **Architecture:** Review of machine learning crop yield prediction methods, features and palm oil applications, proposing a prospective ML architecture for palm oil yield prediction.
- **Data:** Published literature on crop yield prediction and palm oil; no new data.
- **Main result:** Summarizes widely used features and algorithms, advantages and challenges, and covers remote sensing, disease recognition, mapping and tree counting.
- **Open work:** Developing efficient palm oil yield models, optimal feature and algorithm selection, and wider use of remote sensing.
- **Issues:** Proposed architecture is conceptual and not tested; review methodology not quantified in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Crop yield prediction in agriculture: A comprehensive review of machine learning and deep learning approaches, with insights for future research and sustainability](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e40836)
Jabed et al. (2024), *Heliyon*. 276 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews ML and deep learning approaches for crop yield prediction to support food security and resource management.
- **Architecture:** Systematic literature review of machine learning (random forest, ANN, SVM) and deep learning (CNN, LSTM, DNN) for crop yield prediction.
- **Data:** Published studies; highlights inputs such as temperature, rainfall, soil type, humidity and vegetation indices (NDVI, EVI, LAI, NDWI).
- **Main result:** Random forest, ANN and SVM are most used in ML; CNN, LSTM and DNN emerge as promising deep learning candidates.
- **Open work:** Addressing geographical diversity, crop heterogeneity and changing environmental conditions.
- **Issues:** Qualitative synthesis; no quantitative comparison reported in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Forecasting Corn Yield With Machine Learning Ensembles](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2020.01120)
Shahhosseini et al. (2020), *Frontiers in Plant Science*. 274 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts county-level corn yields in the US Corn Belt early in the season with machine learning ensembles.
- **Architecture:** Machine learning ensembles (optimized weighted, average and stacked LASSO ensembles) of base learners, built with blocked sequential procedures.
- **Data:** County-level corn yields and weather, soil and management data for Illinois, Indiana and Iowa.
- **Main result:** Weighted and average ensembles reach RRMSE 9.5%; stacked LASSO has least bias (MBE 53 kg/ha); forecasts with RRMSE 9.2% are possible by June 1.
- **Open work:** Extending to other crops and regions and refining ensemble feature importance.
- **Issues:** Limited to three states; stacked ensembles underperform for time-series data.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Crop yield forecasting on the Canadian Prairies by remotely sensed vegetation indices and machine learning methods](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agrformet.2015.11.003)
Johnson et al. (2016), *Agricultural and Forest Meteorology*. 272 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts crop yields on the Canadian Prairies before harvest using satellite vegetation indices, to support agricultural planning.
- **Architecture:** Bayesian neural network and model-based recursive partitioning (tree-based), compared with multiple linear regression.
- **Data:** MODIS vegetation indices (NDVI, EVI) and other satellite-derived variables, with census-region yields of barley, canola and spring wheat across the Canadian Prairies.
- **Main result:** Nonlinear methods (Bayesian neural network and model-based recursive partitioning) outperform multiple linear regression; vegetation indices provide useful forecasts weeks to months before harvest.
- **Open work:** Adding weather inputs and testing other crops, regions and earlier forecast dates.
- **Issues:** No abstract available; regional yield statistics only, and numbers are not verified here.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Deep Transfer Learning for Crop Yield Prediction with Remote Sensing Data](https://doi.org/10.1145/3209811.3212707)
Wang et al. (2018), *The Compass*. 264 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts soybean yields in data-poor developing countries from satellite imagery, as a cheaper and more scalable alternative to ground surveys.
- **Architecture:** Deep learning models with transfer learning (pre-training on Argentina, fine-tuning on Brazil); the network family is not specified in the abstract.
- **Data:** Remotely sensed satellite imagery with soybean yield data for Argentina (training) and Brazil (transfer target with less data); exact products not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Deep learning gives promising soybean yield predictions in Argentina, and transfer learning achieves satisfactory results in Brazil with less training data.
- **Open work:** Applying the transfer approach to other crops and countries with scarce ground truth.
- **Issues:** Short student/workshop-style paper; quantitative results and baselines are not reported in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Estimating wheat yields in Australia using climate records, satellite image time series and machine learning methods](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isprsjprs.2019.11.008)
Kamir et al. (2020), *ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing*. 259 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates actual wheat yields across the Australian wheat belt to map yield-gap hotspots, where crop growth models are too data-hungry for large-scale actual-yield estimation.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of nine machine-learning regression base learners and two ensembles; support vector regression with an RBF kernel is the best single learner.
- **Data:** Climate records and satellite image time series (NDVI) over the Australian wheat belt, with yield statistics from statistical units for evaluation.
- **Main result:** SVR-RBF achieves RMSE 0.55 t/ha and R2 0.77 at pixel level and explains 73% of national yield variability, largely outperforming peak-NDVI and harvest-index benchmarks.
- **Open work:** Using the yield maps to quantify yield gaps against modelled potential yields and testing in-season forecasting.
- **Issues:** Statistical model without crop physiology; transferability to anomalous seasons or other regions untested; pixel-level reference yields have their own uncertainty.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Integrated phenology and climate in rice yields prediction using machine learning methods](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolind.2020.106935)
Guo et al. (2021), *Ecological Indicators*. 257 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts site-based rice yields in China and quantifies the contribution of phenology alongside climate and geography.
- **Architecture:** Multiple linear regression compared with backpropagation neural network (MLP), support vector machine and random forest over eleven predictor combinations.
- **Data:** Site-based rice phenology observations, growing-season climate variables and geographic information from Chinese agro-meteorological stations.
- **Main result:** ML outperforms MLR; combining phenology, climate and geography is best, with RMSE 800, 737 and 744 kg/ha (R2 0.24, 0.33, 0.31) for BP, SVM and RF; phenology is as important as climate.
- **Open work:** Better representing phenology and climate in crop models and integrating ML for yield prediction under climate change.
- **Issues:** Explained variance is low (R2 at most 0.33); site-level data only; no management or remote sensing inputs.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Dynamic wheat yield forecasts are improved by a hybrid approach using a biophysical model and machine learning technique](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agrformet.2020.107922)
Feng et al. (2020), *Agricultural and Forest Meteorology*. 240 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts wheat yield dynamically during the season, accounting for stage-specific climate extremes missed by crop or regression models alone.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid of the APSIM process-based crop model with random forest or multiple linear regression using growth stage-specific simulated biomass, climate extreme indices, NDVI and SPEI.
- **Data:** Plot-scale wheat yields 2008–2017 in the southeastern Australian wheat belt, with APSIM simulations, NDVI and SPEI.
- **Main result:** Random forest beats linear regression at every forecast date; one month before harvest r=0.85, MAPE 17.6%, RMSE 0.70 t/ha; two months before r=0.62.
- **Open work:** Extending the system to other cropping regions as farming data become available.
- **Issues:** Ten-year record; regional study; skill drops sharply at longer lead times.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Modeling reference evapotranspiration using extreme learning machine and generalized regression neural network only with temperature data](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compag.2017.01.027)
Feng et al. (2017), *Computers and Electronics in Agriculture*. 229 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates reference evapotranspiration when only temperature data are available, a common situation at weather stations in data-scarce regions.
- **Architecture:** Extreme learning machine (ELM, single-hidden-layer feedforward network) and generalized regression neural network (GRNN), compared with temperature-based empirical equations such as Hargreaves.
- **Data:** Not reported in the available metadata; likely daily temperature records from weather stations in China with FAO-56 Penman–Monteith ETo as target.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the available metadata; the title implies both ML models give acceptable ETo estimates from temperature alone, likely outperforming empirical formulas.
- **Open work:** Assess spatial transferability to stations not used in training and in other climates.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable, so data and numbers could not be verified; temperature-only inputs cannot capture radiation, humidity and wind effects, limiting accuracy in some climates.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [A deep learning approach to conflating heterogeneous geospatial data for corn yield estimation: A case study of the US Corn Belt at the county level](https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.14885)
Jiang et al. (2019), *Global Change Biology*. 226 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates county-level corn yield in the US Corn Belt by fusing heterogeneous phenology, meteorology and remote sensing data, including under extreme weather.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network, compared with LASSO regression and random forest.
- **Data:** County-level corn yields, crop phenology (growth phases), meteorological indices and satellite remote sensing indices over the US Corn Belt.
- **Main result:** LSTM explains 76% of yield variation versus 39% from meteorological indices alone; in the 2012 drought RMSE is 1.47 Mg/ha versus 1.93 (LASSO) and 2.43 (RF); silking to dough is the most critical period.
- **Open work:** Extending to in-season prediction, other crops and global regions.
- **Issues:** County-level aggregation; end-of-season estimation rather than early forecast; limited number of extreme years.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [China can be self-sufficient in maize production by 2030 with optimal crop management](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-38355-2)
Luo et al. (2023), *Nature Communications*. 223 citations.

- **Main goal:** China's future maize self-sufficiency under rising food and feed demand and climate change, and how much yield gain optimal crop management could deliver by the 2030s.
- **Architecture:** Data-driven yield projections combined with a machine learning model; the specific ML method family is not specified in the abstract.
- **Data:** Data from 402 stations and 87 field experiments across China, with future climate under the SSP585 scenario.
- **Main result:** Optimal planting density and management roughly double current yields; dense planting plus soil improvement give a 52% yield gain in the 2030s under SSP585, outweighing climate change effects.
- **Open work:** Extend the projections to other crops and scenarios, and test whether the management gains are achievable at farm scale across regions.
- **Issues:** Projections rely on a single high-end scenario and on extrapolating field experiments; the ML model, its uncertainty and its socioeconomic constraints are not detailed in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Incorporating machine learning with biophysical model can improve the evaluation of climate extremes impacts on wheat yield in south-eastern Australia](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agrformet.2019.05.018)
Feng et al. (2019), *Agricultural and Forest Meteorology*. 220 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves assessment of extreme climate event impacts (frost, drought, heat) on wheat yield, which process-based crop models represent poorly.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid model feeding APSIM crop model outputs and growth-stage-specific extreme-event indicators into a random forest; multiple linear regression hybrid used as benchmark.
- **Data:** Observed wheat yields and climate records in the New South Wales wheat belt, south-eastern Australia, plus APSIM simulations; future climate projections for impact assessment.
- **Main result:** APSIM+RF explains 81% of observed yield variation, 33% better than APSIM alone and 19% better than APSIM+MLR; APSIM alone may overestimate future yields by 1–10%.
- **Open work:** Apply the hybrid approach to other regions and crops and to further extreme-event types.
- **Issues:** Regional statistical correction may not transfer outside training conditions; future projections rely on extrapolating learned extreme-event effects.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Remote-Sensing Data and Deep-Learning Techniques in Crop Mapping and Yield Prediction: A Systematic Review](https://doi.org/10.3390/rs15082014)
Joshi et al. (2023), *Remote Sensing*. 220 citations.

- **Main goal:** Systematically review deep learning with remote sensing data for crop mapping and crop yield prediction.
- **Architecture:** Systematic review of 90 papers covering platforms, sensors, input features, deep learning architectures (CNN, LSTM and others), frameworks, training data and performance.
- **Data:** 90 peer-reviewed studies using satellite and other remote sensing data for crop mapping and yield estimation.
- **Main result:** Multiple deep learning solutions with different remote sensing inputs give reliable crop mapping and yield prediction.
- **Open work:** Address scarce training data, build efficient and generalisable models and improve prediction transparency for large-scale use.
- **Issues:** Review restricted to the selected databases and period; performance comparisons across heterogeneous studies are not directly comparable.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Crop Yield Prediction Using Machine Learning Models: Case of Irish Potato and Maize](https://doi.org/10.3390/agriculture13010225)
Kuradusenge et al. (2023), *Agriculture*. 219 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predict Irish potato and maize yields from weather to give early information for food security planning in Rwanda.
- **Architecture:** Random forest, polynomial regression and support vector regression with rainfall and temperature as predictors.
- **Data:** Historical weather and crop yield data for Musanze district, Rwanda, gathered from various sources.
- **Main result:** Random forest is best, with RMSE 510.8 and 129.9 and R2 0.875 and 0.817 for potato and maize; optimal weather conditions are identified.
- **Open work:** Add soil, management and remote sensing predictors and test in other districts.
- **Issues:** Single district with small datasets; only rainfall and temperature as inputs; risk of overfitting.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Machine learning-based integration of remotely-sensed drought factors can improve the estimation of agricultural drought in South-Eastern Australia](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agsy.2019.03.015)
Feng et al. (2019), *Agricultural Systems*. 217 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimate agricultural drought by fusing remotely sensed drought factors to reproduce a ground-based drought index.
- **Architecture:** Bias-corrected random forest, support vector machine and multi-layer perceptron neural network regression.
- **Data:** Thirty drought factors from TRMM and MODIS to reproduce SPEI, 2001–2017, New South Wales wheat belt; station climate data and observed wheat yields for evaluation.
- **Main result:** Bias-corrected random forest gives the lowest RMSE and highest R2 for SPEI prediction.
- **Open work:** Extend to other regions and crops and to drought forecasting.
- **Issues:** Abstract truncated; target is a derived index; TRMM is discontinued; regional study only.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Predictive ability of machine learning methods for massive crop yield prediction](https://doi.org/10.5424/sjar/2014122-4439)
González-Sánchez et al. (2014), *Spanish Journal of Agricultural Research*. 216 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compare machine learning methods for massive crop yield prediction across many crops for agricultural planning.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of multiple linear regression, M5-Prime regression trees, MLP neural networks, support vector regression and k-nearest neighbor.
- **Data:** Ten crop datasets from an irrigation zone in Mexico; tested on two consecutive years.
- **Main result:** M5-Prime and KNN have lowest errors (RMSE 5.14 and 4.91, RRSE about 79%) and highest correlations (0.41 and 0.42); M5-Prime is best overall.
- **Open work:** Add more predictors and test other regions.
- **Issues:** Low correlations overall (about 0.4); short test period; single irrigation zone.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Dynamic Neural Network Modelling of Soil Moisture Content for Predictive Irrigation Scheduling](https://doi.org/10.3390/s18103408)
Adeyemi et al. (2018), *Sensors*. 204 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models soil moisture dynamics to enable predictive, closed-loop irrigation scheduling that saves water.
- **Architecture:** Dynamic neural network (recurrent, NARX-type) predicting one-day-ahead volumetric soil moisture from past soil moisture, precipitation and climate measurements.
- **Data:** Field soil moisture and climate measurements from three sites; AquaCrop simulations of a potato growing season for irrigation evaluation.
- **Main result:** R2 above 0.94 at all sites, with robust predictions at independent sites; predictive scheduling saves 20 to 46% water with similar yield and water use efficiency as rule-based irrigation.
- **Open work:** Field deployment of the closed-loop system and testing for other crops and soils.
- **Issues:** Irrigation benefits are shown in AquaCrop simulations, not field trials; three sites only.
- *Basis: abstract*

### BMC Bioinformatics BioMed Central Methodology article Machine learning techniques in disease forecasting: a case study on rice blast prediction
 (2006), *Venue not recorded*. 201 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts rice blast disease from weather variables to support timely fungicide decisions, comparing machine learning approaches.
- **Architecture:** Support vector machine regression compared with multiple regression, backpropagation neural network and generalized regression neural network; implemented as the RB-Pred web server.
- **Data:** Leaf blast severity records and weather variables (temperature, relative humidity, rainfall, rainy days) from rice-growing locations in India.
- **Main result:** The support vector machine model gives the highest correlation and lowest error for blast severity prediction, outperforming regression and neural networks.
- **Open work:** Extend to other crops and diseases and to more locations and years.
- **Issues:** Limited number of seasons and sites; location-specific relations may not transfer.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Crop yield prediction integrating genotype and weather variables using deep learning](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0252402)
Shook et al. (2020), *PLOS ONE*. 200 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts soybean yield across multiple environments by combining genotype information and weather, to support breeding under diverse climatic conditions.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network with a temporal attention mechanism for interpretability, using pedigree relatedness measures plus weekly weather.
- **Data:** Uniform Soybean Tests (UST) performance records in North America with weekly weather parameters over the growing season.
- **Main result:** Outperforms SVR with RBF kernel, LASSO regression and the data-driven USDA yield model; attention identifies important time windows in the season.
- **Open work:** Incorporate genomic markers and soil/management data, and extend to other crops and breeding programs.
- **Issues:** Pedigree-based relatedness is a coarse genotype representation; weekly weather aggregation may miss extremes; results tied to trial-plot conditions.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Comparative assessment of environmental variables and machine learning algorithms for maize yield prediction in the US Midwest](https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/ab7df9)
Kang et al. (2020), *Environmental Research Letters*. 196 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses which environmental variables, observation frequencies and algorithms best predict county-level maize yield in the US Midwest.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of Lasso, support vector regression, random forest, XGBoost (gradient boosting), LSTM and convolutional neural network (CNN).
- **Data:** County-level maize yields with features from satellite observations, weather data, land surface model outputs, soil maps and crop progress reports (hundreds of features).
- **Main result:** XGBoost is most accurate and stable while LSTM and CNN are not advantageous; best setup improves accuracy by 5% over a Lasso baseline; reasonable forecasts from early June and better than USDA WASDE early in the season.
- **Open work:** Extend to other crops and regions and to in-season operational forecasting.
- **Issues:** County-level aggregation; results specific to the US Midwest; deep models may be data-limited; feature importance is correlational.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Applying machine learning on sensor data for irrigation recommendations: revealing the agronomist’s tacit knowledge](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11119-017-9527-4)
Goldstein et al. (2017), *Precision Agriculture*. 195 citations.

- **Main goal:** Uses sensor data and machine learning to reproduce agronomists' irrigation recommendations, capturing their tacit knowledge.
- **Architecture:** Machine learning regression and classification models; the specific algorithms are not specified here.
- **Data:** Field sensor data paired with agronomist irrigation recommendations; details are not reported here.
- **Main result:** The title indicates ML can reveal and reproduce expert irrigation decisions; quantitative results are not available here.
- **Open work:** Generalization to other crops and farms and integration into decision support systems.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; models learn expert behavior rather than agronomic optimum, inheriting expert biases.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [The use of high‐resolution image time series for crop classification and evapotranspiration estimate over an irrigated area in central Morocco](https://doi.org/10.1080/01431160701250390)
Simonneaux et al. (2008), *International Journal of Remote Sensing*. 193 citations.

- **Main goal:** Classifies crops and estimates evapotranspiration over an irrigated area in central Morocco from high-resolution image time series.
- **Architecture:** Decision tree classifier applied to per-pixel NDVI profiles, followed by the FAO crop coefficient evapotranspiration model with NDVI-derived Kc.
- **Data:** Eight Landsat TM images over one crop season, radiometrically corrected; ALADIN model outputs for reference evapotranspiration (ET0) maps.
- **Main result:** NDVI profiles identify four main land cover types (bare soil, annual crops, trees on bare soil, trees on annual understory), enabling spatial ET estimation over the whole area.
- **Open work:** Validate ET estimates with field measurements and extend to multiple seasons.
- **Issues:** Single season; classification accuracy and ET validation statistics are not reported in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [An LSTM neural network for improving wheat yield estimates by integrating remote sensing data and meteorological data in the Guanzhong Plain, PR China](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agrformet.2021.108629)
Tian et al. (2021), *Agricultural and Forest Meteorology*. 192 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves regional wheat yield estimation for food security by integrating remote sensing and meteorological data across growth stages.
- **Architecture:** LSTM neural network with different time steps, compared with backpropagation neural network and support vector machine.
- **Data:** Meteorological data plus remotely sensed VTCI and LAI at main growth stages for the Guanzhong Plain, China, with yields at irrigated and rain-fed sites 2008–2016.
- **Main result:** Best LSTM (two time steps, all inputs) reaches RMSE 357.77 kg/ha and R2 0.83, far better than BPNN (R2 0.42) and SVM (R2 0.41).
- **Open work:** Application to other crops and regions and in-season forecasting.
- **Issues:** Limited sample of sites and years; single region.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Neural network models in greenhouse air temperature prediction](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0925-2312(01)00620-8)
Ferreira et al. (2002), *Neurocomputing*. 191 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts greenhouse air temperature for climate control.
- **Architecture:** Radial basis function neural networks trained with different off-line and on-line methods.
- **Data:** Measured inside and outside climate variables (e.g. temperature, solar radiation, humidity) from a greenhouse in Portugal.
- **Main result:** RBF networks predict greenhouse air temperature accurately, with training method affecting performance.
- **Open work:** Integrate into model predictive control of greenhouse climate.
- **Issues:** Single greenhouse; limited period; adaptation to seasonal change needs on-line training.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Machine learning approach for forecasting crop yield based on climatic parameters](https://doi.org/10.1109/iccci.2014.6921718)
Veenadhari et al. (2014), *International Conference on Computational Collective Intelligence*. 188 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts crop yield from climatic parameters to support farmers' decisions in India.
- **Architecture:** Decision tree classifier (C4.5-type) relating climatic variables to yield classes, delivered as a decision-support tool.
- **Data:** Historical climate and crop yield records for districts of Madhya Pradesh, India; exact period not confirmed here (abstract missing).
- **Main result:** The decision tree yields interpretable rules and reasonable accuracy in predicting yield categories; specific scores are not available here.
- **Open work:** Adding soil and management inputs and more crops or regions would follow naturally.
- **Issues:** Coarse yield classes; small district-level dataset; climate-only predictors ignore management and soil.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Hybrid Deep Learning-based Models for Crop Yield Prediction](https://doi.org/10.1080/08839514.2022.2031823)
Oikonomidis et al. (2022), *Applied Artificial Intelligence*. 188 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts crop yield, which depends on many weather and soil factors, by evaluating hybrid deep learning models.
- **Architecture:** Compares XGBoost with hybrid CNN-DNN (convolutional neural network with MLP), CNN-XGBoost, CNN-RNN and CNN-LSTM models.
- **Data:** Public soybean dataset with 395 weather and soil features and 25,345 samples.
- **Main result:** CNN-DNN is best (RMSE 0.266, MAE 0.199, R2 0.87); XGBoost is second and much faster.
- **Open work:** Testing on other crops and regions would follow naturally.
- **Issues:** Single dataset; spatial and temporal split strategy not described in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Crops Yield Prediction Based on Machine Learning Models: Case of West African Countries](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4003105)
Saadio et al. (2022), *Social Science Research Network*. 185 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts crop yields in West African countries to support food security planning.
- **Architecture:** Machine learning regression models; the specific method type is not specified here (abstract missing).
- **Data:** Country-level crop yield records with climatic and possibly agricultural inputs for West African countries; details are not available here.
- **Main result:** Relative model performance is compared; specific scores are not available here.
- **Open work:** Finer spatial resolution and inclusion of soil and management data would follow naturally.
- **Issues:** Coarse aggregated data; limited sample size; generalization uncertain.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Rice crop yield prediction in India using support vector machines](https://doi.org/10.1109/jcsse.2016.7748856)
Gandhi et al. (2016), *International Joint Conference on Computer Science and Software Engineering*. 182 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts rice crop yield in India from climate and crop data to support agricultural planning.
- **Architecture:** Support vector machine (SVM) model, implemented as sequential minimal optimization in WEKA.
- **Data:** District-level rice and climate records (precipitation, temperatures, area, production) for Maharashtra, India.
- **Main result:** SVM is reported to give usable yield predictions with accuracy metrics compared against other classifiers; exact values not reproduced here.
- **Open work:** Using more years, remote sensing inputs and other algorithms could improve accuracy.
- **Issues:** Small dataset and short record; yield discretized into classes; limited validation.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Estimation of soil temperature from meteorological data using different machine learning models](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geoderma.2018.11.044)
Feng et al. (2019), *Geoderma*. 175 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates half-hourly soil temperature at several depths from meteorological data on the Loess Plateau, China.
- **Architecture:** Compares extreme learning machine (ELM), generalized regression neural network (GRNN), backpropagation neural network (BPNN) and random forests (RF).
- **Data:** Field experiment on the Loess Plateau: half-hourly soil temperature at 2, 5, 10 and 20 cm with air temperature, wind speed, humidity, solar radiation and vapor pressure deficit as inputs.
- **Main result:** All models perform well: RMSE about 2.3-3.1 °C, NSE 0.84-0.93; ELM is slightly best.
- **Open work:** Testing at other sites and deeper layers would assess transferability.
- **Issues:** Single site; differences between models are small; no soil moisture or prior-time inputs mentioned.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Estimating and understanding crop yields with explainable deep learning in the Indian Wheat Belt](https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/ab68ac)
Wolanin et al. (2020), *Environmental Research Letters*. 174 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates wheat yield while explaining the drivers of yield variability, combining predictive deep learning with interpretability.
- **Architecture:** Deep neural network (1D convolutional neural network) on multivariate time series, interpreted with regression activation maps; compared with ridge regression and random forest.
- **Data:** Vegetation (satellite, e.g., MODIS-derived) and meteorological time series with district-level wheat yields in the Indian Wheat Belt.
- **Main result:** The DL model beats ridge regression and random forest; learned features relate to growing-season length and temperature and light conditions (e.g., high 2012 yields linked to cool, sunny conditions).
- **Open work:** Apply the approach to other crops and regions.
- **Issues:** Limited years of yield data; interpretation via activation maps is qualitative; regional scope.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [New approach to estimate daily reference evapotranspiration based on hourly temperature and relative humidity using machine learning and deep learning](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agwat.2020.106113)
Ferreira et al. (2020), *Agricultural Water Management*. 172 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates daily reference evapotranspiration from limited hourly sensor data (temperature and humidity, or temperature only).
- **Architecture:** Random forest, XGBoost, artificial neural network (MLP) and convolutional neural network (CNN), with different daily vs hourly input strategies.
- **Data:** 53 weather stations in Minas Gerais, Brazil; targets from daily and summed-hourly ASCE Penman–Monteith ETo; regional and local scenarios.
- **Main result:** Using 24 h hourly data directly is best; CNN with hourly data plus hourly Ra is best overall, reducing RMSE by up to 28.2% (0.71 to 0.51) regionally and 22.4% locally.
- **Open work:** Test in other climates and with low-cost sensor networks.
- **Issues:** Single Brazilian state; targets are computed ETo rather than measured; temperature-only inputs limit accuracy.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Climate change impacts on crop yields: A review of empirical findings, statistical crop models, and machine learning methods](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envsoft.2024.106119)
Hu et al. (2024), *Environmental Modelling & Software*. 172 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews how climate change affects crop yields and how statistical crop models and machine learning estimate these impacts, for food security.
- **Architecture:** Review of about 230 statistical crop modelling studies, covering empirical findings, statistical crop models and machine learning methods.
- **Data:** Published studies for major crops (maize, wheat, soybean and others).
- **Main result:** Warming reduces yields: 1 °C warming decreases yields by 7.5 ± 5.3% for maize, 6.0 ± 3.3% for wheat and 6.8 ± 5.9% for soybean.
- **Open work:** Better integration of ML with process understanding, adaptation effects and extreme events; specifics not in the truncated abstract.
- **Issues:** Abstract is truncated; conclusions on ML methods are not visible in the provided text.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Artificial neural networks for rice yield prediction in mountainous regions](https://doi.org/10.1017/s0021859606006691)
Ji et al. (2007), *The Journal of Agricultural Science*. 171 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts rice yield in mountainous regions where conventional models perform poorly.
- **Architecture:** Neural network (MLP) compared with multiple linear regression.
- **Data:** Field and climatic data for rice in mountainous areas of Fujian, China.
- **Main result:** Neural network models predict rice yield more accurately than linear regression.
- **Open work:** Adding more sites and seasons and testing input sensitivity.
- **Issues:** Small dataset; region specific.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Predicting spatial and temporal variability in crop yields: an inter-comparison of machine learning, regression and process-based models](https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/ab7b24)
Leng et al. (2020), *Environmental Research Letters*. 169 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares how well process-based crop models, regression and machine learning reproduce the mean, variability and extremes of US maize yield, and uses the best method to project climate impacts.
- **Architecture:** Inter-comparison of process-based crop models, a traditional regression model and a machine-learning algorithm; the specific ML algorithm family is not specified in the abstract.
- **Data:** Observed US county-level maize yields and climate predictors; harmonized process-based crop model simulations; climate projections for 1.5 °C and 2 °C global warming scenarios.
- **Main result:** Machine learning explains 93% of national yield variability versus 51% for regression and 42% for process-based models, and projects a 13.5% maize yield loss under 2 °C warming.
- **Open work:** Extending the probabilistic risk analysis to more crops, regions and scenarios, and adding adaptation and management effects.
- **Issues:** Statistical models extrapolate to warmer climates outside the training range and lack CO2 fertilization and adaptation processes; ML method details are not given in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Machine learning approaches for spatial modeling of agricultural droughts in the south-east region of Queensland Australia.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2019.134230)
Rahmati et al. (2020), *Science of The Total Environment*. 169 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps agricultural drought hazard in south-east Queensland by identifying the hydro-environmental drivers of drought occurrence, to support drought management and adaptation planning.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of classification and regression trees, boosted regression trees, random forest, multivariate adaptive regression splines, flexible discriminant analysis and support vector machines.
- **Data:** Relative departure of soil moisture for eight severe droughts in south-east Queensland, 1994–2013, as the drought inventory, with eight hydro-environmental predictors such as soil water capacity, rainfall and clay content.
- **Main result:** Random forest performs best (AUC-ROC 97.7%, TSS 0.873) and FDA worst (AUC-ROC 73.9%); about 21.2% of the area falls in high or very high drought hazard classes.
- **Open work:** Applying the mapping to other drought-prone regions and incorporating dynamic climate predictors for time-varying hazard assessment.
- **Issues:** Static hazard map rather than a forecast; few drought events; spatially autocorrelated samples may inflate validation scores.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Development of a neural network model to predict daily solar radiation](https://doi.org/10.1016/0168-1923(94)90103-1)
Elizondo et al. (1994), *Agricultural and Forest Meteorology*. 167 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts daily solar radiation, an input often missing for crop simulation models, from routinely observed weather variables.

- **Main result:** The neural network estimates daily solar radiation with reasonable accuracy from commonly available variables; specific error statistics not reported here.
- **Open work:** Testing at more locations and climates and comparing with empirical radiation models.
- **Issues:** Few training sites; transferability to other climates and cloudy-day accuracy are uncertain.

### [DeepYield: A combined convolutional neural network with long short-term memory for crop yield forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eswa.2021.115511)
Gavahi et al. (2021), *Expert Systems with Applications*. 164 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts crop yield at county scale from satellite imagery before harvest to support food security and agricultural planning.

- **Data:** MODIS satellite products (such as surface reflectance and land surface temperature) and county-level soybean yields in the United States; periods not reported here.
- **Main result:** DeepYield is reported to outperform the compared deep learning models in yield forecasting; exact scores are not reported here.

### [Using machine learning for crop yield prediction in the past or the future](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2023.1128388)
Morales et al. (2023), *Frontiers in Plant Science*. 160 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses how algorithm choice, data volume and partitioning affect ML crop yield forecasting.

- **Data:** Synthetic sunflower and wheat yields simulated with DSSAT (OilcropSun, Ceres-Wheat), 2001–2020, five areas of Spain.
- **Main result:** Random forest performs best (RMSE 35–38%) but is only modestly better than a farm-average baseline (42%).

### [Deep learning for crop yield prediction: a systematic literature review](https://doi.org/10.1080/01140671.2022.2032213)
Oikonomidis et al. (2022), *New Zealand Journal of Crop and Horticultural Science*. 158 citations.

- **Main goal:** Systematically reviews deep learning for crop yield prediction to identify motivations, methods, features, data sources and gaps.
- **Architecture:** Systematic literature review of deep learning methods (CNN, LSTM and others) for crop yield prediction.
- **Data:** 456 retrieved studies, 44 selected primary studies analyzed for crops, algorithms, features and data sources.
- **Main result:** CNN is the most common algorithm and performs best in RMSE; lack of large training datasets and overfitting risk are key challenges.
- **Open work:** Larger datasets and work on under-studied topics identified in the review are needed.
- **Issues:** Review limited to 44 studies; heterogeneous metrics hinder quantitative comparison.

- **Issues:** Methods and metrics are not described in the abstract; aggregated statistics limit field-level use.

### [Comax: An Expert System for Cotton Crop Management](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.233.4759.29)
Lemmon (1986), *Science*. 156 citations.

- **Main goal:** Supports cotton crop management decisions on irrigation, fertilization and harvest timing by coupling expert knowledge with crop simulation.

### [An interaction regression model for crop yield prediction](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-97221-7)
Ansarifar et al. (2021), *Scientific Reports*. 150 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts corn and soybean yield accurately while providing interpretable environment-by-management interactions.

- **Main result:** Relative RMSE of 8% or less for both crops, outperforming ML benchmarks; identifies about a dozen environment-by-management interactions and decomposes yield contributions.

### [A GNN-RNN Approach for Harnessing Geospatial and Temporal Information: Application to Crop Yield Prediction](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v36i11.21444)
Fan et al. (2021), *AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence*. 147 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts county-level crop yields across the US by exploiting both geospatial and temporal information, as climate change raises food-security concerns.

- **Data:** Over 2,000 counties in 41 US states, 1981–2019, with weather, land surface and soil features.
- **Main result:** The GNN-RNN consistently outperforms linear, tree-based and deep learning baselines on multiple metrics, presented as the first nationwide county-level ML yield model embedding geographical knowledge.

### [Exploring uncertainties in global crop yield projections in a large ensemble of crop models and CMIP5 and CMIP6 climate scenarios](https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/abd8fc)
Müller et al. (2021), *Environmental Research Letters*. 143 citations.

- **Main goal:** Quantifies uncertainty in projected global crop yields from both climate models and crop models under climate change.
- **Architecture:** Statistical crop model emulators of nine process-based global gridded crop models (GGCMI), used to run a large ensemble; not a deep learning method.
- **Data:** Up to 45 CMIP5 and 34 CMIP6 climate projections under three forcing scenarios, for maize, spring and winter wheat, rice and soybean.
- **Main result:** Climate and crop models contribute roughly equally to uncertainty; median caloric production impact is more negative under CMIP6 (+1% to -19%) than CMIP5 (+5% to -13%); wheat and maize are dominated by crop-model spread, soybean and rice by climate.
- **Open work:** Developing consistent, process-level crop model testing and weighting ensembles by plausibility.
- **Issues:** Unbalanced crop model ensemble with an equal-plausibility assumption; emulators simplify process-model behaviour.
